Read this:

Playgroup note, Thursday, from Uma. Nikita (2 years) rubbed her eyes twice during story time and slumped against my knee. When I asked, "Sleepy?" she nodded and pointed to the nap mats. Before lunch she patted her tummy and said, "Hungry, khana." After lunch she tugged at her shorts and did a little dance; we reached the potty just in time. 👍 I'll tell her father she's starting to put words to what her body feels.

Where did Nikita point when asked if she was sleepy?
To the nap mats.
What does Nikita patting her tummy and saying "khana" show she understood?
It shows she noticed the hungry feeling inside her and wanted food.
What could Nikita's father do at home to build on this?
He could name her body feelings in simple words, like sleepy or hungry, and respond when she signals them.
How might Uma's day change as Nikita names her needs?
Uma can meet Nikita's needs sooner, with fewer meltdowns and fewer accidents. 🙂

Read this:

On the local bus home from the weekly haat, Aparna, two, stops chattering. She pulls at her sandal strap and whimpers, then pushes her face into Bidisha's sari. Her mother loosens the strap; a red line shows on the small foot. Aparna sighs, then yawns wide and curls up in Bidisha's lap. By the next stop she is asleep, one fist still holding a paper packet of roasted chana.

What mark did Bidisha find on Aparna's foot?
A red line from the sandal strap.
Why did Aparna whimper and pull at her sandal?
The strap was hurting and she was tired, and she wanted the discomfort to stop.
What could Bidisha try after this trip?
She could check how the sandals fit and plan a rest before long outings, while watching for these signals.
What would change if Bidisha had scolded Aparna for fussing?
The signal about the strap might have been missed, and Aparna could have stayed sore and cried harder.

Read this:

At the playground in Leeds, Tariq, nearly three, stops halfway up the climbing frame and grabs the front of his trousers. "Wee-wee," he says, climbing down fast. Fatima, his mother, takes his hand and they hurry to the cafe toilet. Back outside, he shivers and holds out his arms. "Cold." She zips up his coat. He nods, pats the zip, and runs back to the frame.

Which word did Tariq use when he felt cold?
He said "Cold."
Why did Tariq climb down so fast?
He felt he needed to wee and wanted to reach the toilet in time.
What went right, and how could Fatima keep it going?
Tariq named his need early; she can keep responding quickly and noticing when he tells her.
What is it like for Fatima when Tariq can say what his body needs?
Outings feel easier and calmer because she doesn't have to guess.

Read this:

I'm Neelam, Seema's grandmother. At two, Seema has started telling us about her body. This morning she stopped playing, tugged at her nappy and said, "Wet." At lunch she pushed her plate away and rubbed her eyes. "Sleepy," she whispered, and crawled onto my lap. Later she held her tummy and made a face. I checked; she needed the toilet. She is learning what her body is saying.

What did Seema say when she tugged at her nappy?
She said, "Wet."
What did Seema's rubbing her eyes and whispering "Sleepy" suggest?
It suggests she felt tired and knew she needed rest.
How can Neelam support Seema in noticing her body signals?
By naming the feelings back to her and responding quickly, like helping her rest or go to the toilet.
How does Neelam see Seema's new words?
Neelam sees them as Seema learning to understand what her body is telling her. 😊

Read this:

Tuesday: Abhinav, twenty months, whines and throws his toy car. His father Chinmay tries to play, but Abhinav cries louder.

Thursday: Abhinav whines again at the same time. Chinmay asks, "Hungry?" Abhinav points to the kitchen.

The next Monday: Before lunch, Abhinav walks to the kitchen, pats his tummy and says, "Eat!" Chinmay smiles and hands him a banana.

What did Abhinav say on Monday before lunch?
He said, "Eat!"
What was Abhinav likely feeling when he whined and threw his car on Tuesday?
He was likely hungry and upset but didn't know how to show it yet.
What helped Abhinav connect his feeling to food?
His father asking "Hungry?" helped him link the uncomfortable feeling to eating.
How might Chinmay feel on Monday when Abhinav says "Eat!"?
He probably feels relieved and happy that Abhinav can now tell him what he needs.

Read this:

Keerthana stopped in the middle of the building's play area, crossed her legs and went very still. Her uncle Saurabh, visiting from Pune, didn't notice at first. "Susu," she said, tugging his kurta. "Susu now!" He grabbed her hand and ran for the lift. They made it, just. Back downstairs, she yawned, rubbed her eyes with both fists and climbed into his lap, the swing forgotten.

What did Keerthana say while tugging Saurabh's kurta?
She said, "Susu now!"
What does Keerthana rubbing her eyes and climbing into Saurabh's lap suggest?
She was tired and wanted comfort; her body's signals mattered more to her than the swing.
What could Saurabh watch for next time he looks after Keerthana?
Early signs like crossing her legs or going still, so he can take her to the toilet before it becomes urgent.
How might Saurabh feel after the rush to the lift?
Relieved they made it in time, and maybe surprised at how clearly she told him what she needed.

Read this:

"Tummy," Vikas said, pressing his hand flat on his shirt.
"Your tummy hurts?" Vandana asked, putting down her laptop.
"No. Tummy empty."
She laughed. "Empty! You mean hungry?"
"Hungry. Banana."
"You had lunch an hour ago."
"Banana, Mummy." He leaned on her knee, eyes half shut.
"Hungry and sleepy, both?" she said. "Half a banana, then nap."
He ate it in four bites and was asleep on the mat before she had dropped the peel in the bin.

What did Vikas ask for?
A banana.
How can you tell that Vikas felt tired as well as hungry?
He leaned on her knee with his eyes half shut and fell asleep right after eating, so he was sleepy and worn out.
What did Vandana do well when Vikas said "tummy"?
She stopped to ask what he meant instead of guessing, which helped him find the right word, hungry.
What would change if Vandana had refused the banana because lunch was recent?
Vikas might have got upset and cranky, and he would learn that telling her his body's signals doesn't help.

Read this:

Creche note from Payal, a hot afternoon in May
Mehak came in from the shaded yard with red cheeks and went straight to the water jug, patting it and saying "paani, paani." She drank a full cup. After lunch she pulled at her dress and said "hot." I changed her into a cotton frock and put her mat under the fan. She was asleep in minutes. I've told her mother she is naming more of what her body feels now 😊

What did Mehak say while patting the water jug?
She said "paani, paani."
What was Mehak feeling when she pulled at her dress and said "hot"?
She felt uncomfortable and too warm, and she wanted Payal to fix it.
How could Payal keep supporting Mehak's naming of body signals?
Keep answering quickly when Mehak names a need, and give her words for new signals like "thirsty" or "sleepy".
How might Mehak's mother feel reading the note?
Glad and reassured that Mehak is learning to tell carers what her body needs.

Read this:

Winter in their village near Mandi meant layers: woollen pyjamas, socks, a thick sweater. Sumit, two, was playing with pine cones on the sunny steps when he suddenly stopped, tugged at the waist of his pyjamas, and wriggled. "Su-su!" he shouted. His mother, Vidya, dropped the washing and ran him to the bathroom. They made it, just. "You told me! Well done." Sumit looked very serious, then went back to his pine cones.

What was Sumit playing with?
Pine cones on the sunny steps.
What does Sumit's serious look afterwards suggest?
Sumit seemed proud and a little surprised that telling his mother worked.
How could Vidya help Sumit keep noticing this signal in winter?
She could dress him in pyjamas that pull down easily and keep praising him for telling her early.
How might Vidya feel after they made it in time?
Vidya probably felt relieved and pleased, seeing Sumit notice and name the signal.

Read this:

During the June street festival in Lisbon, the whole neighbourhood smelled of grilled sardines, and music played till late. Sofia, two, danced on her mother's feet until almost ten. Then she stopped, rubbed her eyes, and pulled at Beatriz's skirt. "Cama," she said. "Bed." Beatriz knelt. "You're tired?" Sofia nodded and leaned her head on her mother's shoulder. Beatriz carried her home under the paper garlands, and Sofia was asleep before the second corner.

What did the neighbourhood smell of?
Grilled sardines.
How was Sofia feeling when she said 'Cama'?
Sofia felt tired and sleepy, and knew she needed to rest.
Why was it good that Beatriz asked 'You're tired?'
It named the feeling for Sofia, helping her link the body signal to the word.
How might Beatriz feel carrying Sofia home?
Beatriz probably felt tender and glad that Sofia could tell her she was tired.

Read this:

I'm Pradeep, Lavanya's uncle. At our Onam lunch, the sadya took forever to be served. Lavanya, not quite two, was fine for the first hour. Then she stopped patting the flower pookalam, came to me, patted her tummy and said, "Mum-mum." She opened her mouth like a little bird. I don't know if she was really hungry or had just seen the payasam. But I gave her a bit of banana from the leaf, and she stopped fussing at once.

What did Pradeep give Lavanya from the leaf?
A bit of banana.
What might Lavanya have been feeling when she patted her tummy?
Lavanya was probably hungry and impatient after the long wait.
How could adults help Lavanya connect her tummy signal to eating?
Respond to her 'mum-mum' quickly and name it, 'You're hungry', so she learns the signal works.
How does Pradeep read Lavanya's signal?
Pradeep isn't sure whether she was hungry or had just seen the payasam, but responds kindly and notices she settles.

Read this:

First week of Onam holidays: Jomon squats behind the sofa and wets his shorts. Ganga cleans him up and says, "Next time, tell Amma."

Four days later: in the middle of playing, he stops, grabs the front of his shorts and looks at Ganga. She takes him to the potty, just in time.

Thiruvonam morning, in his new mundu: "Amma, soo-soo!" Ganga laughs and runs with him.

What did Jomon say on Thiruvonam morning?
He said, "Amma, soo-soo!"
How did Ganga likely feel on Thiruvonam morning?
Ganga was probably delighted and relieved, laughing as she ran with Jomon.
How did Ganga support Jomon in noticing his body's signal?
She stayed calm after the accident, gave him simple words to use, and responded quickly when he signalled.
What might Jomon feel when Ganga responds quickly to his signal?
Jomon may feel proud and understood, which helps him keep telling her.

Read this:

During Ramzan, the evenings in the Hyderabad flat were loud with guests arriving for iftar. By eight, Yusuf, two, was rubbing his eyes and pulling at his ear.

Gurpreet Aunty from next door tried to give him a sweet. He pushed it away and flopped on the carpet, whining.

His mother noticed. "He's not hungry, he's sleepy," she said, and carried him to the quiet bedroom. Within minutes he was asleep.

What was Yusuf doing by eight?
He was rubbing his eyes and pulling at his ear.
What was Yusuf feeling when he pushed away the sweet and whined?
Yusuf was tired and cranky, overwhelmed by the noise and ready to sleep.
How did Yusuf's mother respond well to his signals?
She read the eye-rubbing and whining as tiredness, not hunger, and took him somewhere quiet to sleep.
How might Gurpreet Aunty have understood Yusuf's whining?
Gurpreet Aunty may have thought he wanted a treat, and then learned it was tiredness when his mother explained.

Read this:

"Manoj, why is she hitting her tummy?" Ganga asked.

Their daughter Chinni stood by the fridge in the May heat, patting her stomach and saying, "Ow."

"It's two hours since lunch," Manoj said. "Hungry?"

"Chinni, are you hungry?"

Chinni nodded hard and pointed at the fridge.

Ganga gave her a slice of watermelon. Chinni ate it, then patted her tummy again and smiled. "Ow gone."

Manoj laughed. "She's learning what her tummy is telling her."

What did Ganga give Chinni?
Ganga gave her a slice of watermelon.
How did Chinni feel after eating the watermelon?
Chinni seemed satisfied and happy, smiling and saying "Ow gone".
How did Manoj and Ganga help Chinni understand her body signal?
They noticed her gesture, asked a simple question, and responded quickly, so she linked the feeling to hunger.
How did Manoj feel about Chinni's words?
Manoj was amused and pleased, seeing that she was learning what her tummy was telling her.

Read this:

Note for Ojas's Papa, from Nani, Saturday
Before lunch Ojas patted his tummy and said "mum-mum", so he knows when he's hungry now. After lunch he rubbed his eyes and dragged his blanket to me, and he went down for his nap without a fuss. Earlier he'd stopped playing, held his nappy and fussed; he needed changing. His cousin Suraj kept wanting to play trains and sulked when Ojas lay down, so I let Suraj choose the nap-time story. 🙂

What did Ojas drag to Nani after lunch?
He dragged his blanket to her.
What was Ojas feeling when he rubbed his eyes?
He was tired and sleepy, and bringing his blanket showed he knew he wanted rest.
How could Nani keep helping Ojas notice his body's signals?
She could name each signal out loud, like "you're hungry" or "you're sleepy", whenever he shows it.
What is it like for Suraj when Ojas lies down for his nap?
Suraj feels disappointed to lose a playmate, but choosing the story helps Suraj feel included.

Read this:

Guests were due any minute, and the tin of buttons had spilled across the floor. Dilnaz Ammi groaned. "No time, beta." But Nirmala was already crouching. "Reds here, whites here, blacks here." Then she stopped. "This red one is big, it goes with the big ones." She made a line of big buttons and a pile of tiny ones. When the doorbell rang, three neat heaps sat back in the tin.

What had spilled across the floor?
The tin of buttons had spilled.
How was Dilnaz Ammi feeling when she saw the spill?
She felt stressed and hurried, groaning and saying there was no time because guests were due.
How could Dilnaz Ammi encourage Nirmala's sorting later?
She could ask her to explain her groups, like why the big red button went with the big ones.
What would change if there had been no rush?
Nirmala might have had time to try more ways of grouping, maybe by shape, and talk about each choice.

Read this:

In their Kolkata flat, Bhupen Dadu dumped a basket of dry socks on the bed. "Help me pair these, Maria." Maria, five, made piles. "Big ones are Papa's. Medium are Dadu's. Tiny ones are mine!" Then she held up two blue socks of different sizes. "Same colour, but not same size," she said, and put them in different piles. Dadu raised his eyebrows. "Clever girl."

How did Maria sort the socks at first?
She made piles by size: big for Papa, medium for Dadu and tiny for herself.
How did Dadu feel about Maria's sorting?
He seemed impressed, raising his eyebrows and calling her a clever girl.
What small step could Dadu add to stretch her thinking?
He could ask her to sort the same socks by colour next and compare the two ways.
How might Papa benefit from Maria's sorting?
His big socks end up together in one pile, making it easier for him to find a pair. 👍

Read this:

"Nandini, triangles go in this box."
"And circles here. What about this one, Anirban?"
"That's half a circle. It's round on one side."
"But it's flat on this side. It's not a circle."
"Make a new box for half-circles?"
"Yes! And squares go with... wait, this is long."
"That's a rectangle. It has four sides but it's longer."
"Rectangles get their own box too."
They lined up four boxes on the floor.

How many boxes did they line up on the floor?
They lined up four boxes.
Why did Nandini disagree that the half-circle was a circle?
Nandini felt doubtful that it was a circle because it was flat on one side, not round like the others.
What was good about how they solved the half-circle problem?
Instead of forcing it into a box, they made a new group for half-circles, which fit its shape.
What would change if they sorted by colour instead of shape?
The half-circle and rectangle puzzles might disappear, but new questions about colour groups would come up.

Read this:

Classroom note by Shalini Ma'am, Nursery
Today I gave Vaibhav a tray of mixed buttons. First he made a red pile, a blue pile and a yellow pile. Then, without my asking, he pulled the big buttons out of each pile and put them in a row. 'Big ones are the daddies.' I gave him a second tray of shells, and he started sorting those by shape. 👍

What did Vaibhav sort first on the tray?
He sorted mixed buttons into red, blue and yellow piles.
What does Vaibhav's 'daddies' comment suggest about how he was thinking?
It suggests he was enjoying finding patterns and noticed size as a new way to group, giving it his own playful meaning.
How could Shalini Ma'am challenge Vaibhav a little further?
She could ask him to find another way to sort the same shells, like by texture, to stretch his thinking.
How might Vaibhav's parents feel reading this note?
They would likely feel pleased and curious, and might try sorting games at home too.

Read this:

At her mother's small vegetable shop in the kasba, Vidya squatted beside a heap of mixed potatoes, onions and tomatoes. 'Vidya, help Ma sort,' said Gurleen. Vidya put all the red ones in one basket. 'Tomatoes!' Then she paused over an onion. 'This is red too.' She held it up next to a tomato, felt its papery skin and moved it to the onion basket. 'Round but not the same.'

What did Vidya put in one basket first?
She put all the red ones, the tomatoes, in one basket.
Why did Vidya pause over the onion?
She was unsure because it was red like the tomatoes, so she had to think about which group it really belonged in.
What could Gurleen say to encourage Vidya's thinking?
She could ask Vidya how she knew it was an onion, so Vidya explains the papery skin and shape herself.
How might Gurleen see her daughter's help at the shop?
She may be glad for the help and quietly impressed that Vidya checked more than colour.

Read this:

On a grey autumn morning in Manchester, Emeka, five, sat on the bedroom floor with his mother Clara and a pile of clean socks. "Find the partners," Clara said. Emeka made a red pile, a blue pile and a black pile. Then he stopped. "Black big, black small," he said, splitting the black pile into Daddy's and his own. Clara raised her eyebrows. "Two ways at once! Clever."

What piles did Emeka make first?
A red pile, a blue pile and a black pile.
How might Emeka have felt when Clara said "Clever"?
He probably felt proud that she noticed his extra sorting by size.
How could Clara build on this at home?
Give him other things to sort, like spoons or toys, and ask him to find another way to group them.
What would change if Clara had simply paired the socks herself?
It would be quicker, but Emeka would miss the chance to practise sorting by colour and size.

Read this:

The preschool maths table had a bowl of buttons. "Can you sort them, Harish?" asked Yamini, his teacher. Harish, four, made two heaps: round and square. A tiny star-shaped button didn't fit either. He held it up, frowning. "This one has no family." "What could you do?" Yamini asked. He thought, then made a third heap: "Star family." He looked up at her with a big smile.

What was in the bowl on the maths table?
Buttons.
What was Harish feeling when he held up the star-shaped button?
He seemed puzzled and a bit stuck, since it didn't fit his two heaps.
Which choice by Yamini helped, and why?
Asking "What could you do?" instead of telling him, so he found the answer of a new group himself.
How might Yamini see Harish's star family?
She likely feels pleased that he worked out a new category on his own.

Read this:

I'm Rekha, and I sell vegetables beside Seema's mother's bangle stall at the weekly market. Seema is five. Last Thursday the bangles got mixed up in a box, and she sat on the mat sorting them without being asked. First all the red, then the green, then the gold. Then she lined each colour up from big to small. Her mother only smiled. I can't say what Seema was thinking, but she didn't look up once until it was done.

What colours did Seema sort first?
First all the red, then the green, then the gold.
What might Seema have felt as she sorted the bangles?
She seemed absorbed and content, maybe proud, as she didn't look up until it was done.
How could Seema's mother build on this at the stall?
Let her help with sorting jobs regularly and ask her to explain how she grouped them.
How does Rekha see Seema's work?
Rekha is impressed by the careful colour and size order but doesn't claim to know Seema's thoughts.

Read this:

Sunday. Anjali, four, helps Papa with the laundry. Yogesh hands her the socks. She piles them all together, then throws them in the air.
Wednesday. "Can you put red with red?" Papa asks. Anjali sorts slowly: red, blue, white. One striped sock confuses her. "Is this red or white?" "It's both. Where should it go?" "Its own house."
Saturday. Anjali sorts the shoes by size without being asked: "Papa big, Mamma middle, Anjali small."

What did Anjali do with the socks on Sunday?
Piled them together and threw them in the air.
How did Anjali feel about the striped sock?
Anjali felt confused, unsure whether it was red or white.
How did Papa help Anjali think about categories?
He gave a simple rule, red with red, and asked her to decide where the tricky sock should go.
How might Yogesh feel when Anjali sorts the shoes by size unasked?
Yogesh would likely feel delighted and proud of her new thinking.

Read this:

Guests were coming for Diwali dinner in half an hour when Pradeep, five, knocked over Madhuri's button tin. Hundreds of buttons rolled across the floor. "Sorry!" Madhuri took a breath. "Help me, fast. Big ones in this bowl, small ones in that." Pradeep scooped. Then he stopped. "Some are shiny. Shiny ones separate?" "Good idea, but quick!" By the time the doorbell rang, there were three bowls: big, small and shiny.

How long until the guests arrived?
Half an hour.
What was Pradeep feeling when he said 'Sorry!'?
Pradeep felt worried and guilty for knocking over the tin.
How did Madhuri turn the mess into learning?
She gave clear size categories and welcomed his own idea of sorting shiny ones separately.
How might Madhuri feel when the doorbell rings?
Madhuri probably felt relieved and amused, with the buttons sorted into three bowls.

Read this:

In mango season, Kamal Dadu took Varun, five, to the fruit market in Dadar. At home, Dadu tipped the bag onto newspaper. "Help me. Which ones are ready?" Varun sorted: yellow ones in one pile, green in another. Then he made a third pile. "These are yellow and green." Dadu laughed. "In-between ones. We'll eat them tomorrow." Varun lined up the yellow ones by size, biggest to smallest. "The big one is for Dadu."

Where did Kamal Dadu take Varun?
To the fruit market in Dadar.
How might Varun have felt making the third pile?
Varun probably felt thoughtful and pleased, noticing the in-between mangoes.
How could Dadu keep building Varun's sorting skills?
Ask him to sort by other traits, like size or shape, and explain his choices, as he did with the in-between pile.
How might Dadu feel when Varun gives him the biggest mango?
Dadu would likely feel touched and amused by his grandson's generosity.

Read this:

"Papa, look," said Chinmay, spreading out the Diwali diyas on the floor.

"What are you doing?" Vikas asked.

"Big ones here. Small ones here."

"And the painted ones?"

Chinmay frowned. "Hmm." He made a third pile. "Painted ones here."

"What about the big painted one?"

Chinmay thought hard, then put it between two piles. "It's both!"

Vikas laughed. "Clever."

How did Chinmay first sort the diyas?
He put big ones in one pile and small ones in another.
How did Chinmay feel when he couldn't decide where the big painted diya went?
Chinmay felt puzzled and thoughtful, then pleased when he decided it was both.
How can Vikas keep supporting Chinmay's sorting skills?
Give him more things to sort and ask questions like "What about this one?" to stretch his thinking.
How did Vikas feel about Chinmay's answer?
Vikas was amused and impressed, calling him clever.

Read this:

Nursery note, autumn.

Zeenat collected leaves in the garden today and sorted them on the mat without being asked: red leaves, yellow leaves, and brown leaves.

Then she sorted them again, big and small. When a friend added a green one, she said, "That goes by itself."

I'll set out a tray of shells next week for sorting by shape. — Kalyani

How did Zeenat sort the leaves first?
Zeenat sorted them into red leaves, yellow leaves, and brown leaves.
How might Zeenat have felt sorting the leaves on her own?
Zeenat was likely interested and absorbed, enjoying the task without being asked.
How is Kalyani planning to support Zeenat's sorting?
Kalyani will set out a tray of shells for sorting by shape.
How might the friend feel when Zeenat put the green leaf by itself?
The friend might be curious or pleased to see the leaf get its own group.

Read this:

At harvest time, Gopika Paati's shop in the village near Salem was full of beans. Mahima, five, sat on a sack and helped.

"Red beans in this tin, white beans in that tin," Paati said.

Mahima sorted quickly. Then she found some spotted beans. She made a new pile.

"Why a new pile?" Paati asked.

"They're not red and not white. They're spotty."

Where did the white beans go?
White beans went in that tin.
How did Mahima feel when she found the spotted beans?
Mahima was confident and thoughtful, deciding they needed their own pile.
How can Paati keep encouraging Mahima's sorting?
Ask her to explain her groups and give her new things to sort in the shop.
How might Paati feel about Mahima's new pile?
Paati was likely pleased and amused by Mahima's clear reasoning.

Read this:

In April, when autumn leaves covered the park in Cape Town, Tomas and his cousin Zanele filled a shoebox with treasures. At home they tipped it out on the floor. Tomas made piles: "Red here. Yellow here. Brown here." Zanele had a different idea. "Big ones and small ones!" They argued, then Tomas said, "Both!" So they made a big-red pile, a small-red pile, and so on. Zanele found one stone and frowned. "It's not a leaf." She gave it its own pile.

Where did the children collect their treasures?
They collected them in the park in Cape Town, where autumn leaves covered the ground.
Why did Zanele frown at the stone?
She was puzzled because it didn't fit any leaf group, and felt it needed its own place.
How could an adult build on this sorting game?
They could ask the children to sort the same leaves a new way, such as by shape, and explain their groups.
How does Tomas feel when Zanele wants to sort a different way?
Tomas is annoyed at first, but then finds a way to use both ideas, which keeps the game fun for him too.

Read this:

I'm Dilnaz, Arohi's friend since primary school. This term she's changed. She started wearing the same chunky white sneakers the senior girls wear, even though she told me they hurt her feet. She posts photos from the cafe where the popular group goes, but I know she only ordered water. She laughs a bit louder at their jokes. Yesterday she dropped the science club, which she loved, because "it's for kids." I don't know what she's feeling. Maybe she's happy. But when we walk home she's quiet, and she keeps checking how many people liked her photo.

Which club did Arohi drop?
The science club.
What might Arohi's checking her likes on the way home suggest?
She may be anxious about whether her new image is working and whether she is rising in the group's eyes.
What could Dilnaz do as a friend?
Tell Arohi gently that she misses the old Arohi and that she is still welcome, without lecturing her.
How does Dilnaz see these changes differently from how Arohi might present them?
Dilnaz sees the costs, like sore feet and a dropped club, while Arohi may be focused on fitting in with the popular group.

Read this:

Week one: Sachin, sixteen, noticed that the boys who got the most attention in class all posted gym photos. He started doing push-ups every night and asked his sister Rajni to take pictures. "From this angle. No, lower."
Week three: His posts got more likes. Two seniors started saying "Hi, bro" in the corridor. He walked taller. He skipped Rajni's birthday dinner to film a workout video.
Week six: One of his videos flopped. He deleted it within an hour. At dinner he was snappy. Rajni asked, "Do you actually like the gym, or just the likes?" Sachin didn't answer. But the next evening he went cycling instead, with no phone.

What did the seniors start saying to Sachin in the corridor?
"Hi, bro."
Why did Sachin delete the video within an hour?
He was embarrassed it didn't get attention and worried it would hurt his new standing.
How might Rajni's question help Sachin?
It made him think about whether he was working out for himself or only for status, without scolding him.
How might Rajni have felt when Sachin skipped her birthday dinner?
Hurt and pushed aside for something that seemed shallow to her.

Yamini, when I was fifteen, the cool boys in my school all rode loud motorbikes and wore flashy watches. I didn't even have a bike. Arohi said privately that Arohi would have been happy for Hansa to choose differently, so Arohi may not have expected Hansa to follow for the group's sake.

In Class 10, our group of five did everything together: tuition, lunch, cricket on Sundays. When stream selection came, Tejas said, "PCM, all of us, obviously. Same class, same tuition." Everyone nodded. So did I, even though I'm Reena and I'd been drawing buildings in the margins of my notebooks for years.

I filled PCM. For the first three weeks of Class 11, I sat in physics feeling like I was drowning in a language I didn't speak. And the funny thing? The group was already splitting. Tejas was in a different section. Two of them joined a different tuition.

One night I realised I was about to spend two years in a stream I didn't want, for friends who were drifting anyway. And if I stayed, I'd blame them for it later.

I went to the office the next morning and switched to humanities with maths. I told the group at lunch. Tejas said, "Traitor," but he was grinning. We still play cricket on Sundays.

What did Reena draw in the margins of notebooks?
Reena drew buildings in the margins of notebooks.
What was Reena feeling in physics during the first weeks of Class 11?
Reena felt lost and overwhelmed, like drowning in a language Reena did not speak.
What did Reena notice that helped make a better choice?
Reena noticed the group was splitting anyway, so following them would mean regret and blame later, and chose humanities with maths instead.
How does Tejas seem to see Reena's switch?
Tejas teases Reena as a traitor but is grinning, which suggests he is not really upset and the friendship holds.

Career counsellor's note, Class 10, stream choice week

Baljeet came to fill in his form with three friends, including Tushar. All four wrote "Science (PCM)." Baljeet's pen hovered for a long time before he wrote it.

I asked him to stay back. He said, "We've been together since nursery. If I take commerce, I'll be alone in a new section." When I asked about his marks, he said his best subjects are accounts and economics, and physics is his weakest.

I asked him to picture the day two years from now when he is stuck in a subject he doesn't like. Would he blame his friends? He said, "Probably. That's not fair on them, is it?"

We talked about how groups change after Class 10 anyway, new sections, new tuitions, new friends.

He came back the next day and asked for a new form. He wrote "Commerce." Tushar came with him and said, "We'll still have lunch, idiot." Baljeet laughed. I have noted his change in the office register.

How many friends came with Baljeet to fill in the form?
Baljeet came with three friends, including Tushar.
What was Baljeet worried about as his pen hovered?
Baljeet was anxious about being alone in a new section and losing his friends if he chose commerce.
How did the counsellor help Baljeet choose for himself?
The counsellor asked him to picture being stuck in a subject he disliked and whether he would blame his friends, which helped him see the real cost.
How does Tushar see Baljeet's change of stream?
Tushar seems supportive and relaxed about it, joking that they will still have lunch together.

At the athletics club the floodlights were still on when Afreen finished her last 200 metres. It was the fourth dawn practice in a row. Her legs shook, but her mind raced: the state trials in March, a national place, and the sick feeling that everyone else was better. "Log," said Coach Jagdish, tapping the notebook. Afreen wrote: "Four sessions, all done. Two clean starts." The coach pointed at the corner. "Chemistry test Thursday?" "Yes." "Then that goes in the log too. Trials are your goal, not your whole life." Afreen exhaled. "I want it so much I'm scared of it." "Good. Keep counting sessions, not medals."

How many dawn practices in a row had Afreen done?
It was the fourth dawn practice in a row.
What does Afreen mean by wanting it so much that Afreen is scared of it?
That the wish to reach the trials burns strongly, and so does the fear of not being good enough; the racing mind and the sick feeling show both.
Why does Coach Jagdish put the chemistry test in the log too?
It keeps a backup plan and the rest of Afreen's life in view, since the trials are a goal and not the whole of life. 😊
How might Coach Jagdish see Afreen's fear?
As a normal companion to a big goal, best handled by counting sessions instead of medals.

Shankar had wanted the civil services since Class 8, when a young collector visited their school in Hyderabad and spoke about fixing the water supply in a village. Now in Class 11, the goal felt like fire in his chest on good days and a stone on bad ones.

"Lakhs of people apply," his sister Himani said, reading over his shoulder. "Only a few hundred get in."

"I know." He'd looked it up at two in the morning, heart pounding.

That weekend he stopped only dreaming about it and made a small plan on a sheet taped above his desk. One newspaper editorial every morning, notes in a register. Thirty minutes of general studies after school. And at the bottom, in smaller letters: backup, economics degree, then decide.

Himani tapped the sheet. "And if you don't make it?"

"Then I'll still know economics, and I'll have read two thousand editorials." He ticked off the first box. "Today I just count whether I did it."

What did Shankar tape above his desk?
Shankar taped a sheet with a small plan above his desk.
What was Shankar feeling about his goal?
Shankar felt both fired up and full of dread, excited on good days and anxious enough to research it at two in the morning.
Why is counting whether he did the daily tasks a wise habit?
It measures effort he can control, so he keeps going even though the final result is uncertain.
How does Himani see Shankar's goal?
Himani seems worried about the odds, which is why she mentions how few get in and asks about the backup.

"Coach, can I be honest?" Asif said, sitting on the bench after practice.

Thomas sir sat next to him. "Go on."

"I want to play professionally. Like, really. But every time I say it, my stomach goes weird. What if I'm not good enough? Out of our whole academy, maybe one person makes it."

"That feeling's normal. Anyone chasing something big feels it." Thomas sir pulled a notebook from his bag. "So let's make it smaller. What can you do every single day?"

Asif thought. "Juggling, two hundred touches. Sprints. Stretching."

"Write it down. Tick it every night. Not the goals you score. What you did."

"And if I don't make it?"

"You finish school properly. Maybe sports science, maybe coaching. That's the backup. It doesn't cancel the dream."

Asif wrote it all down. "It's less scary on paper."

"It usually is."

How many touches did Asif say he would juggle every day?
Asif said he would do two hundred touches.
What does Asif's stomach going weird suggest?
It suggests he feels dread and fear of not being good enough, even while he really wants to play professionally.
What plan did Thomas sir help Asif make, and why is it wise?
They listed daily habits to tick off each night and a backup of finishing school and maybe sports science, which keeps the dream while lowering the risk.
How does Thomas sir see Asif's fear?
Thomas sir sees it as normal for anyone chasing something big, not as a sign Asif should give up.

Tuesday. Nilesh had started turning his phone face down at dinner and taking calls on the balcony. Gurleen noticed, and then told herself she was imagining it. He'd said he was busy with his project, and he was, wasn't he?

Friday. His bag sat open by the door, phone at the top. Gurleen's hand hovered, then dropped. She sat on the bed and wrote what she had actually seen: phone face down, balcony calls, shorter replies. The list was small, but it was real, and it wasn't only in her head.

Sunday. Over chai she said, "Something has changed. You take calls outside and you seem far away. Is there something you want to tell me?" Nilesh put his cup down and looked at her. "Yes," he said slowly. "Let me tell you properly." She listened, and decided she would watch whether his words matched what she saw.

Where did Nilesh take his calls?
Nilesh took his calls on the balcony.
What was Gurleen feeling on Tuesday when she told herself she was imagining it?
She was doubting her own perception, uneasy about what she noticed but unwilling to trust it yet, so she explained it away with his busy project.
What did Gurleen do instead of going through the bag, and why did it help?
She wrote down what she had actually seen and then asked Nilesh directly, so she acted on real observations without spying.
How might Nilesh have felt when Gurleen asked her question over chai?
He might have felt caught or nervous, but the plain and calm question gave him a clear chance to answer honestly.

Thursday. Something's off with Ganga, and I'm tired of pretending it isn't. For a month she's been 'at the library' till ten, but her library card shows no entries, she's changed her phone password, and last Sunday she flinched when a message popped up. Every time, I make an excuse for her. Exams. Stress. I'm being paranoid. Then I lie awake doubting myself. Today Meera asked me, 'If a friend told you all this, what would you say?' I'd say: that's not paranoia, that's noticing. I thought about reading her messages while she slept. I didn't. That's not who I want to be. So tonight at the tea stall I asked her straight: 'Ganga, things have changed. The late nights, the password, the flinch. Is there something you need to tell me?' She went quiet for a long time. Then she said, 'Can we talk tomorrow? Properly.' My stomach dropped. But at least I asked.
- Anand

Where did Ganga say she had been till ten?
At the library.
What was Anand feeling while lying awake?
Anand felt anxious and full of self-doubt, making excuses for Ganga while sensing something was wrong.
What did Anand do instead of spying?
Trusted what had been observed and asked Ganga directly and calmly at the tea stall.
How does Meera see Anand's worries?
As noticing real changes, not paranoia.

"Kavitha, can I ask you something awkward?"
"That face means money."
"It does. My hostel fee is due Friday and my stipend is late. Could I borrow some for two weeks? I'll return it on the tenth, when the stipend comes."

Being embarrassed. Shalini nearly waited until Thursday to bring it up.

Monday: Sharmila's scholarship was delayed again, and the hostel mess fee of 3,000 was due on Friday. She spent the evening scrolling past Parveen's name, cheeks hot. Asking felt like admitting she had failed.
Wednesday: Avoiding it wasn't working; she'd started skipping dinner. On the library steps she said it straight: "Parveen, I need to borrow 3,000 for the mess fee. My scholarship comes on the 20th, and I'll pay you back on the 21st. If that's hard for you, just say no, really." Parveen transferred it that night. "Stop looking so guilty," she said.
The 21st: The scholarship landed at noon. By one, Sharmila had sent the 3,000 back with a message: "Returned. Thank you for trusting me." That evening she bought two plates of momos near the gate. "Not interest," she said. "Just momos." Parveen laughed and took the bigger plate.

How much was the hostel mess fee?
3,000, due on Friday.
Why did Sharmila keep scrolling past Parveen's name on Monday?
She felt embarrassed and ashamed; asking felt like admitting she had failed.
What made Sharmila's request a fair one?
She asked clearly, named the amount and a repayment date, left Parveen free to say no, and repaid on the day she promised.
How might Parveen see the returned 3,000 on the 21st?
As proof that her trust was well placed, which keeps the friendship easy and warm.

Nikita, you're worried about asking Divya for that money? Let me, your Irawati Masi, tell you what I did wrong at your age.
I was twenty, in Pune, learning typing and shorthand. My father's money order was late, and my friend Sushma lent me eighty rupees without a question. Eighty was a lot then. I said, "I'll return it soon." Soon. No date.
Then the money order came, and there were books to buy, and I told myself next month. And the month after that I started taking the other staircase so I wouldn't meet her. Imagine. Sushma hadn't asked once, and I was hiding like a thief.
Finally she came to my room and said, "I don't care about the eighty. I miss you." I cried and gave it back that same day, from the money for my new sandals.
So when you ask Divya, say the amount, say the date, and keep it. The money is small. The friendship isn't.

How much did Sushma lend Irawati?
Eighty rupees.
Why did Irawati start taking the other staircase?
She felt guilty and ashamed about the unpaid loan and avoided Sushma rather than face her.
What was the turning point in Irawati's story, and what did she choose then?
Sushma coming to her room to say she missed her; Irawati returned the money that same day.
How did Sushma see the unpaid loan?
She cared far more about the lost friendship than the eighty rupees, and simply missed Irawati.

My name is Vijay, and for three weeks I crossed the corridor to avoid Professor Sarita's room. Everyone said she failed people for fun. My thermodynamics assignment was half done and I could not understand the second question, yet my stomach turned every time I saw her door. Finally I wrote down three specific doubts, read the chapter again, and went during office hours with sweaty palms. She looked up, said "Sit," and asked me to show my working. I expected a scolding. Instead she circled one line and said, "Good start, wrong sign here." Ten minutes. I walked out lighter, almost laughing. She still scares me a little, but now I know she forgets her glasses on her forehead.

How many specific doubts did Vijay write down before going?
He wrote down three specific doubts.
Why did Vijay's stomach turn every time he saw her door?
He was scared of her strictness, having heard she failed people, and feared a scolding about his half done assignment.
What would you advise Vijay to do if he gets stuck again?
Go early to office hours again with specific doubts and his own working, instead of avoiding her until the problem grows.
How might Professor Sarita see a student turning up at office hours?
She probably sees a student who wants to learn; her calm "Sit" and quick correction suggest she is glad to help, not eager to scold.

By the fourth week of the semester I hadn't understood a single lecture in Dr. Nitin Sharma's Control Systems, and I'd done the worst possible thing: nothing. He had a reputation for sending students out over late assignments, so I skipped his office hours and hoped it would click on its own. It didn't. My first quiz came back at 4 out of 20.
That scared me more than he did. So on Monday I wrote down exactly where I was stuck, three examples, page numbers, and went at 4 p.m.
He was eating a banana. He had a small plant on his desk and a photo of a dog. He listened, drew one diagram, and said, "Everyone gets lost at transfer functions. Come every Monday until you don't."
I've gone five Mondays now. I got 14 on the second quiz. He's still strict. He's also a person who named his dog Resistor.
— Vikas

What did Vikas score on the first quiz?
4 out of 20.
Why did Vikas avoid Dr. Sharma's office hours at first?
Vikas was scared of Dr. Sharma's strict reputation and hoped the subject would click without help.
What did Vikas do to make the visit work?
Wrote down exactly where the confusion was, with three examples and page numbers, and went to office hours on Monday.
How does Dr. Sharma see Vikas's struggle?
As normal ("Everyone gets lost at transfer functions"), and he invites Vikas to come every Monday.

Academic advisor's note, MSc first year, 11 October
Neelam has missed two thesis check-ins with Prof. Vinita Kulkarni. Today she came to me instead, pale, saying she was "too scared to face her now" because the delay had grown so long. She admitted she had been avoiding the department corridor for three weeks.
I asked what she was afraid of. "That she'll say I'm not serious." I pointed out that each missed week made that more likely, not less.
We prepared together: a one-page summary of what she had done, where she was stuck, and a realistic new timeline. I suggested she open with an apology, not excuses.
At 3 p.m. I walked with her as far as the professor's door and waited in the corridor. She came out twenty minutes later, flushed but smiling. "She said, 'Next time, come when you're stuck, not when you've finished being scared.'" They have fixed weekly Tuesday meetings.

How many thesis check-ins had Neelam missed?
Two.
What was Neelam afraid of?
That Prof. Kulkarni would think she wasn't serious; she was pale and too scared to face her.
How did the advisor help Neelam face the professor?
By preparing a one-page summary, stuck points and a new timeline with her, suggesting an apology instead of excuses, and walking her to the door.
How does Prof. Kulkarni respond to Neelam?
Firmly but kindly, telling her to come when stuck and setting weekly Tuesday meetings.

Counselling note, Tuesday. Vikas came in because his friend Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago, without a word. He said he felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone during our talk. He told me he had sent many messages and had not stopped rereading the last ones. We talked about how someone's silence can be about their own reasons, not about Vikas's worth. I did not tell him what Deepak thinks, because I do not know. He said the hardest part is never getting an answer. We agreed that he would stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday, and come back next week to tell me how it went. I will check in then.

How long ago did Deepak stop replying?
Deepak stopped replying three weeks ago.
What did Vikas feel, and what shows it?
Vikas felt confused and small, and he kept checking his phone and rereading the last messages.
What did Vikas and the counsellor agree that he would do next?
Stop sending messages for now, leave the phone in his bag at cricket practice on Saturday and come back to report.

The counsellor does not know Deepak's reasons, and guessing could pull Vikas further into chasing answers.

Day 1: Aditi, who had messaged Himani every night for a month since they met at the book club, stopped replying mid-conversation. Himani's last message, "haha same! coffee saturday?", sat there unanswered.

Day 20: Still nothing. Walking home from book club, Himani told her friend Tsering, "I keep thinking it was me." Tsering said, "Maybe Aditi just couldn't say whatever it was. What was Himani's last message before Aditi stopped replying?
"haha same! coffee saturday?"

Small and stupid, replaying every joke and wondering what she had done wrong.

Sending one kind message instead of six, putting the phone away, talking to Tsering, and archiving the chat.

Vaibhav, beta, you keep checking your phone. Someone stopped replying? Let me, your Binita pishi, tell you a story from before phones.
In 1985 I was twenty, in Shillong, writing every week to a boy called Arun whom I'd met at a cousin's wedding. For six months he wrote back, long letters with pressed leaves inside. Then nothing. I wrote three more letters. Then a fourth, angry. Then I walked to the post office every day for a month, asking the postman if something had got lost.
I decided I'd been too boring. Too forward. Too something.
Years later a friend told me Arun had simply got engaged and hadn't known how to tell me. So he told me nothing. It had nothing to do with my letters.
I wish I had stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept my own peace. His silence was about his courage, not my worth. So, beta, put the phone down and come and eat. Your pishi has made luchi.

What did Arun put inside his letters?
Pressed leaves.
How did Binita feel about herself when the letters stopped?
That she had been too boring or too forward; she felt small and blamed herself.
What does Binita wish she had done?
Stopped at the first unanswered letter and kept her own peace, instead of writing more and asking the postman every day.
Why had Arun stopped writing?
He had got engaged and didn't know how to tell her, so he said nothing.

The phone buzzed on the accounts-office desk and Mridul's stomach dropped before he read a word. The message from Sir said: "Send the ledger. Now." Same tone as always, and no threat in it. At the next desk, Sumit saw the colour leave his face. "Again?" Sumit asked quietly. "It's my body," Mridul said. "It jumps at every ping." He sent the file, then opened his notebook and drew two columns: things that had really happened (two shouted meetings, one late call) and things his mind said might happen (being sacked tomorrow). The second column was longer. Under it he wrote the start of a safety net: three months of rent set aside, and two contacts at other firms. Sumit slid over a name of an accountant worth calling.

What did the message from Sir say?
It said, "Send the ledger. Now."
What does Mridul's stomach dropping before he read a word suggest?
It suggests Mridul dreads the boss's messages, and his body reacts before his mind does, which he treats as information.
What did Mridul do with his notebook, and how does it help?
He listed what had really happened and what his mind said might happen, which helps him separate real risk from imagined risk.
How might Sumit see Mridul's reaction?
Sumit noticed the colour leave Mridul's face and asked quietly, so Sumit seems concerned and supportive, and offered a name worth calling.

Trisha, when your phone buzzes and you jump like that, it reminds me of myself at twenty-two. Your Suraj-mama had a supervisor at a medicine warehouse in Baddi who shouted on every call. After a month, just the ringtone made my stomach drop. I froze. For three years I stayed, telling myself any other place would be worse. Then one night my friend Pinto made me write two lists: what could really happen if I left, and what I only imagined. Real: a few lean months. Imagined: that nobody would ever hire me again. After that I did boring things. I put a little aside each month. I called four old classmates and asked about openings. When the next shouting call came, my stomach still dropped, but now I knew it was telling me something. Eight months later I left. So listen to that stomach, Trisha. Then make your lists.

Where was the warehouse?
The warehouse was in Baddi.
How did young Suraj feel when the ringtone went off?
Suraj felt dread and fear, with a dropping stomach at the sound.
What turning point in the story helped Suraj stop freezing?
Pinto's two lists, separating real risks from imagined ones, which led him to build a cushion and contacts before leaving.
Why might Pinto have suggested the two lists?
Pinto likely saw that Suraj's fear was mixing real and imagined dangers, and wanted Suraj to see which ones could actually be planned for.

Deepak was at his cousin's wedding in Jaipur, dhol thumping, when his phone buzzed for the ninth time that day. 'Call me. Now.' His manager, Mr. Batra, again. Deepak's stomach dropped the way it always did, and he slipped behind the tent, where it was only slightly quieter. His friend Simran followed him out. 'You've gone grey. What's he going to do, fire you at a wedding?' Deepak laughed weakly, then didn't. 'He could block my confirmation.' 'Could he, really? Or is that the fear talking?' Between the generator and the catering vans they sorted it out: real risk, a bad review next month; imagined risk, being ruined forever. Simran made him name three college friends who could tell him about openings, and suggested he talk to his elder brother about a backup for a few lean months. Deepak texted Mr. Batra: 'At a family wedding today, will call at 9 a.m. tomorrow.' Then he went back in and danced, badly.

How many times had Deepak's phone buzzed that day?
Deepak's phone had buzzed nine times that day.
What does Deepak's stomach dropping suggest about his feelings?
It suggests Deepak feels dread and fear whenever Mr. Batra messages, even at a family wedding.
Why was sorting real risks from imagined ones useful?
It showed the likely worst case was a bad review, not ruin, and led to a plan with college contacts and a backup for lean months.
How does Simran see Deepak's fear?
Simran sees it as partly real and partly the fear talking, and helps pull the two apart.

I'm Ayesha, at the next desk in the design team. For weeks Kavitha had looked worn out. Then on Thursday at the tea point I saw her and Rohit talking in low voices. Rohit was showing her notes on his phone; then she showed him hers. I caught "dates", "same words" and "same here", and by the end her shoulders had come down and she laughed once. Ayesha saw them at the tea point on Thursday.

They can share facts and dates rather than gossip, and support each other without pulling anyone into a risky move, as Kavitha and Rohit agreed.
How might Rohit have felt while sharing notes?
Rohit may also have felt relief at finding he was not alone, since Ayesha heard "same here" and Rohit agreed to go to HR only if both wanted to.

At the dairy cooperative's collection centre outside Anand, the supervisor, Mr. Parmar, had a habit of shouting at whoever handled the evening milk register. Dear Uday Sir,
I wanted to explain why I speak so softly in class. I know you asked me to speak up during my presentation yesterday, and I tried, but my voice just got smaller.
I'm not bored or uninterested. I really like geography. But when the whole class is looking at me, my throat tightens. I've always been shy.
Could I present to you and a small group first? I think if I practise with fewer people, my voice will get stronger.
Thank you for always being patient.
Farhan

What subject does Farhan really like?
Geography.
What was Farhan feeling when the voice got smaller during the presentation?
Farhan felt shy and nervous with the whole class looking, which made the throat tighten.
What did Farhan suggest to Uday Sir?
Presenting to a small group first to build confidence gradually.
How might Uday Sir have seen Farhan's soft voice before this letter?
Uday Sir might have thought Farhan was uninterested or not confident, not knowing about the shyness.

Read this:

Pradeep, you said this school radio show is about voices we don't hear enough, so, okay: I'm Dhruv, famous for being the one nobody can hear. In Class 8, our English teacher said, "Speak up, Dhruv, or do you just not care?" in front of everyone. I cared a lot. At home, in our family, you don't raise your voice at elders, so a soft voice meant respect. At school it meant I didn't care. And when she told me off for it, my voice went even smaller, because I was scared. This year Mr Iqbal tried something different. He let me read my answer to him first, just the two of us at his desk. Then to a small group. By October I read a poem to the whole class. Still not loud. But everyone heard it.

By when did Dhruv read a poem to the whole class?
By October.
What was Dhruv feeling when the English teacher asked if Dhruv didn't care?
Dhruv felt hurt and scared, which made the voice even smaller, though Dhruv cared a lot.
What did Mr Iqbal do that worked?
He started in a quiet, private setting at his desk, then a small group, building up to the whole class instead of criticising.
How did the Class 8 English teacher read Dhruv's soft voice?
She read it as not caring, missing both the family habit of speaking softly out of respect and Dhruv's fear.
