messages.content:
Read this:

Subject: sorry about yesterday
Sumit,
I know I yelled at you in the canteen. You only asked if I'd done the chemistry assignment and I told you to mind your own business in front of everyone. I haven't done it. I haven't done anything since Ma died. I come home, shut my door and lie there. Papa knocks and I say I'm studying.
The thing is, I'm not even angry at you. I'm angry that the doctors couldn't fix it, that Papa couldn't, that everyone keeps saying 'be strong' like it's a switch. Mostly I'm scared. Of what happens to us now. Of forgetting her voice.
Don't tell anyone. But don't give up on me either.
Mridul

What had Sumit asked Mridul in the canteen?
He only asked if Mridul had done the chemistry assignment.
What feelings does Mridul reveal beneath his anger?
Fear about what happens to his family now and of forgetting his mother's voice, along with helplessness that no one could fix it.
What could help Mridul at this stage besides Sumit's friendship?
Talking to a trusted adult, like his Papa or the school counsellor, so he isn't carrying the fear alone behind a closed door.
How might Sumit feel reading this email?
Probably relieved the anger wasn't really about him, and worried for Mridul, wanting to stay close while hoping he gets more support.

Read this:

You want to know why I've been such a monster, Gautam? Fine. Since Papa died in March, everything makes me furious. Kirti laughs too loud at lunch and I want to throw my tray. The class teacher says 'take your time with the syllabus' and I want to scream that time is exactly what we didn't have. I skipped two tests. I stay in my room with the door locked and headphones on, even when Ma knocks and says, 'Jaya, eat something.' Everyone says he's in a better place. Better than here? With us? I'm angry at the doctors, at everything, at the grown-ups who kept saying it'd be okay. And under all that... I'm scared. Of Ma crying at night. Of it happening again. There. Happy now?

How many tests has Jaya skipped?
She skipped two tests.
What is Jaya really feeling beneath the fury?
She's scared, of her mother crying at night and of losing someone again, and helpless because the adults couldn't keep their promise that it would be okay.
What could Gautam do after hearing this?
Stay with her without arguing, and gently encourage her to talk to her Ma or a school counsellor so she isn't alone with the fear.
What might Jaya's Ma be going through when she knocks on the locked door?
She is grieving too and probably worried and lonely, wanting to reach her daughter but not knowing how.

Read this:

In the village near Ujjain, Vaibhav hadn't been to the tuition class since his father's death two months ago. When his friend Ritesh came by with notes, Vaibhav snapped, "Who asked you?" and shut the door of his room.
His mother, Indu, heard the bolt slide. She knocked softly. "Vaibhav?"
"Leave me alone!"
Inside, he sat on the floor with his back against the bed. He wasn't really angry at Ritesh. He was angry at the hospital, at the doctors, at the whole unfair world. And underneath, he was scared. If Papa could just be gone, what else could?
Indu sat down outside his door, her back against it too, and waited.

How long ago did Vaibhav's father die?
Two months ago.
What feelings sat underneath Vaibhav's anger?
Fear and helplessness; he felt the world was unfair and was scared that anything could be taken away.
What turning point does Indu's choice to sit by the door offer?
It shows she is there without forcing him, so when he is ready, he can talk or let her in.
How might Ritesh feel after being snapped at?
Ritesh may feel hurt and unsure, but could understand it isn't really about him.

Read this:

In Oslo it was already dark at three. Rosa hadn't been to school for four days. Her mother had died in the spring, and now, in November, Rosa was angrier than ever.
When Ulla knocked with a bag of cinnamon buns, Rosa opened the door a crack. "I don't need your pity."
"It's not pity. It's buns."
"Just go, Ulla."
She shut the door and leaned on it. She could hear Ulla still standing there. Rosa pressed her fists against her eyes. Why were the adults useless? Why couldn't the hospital have done something? It wasn't fair.
After a minute she opened the door again. Ulla was still there. Rosa took the bag without a word.

What did Ulla bring?
A bag of cinnamon buns.
What was Rosa feeling as she leaned on the door?
She felt angry and helpless, furious that adults and the hospital couldn't save her mother and that life is unfair.
What small turning point happened when Rosa opened the door again?
Taking the bag let a little connection back in, even without words.
What is it like for Ulla to be told to go?
Ulla probably feels hurt but understanding, choosing to stay by the door because she cares.

Read this:

The school counsellor's room was small, with one plant and two chairs. Sunaina sat with her arms folded.
"Your teachers say you've stopped handing in work," Seema ma'am said gently. "And that you shouted at your friends in the canteen."
"So?"
"It's been three months since your father died."
"What's that got to do with anything?" Sunaina's voice cracked on the last word. "Everyone keeps saying it'll get better. The doctors said he'd get better too."
Seema ma'am waited.
"Nobody could fix it," Sunaina whispered. "Not even the adults." She put her face in her hands.
"No," Seema ma'am said. "Nobody could. I'm here, and we'll meet every week."

How long ago did Sunaina's father die?
Three months ago.
What does Sunaina's cracking voice suggest about her anger?
Underneath the anger she feels helpless and betrayed, since even the adults and doctors could not fix it.
What support does Seema ma'am offer at this stage?
Honest words that nobody could fix it, her calm presence, and a regular weekly meeting.
How might Sunaina's friends see her shouting in the canteen?
They may feel hurt and confused, not knowing her anger comes from grief about her father.

Read this:

Imran,
I'm writing this because I can't say it out loud without getting angry again. Sorry for yelling at you at the nets on Friday. You only asked if I was coming to practice, and I told you to mind your own business, in front of everyone.
Since Appa died in March I've been like this. I slam my door. I haven't opened my physics book in three weeks. Amma knocks and I say "leave me," and then I feel horrible. Everyone keeps telling me to be strong. The doctors couldn't fix him, the adults couldn't fix anything, so what is the point of strong?
I don't think I'm really angry at you. I think I'm scared all the time. Of Amma being alone. Of forgetting his voice.
The school counsellor asked me to come on Monday. I said yes. Will you walk there with me?
Lokesh

When did Lokesh yell at Imran?
At the nets on Friday, in front of everyone.
What feelings does Lokesh say sit beneath the anger?
Lokesh feels scared all the time: afraid of Amma being alone and of forgetting Appa's voice.
What step has Lokesh already taken, and why does it matter?
Lokesh agreed to see the school counsellor on Monday, which brings a trusted adult in to help with the grief.
How might Imran feel reading this letter?
Imran may feel relieved and moved, understanding the yelling came from grief and fear, not from anything Imran did.

Read this:

At the Sri Rama Navami fair in Chaitanya's village, Lalit anna played the harmonium on the temple steps, fingers flying, and the whole crowd clapped along. Chaitanya, nine, forgot all about his cotton candy.
On the walk home he announced to Ammamma, "From tomorrow I will practise harmonium every single day. Like Lalit anna!"
Ammamma's old harmonium sat under a cloth in the storeroom. Next morning Chaitanya dragged it out before brushing his teeth and pumped the bellows till dust flew. He played the same three notes over and over, grinning. After school he played again. After dinner he played on the veranda until the neighbour's dog howled.
"Every day," he told Ammamma, tapping her arm. "You'll see."

Where did Lalit anna play the harmonium?
On the temple steps at the Sri Rama Navami fair.
What made Chaitanya want to practise every day?
He admired Lalit anna and was thrilled by the clapping crowd, so excitement made him want to play like him.
How could Ammamma help this excitement turn into a lasting habit?
She could help Chaitanya choose a short, fixed practice time, so a routine is ready for the days when the thrill wears off.
How might Ammamma feel hearing the same three notes all day?
Ammamma may be amused and touched to hear her old harmonium played again, while wondering how long the excitement will last.

Read this:

On Saturday, Jana's cousin Camila visited from Lisbon and drew everyone around the kitchen table in Berlin: Oma in her reading glasses, Papa mid-yawn, even the cat. The drawings looked alive. Jana, ten, couldn't stop staring at the moving pencil.
That night she found an empty notebook and wrote on the first page in big letters: JANA'S DRAWING BOOK. ONE DRAWING EVERY DAY.
On Sunday she drew her shoe, her lamp and the view from her window. On Monday she drew on the bus to school and again after homework.
"Look, Mama, I've done six already!" she said, holding up the book with smudgy grey fingers.
Mama smiled. "Every day, hm?"
"Every single day, like Camila," Jana said, already sharpening the pencil.

What did Jana write on the first page of her notebook?
JANA'S DRAWING BOOK. ONE DRAWING EVERY DAY.
What does Jana's 'I've done six already!' show about how she feels?
It shows she is proud and excited, eager to draw like Camila.
What could Mama do to help the habit last once the excitement fades?
Mama could help Jana pick a small daily drawing time and keep the book somewhere easy to reach, so it is simple to continue on duller days.
How might Camila feel on hearing that Jana draws every day because of the visit?
Camila might feel flattered and happy to have inspired Jana 😊, and could encourage her by drawing together next time.

Read this:

Looking back, it started at my cousin Pradeep's match. He hit a six, and the whole ground cheered. I decided right then: I would practise cricket every single day.
The next morning I woke up before the alarm. I bowled against the wall for an hour. I told Mummy, "I'm going to be like Pradeep bhaiya." I told my class teacher. I told the watchman.
For the first week it was so easy. I didn't even need anyone to remind me. I just jumped out of bed, grabbed the ball, and ran.
I'm Parul, and that was my cricket week. My arm still remembers.

Where did Parul see Pradeep hit a six?
At Pradeep's match.
What was Parul feeling after seeing the six?
Parul felt excited and full of admiration for Pradeep bhaiya, wanting to be just like him.
What could help Parul keep practising once the excitement fades?
Choosing a set small time each day, like ten minutes after school, so practice doesn't depend on feeling excited.
How might Pradeep feel if he heard about Parul's week?
Pradeep would probably feel proud and flattered that his six inspired his young cousin.

Read this:

Harmonium teacher's note, Saturday
Gurleen came to class today practically bouncing. Last weekend she heard an older student play at the gurdwara and announced, "I'm going to practise every single day, like her!" Her mother says she has practised every morning this week, before breakfast, without being asked.
Today she played her scales twice as long as usual and asked for a new song. Her eyes lit up when I played it for her.
I praised her effort. I also suggested we choose a fixed ten-minute slot, so practice becomes a habit that still happens on days she doesn't feel so excited. She wrote "10 min after school" on her book herself.
Jatin

When has Gurleen been practising this week?
Every morning, before breakfast.
What was Gurleen feeling when she came to class?
She felt excited and inspired, full of admiration for the older student she heard.
Why did Jatin suggest a fixed ten-minute slot?
So practice becomes a habit that still happens when the excitement fades.
How might Gurleen's mother feel watching her practise every morning?
She is probably pleased and a little amused at how eager Gurleen is.

Read this:

Dear Diary,
Today Ojas bhaiya from the third floor showed me his drawings. He draws cars that look REAL. I want to draw like that.
So I decided. I will draw every day. Every single day! I drew three cars today, one before school, one at lunch, and one now. The wheels were wobbly but I don't care.
I asked Mumma to buy a new sketchbook and she said yes. I am going to fill it by the end of the month.
I'm so excited I can't sleep. Tomorrow I will draw a truck.
Raghav

How many cars did Raghav draw today?
Three cars.
What is Raghav feeling as he goes to bed?
Raghav feels excited and inspired by admiration for Ojas bhaiya's drawings, too excited to sleep.
What small plan could help Raghav keep drawing after the excitement fades?
Picking one fixed time each day, such as ten minutes after dinner, and keeping it even on dull days.
How might Ojas feel knowing Raghav wants to draw like him?
Ojas would probably feel flattered and proud to have inspired a younger neighbour.

Read this:

At the Ram Navami bhajan in the village temple, a girl only a few years older than Anjali played the harmonium so fast her fingers blurred, and the whole courtyard clapped along. Walking home under the neem trees, Anjali could not stop talking. "Indu Bua, I'm going to play harmonium every single day. Every day! Even Sundays. Even when it rains." At home she pulled Dadi's old harmonium out from under the cot, blew off the dust and pumped the bellows until it wheezed. She pressed the same three keys for an hour, grinning, and drew a chart with thirty boxes on the back of a calendar page. Indu Bua smiled. "Let's see how the boxes look after the mela is over."

How many boxes did Anjali draw on her chart?
Thirty boxes, on the back of a calendar page.
What feeling was driving Anjali's big promise?
She was excited and inspired after watching the older girl play so fast, and wanted to play like her.
What could help Anjali keep going once the excitement fades?
A small, fixed practice time and someone to play for now and then, so it does not depend on excitement alone.

Indu Bua enjoys Anjali's excitement but hints, with the remark about the mela, that the promise will be harder to keep later.

Third week of the monsoon holidays in Bishnupur, and Anirban's tabla practice had gone grey. The first days had been thrilling: new bols, Baba recording him on the old phone, Thakuma clapping from the veranda. Now it was the same teen-taal, round and round, and his fingers still stumbled on the same fast phrase. Ustadji said it would take months.
From the lane came Jeevan's whistle. "Anirban! Fishing at the big pond, everyone's going!"
Anirban looked at the tabla, then at the rain-washed lane. One day off won't matter, he thought. I practised yesterday. I'll do double tomorrow.
He didn't feel like practising at all. Nothing of the early excitement was left to pull him to the mat. He sat there, half up and half down, listening to Jeevan's footsteps slow outside the gate.

What did Anirban's fingers still stumble on?
His fingers still stumbled on the same fast phrase.
How does Anirban feel when Jeevan whistles, and what bargain does his mind make?
He feels bored and torn, so he tells himself one day off won't matter because he practised yesterday and can do double tomorrow.
What could help Anirban keep going now that the excitement has worn off?
He could do a short, fixed practice before joining Jeevan, so the habit rests on a simple rule rather than on whether he feels like it.
What might Jeevan think, waiting outside the gate?
Jeevan probably just wants his friend at the pond and may not realise Anirban is torn between fun and a practice that has gone dull.

Day nineteen of the plan Lars had copied into his notebook: jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening. In week one he'd felt like an athlete. Now, on Bergen's third straight day of rain, he checked his arms in the bathroom mirror and saw exactly the same arms.
His brother Daniel, home from university, glanced up from the sofa. "Going out in that?"
Lars pulled on one shoe and stopped. It's just rain, he told himself. Then another voice: skip today, the plan says rest days are fine anyway. It didn't, actually.
He sat on the bottom stair, one shoe on and the other in his hand, feeling nothing like the boy who had started this. Daniel said nothing, just raised an eyebrow.
Lars tied the second lace slowly, not because he wanted to, but because he'd said he would.

What was Lars's evening plan?
Jog to the harbour and back, forty push-ups, every evening.
What does Lars's thought 'the plan says rest days are fine anyway' reveal?
He feels discouraged and bored, so his mind bargains for a skip, even inventing a rule, because his arms look exactly the same.
Why did tying the second lace matter, and what might help on the next rainy day?
Lars went because he'd said he would, not because he felt like it; a shorter indoor version for rainy days could make discipline easier when mood is low.
How might Daniel see his brother on the bottom stair?
Daniel may recognise the struggle and chooses a raised eyebrow over a lecture, leaving the decision to Lars.

Okay, Parveen, honest update on the "I'll practise guitar every day" thing? Week one, amazing. Week two, still good. Week three... I don't know. It's the same chords. My fingers hurt. I'm not getting better as fast as the videos said.

Twenty days.

Zubin feels bored and discouraged, the practice dull and progress slow, and tempted by the voice saying one day off won't hurt.

Choosing to practise because of the promise, even without the mood for it, perhaps with a smaller daily target.
How might Parveen respond to this honest update?
Parveen might feel sympathetic and amused, and could encourage Zubin to keep a short daily practice.

Week one: Usha started studying physics for thirty minutes every evening. She loved it. She made colour-coded notes and felt clever.
Week two: Still going, but slower. The notes were less colourful. Her cousin Jahnavi texted, "How's the physics habit?" "Great!" Usha replied.
Week three: The chapter on electricity was hard. The test marks hadn't gone up yet. One evening Usha opened the book, stared at a diagram and thought, one day off won't hurt. She closed it. The next evening she opened it, stared, and closed it again. On Sunday she wrote to Jahnavi: "It's so boring now." Jahnavi replied, "That's when it starts to count."

How long did Usha study physics each evening?
Thirty minutes.
What was Usha feeling in week three when she closed the book?
She felt bored and discouraged, since the chapter was hard and her marks hadn't gone up.
What turning point does Jahnavi's reply point to?
That now the habit depends on discipline rather than mood, so Usha could keep a small daily session anyway.
What might Jahnavi be thinking when she replies?
Jahnavi seems encouraging and wise, understanding that boredom is normal once the novelty fades.

Chinmay, beta, you've stopped your swimming? Let me tell you about my yoga, when I was sixteen.
My teacher at school showed us sun salutations. I loved it. For two weeks I did them every morning on the terrace. I felt like a saint!
Then the third week came. Same moves. Same stiff back. No magic. One morning I thought, "Tarun, you've done fourteen days. One day off won't hurt." Then the next day, same thing.
My grandfather saw me sleeping late and said, "Now the real practice begins. When you don't feel like it."
I grumbled. But I went back up to the terrace the next morning. I still do those salutations, beta. Not because I feel like it. Because I do them.

Where did Tarun do the sun salutations?
On the terrace.
What was young Tarun feeling in the third week?
Young Tarun felt bored and a bit disappointed, since the moves were the same and there was no magic, so a day off seemed harmless.
In the story, what turning point kept Tarun going?
The grandfather's words that real practice begins when you don't feel like it, and going back the next morning.
How might Tarun's grandfather have felt seeing him sleep late?
The grandfather was probably understanding but firm, wanting Tarun to learn that habits run on discipline, not mood.

Week three, and the power had been out in the colony since the evening thunderstorm. Sarita sat on the steps with her English vocabulary cards and a candle stub. Eighteen days of ten new words a day, and her mock-test score had moved by exactly two marks. The cards felt like chewing paper. Just skip today, a voice in her head said reasonably. It's dark. One day won't matter. You'll do double tomorrow. Her younger brother Sumit was already lying on the cool floor, fanning himself with a notebook. "Didi, you're not doing cards in this, are you?" She almost said no. Instead she picked out five cards, not ten, and read them aloud to the candle. It was boring. She did it anyway, then blew out the flame.

How much had Sarita's mock-test score moved?
By exactly two marks.
What does the voice telling Sarita to skip suggest about her mood?
She is bored and discouraged, so her mind bargains that one skipped day in the dark will not matter.
Why was doing five cards instead of ten a wise choice?
A smaller version kept the habit going on a hard, boring day, relying on discipline rather than mood.
What would change if Sarita had taken Sumit's hint and skipped?
The first skip could make the next one easier, and the routine might quietly fade.

For five weeks Uma had read the Tamil and English newspapers aloud on the thinnai at six every morning, preparing for the bank exam, while the milkman slowed his cycle to listen.
Then came the Pongal trip to Periyamma's village: three days of kolams, cooking and cousins, and no newspaper at all.
Back home in Tiruvarur, the pile of unread papers sat by the door. Uma walked past it on the first morning. And the second.
"Five weeks of work, and I broke it in three days," she told her older sister Jaya, who was stringing jasmine. "What's the use now? I'll start properly after the exam."
"The exam is in March, Uma."
Uma shrugged, the guilt sitting heavy under the shrug, and went inside. By the end of the week the papers had spread into a small, yellowing hill.

Where did Uma read the newspapers every morning?
On the thinnai at six every morning.
What does Uma's 'What's the use now?' reveal about how she sees the break?
She feels guilty and treats three days away as having ruined five weeks, so she thinks the routine may as well stop.
What small step could turn this slip around?
Uma could read just one paper aloud the next morning, counting the Pongal days as a pause rather than a failure, and let Jaya remind her of the five weeks already done.
How might Jaya feel watching the pile of papers grow?
Jaya, who gently pointed out that the exam is in March, may be worried to see her sister's hard work slip away over a short festival break.

In the small town of Sirsi, Rukmini had walked for forty minutes every morning for six weeks. Then her cousin's wedding came: four days of travel, late nights and no walks.
When she got home, she looked at her walking shoes by the door and felt a wave of guilt. "Six weeks, gone."
"Gone?" said her friend Urmila, who walked with her. "You missed four days."
"The streak's broken. What's the point now?"
The next morning she didn't go. Or the next. By the end of the week, the shoes had been pushed under the bench.
Urmila came by. "Rukmini, four missed days don't cancel six weeks. But four weeks will."

How long had Rukmini walked every morning before the wedding?
Six weeks.
What was Rukmini feeling when she looked at her walking shoes?
She felt guilty and defeated, as if missing four days had wiped out six weeks.
What turning point does Urmila offer?
Reminding Rukmini that a few missed days don't cancel the habit, so she can simply start again the next morning.
What might Urmila be feeling when she comes by?
Urmila seems concerned and a little frustrated, not wanting her friend to throw away six weeks of walking.

In Amman, Omar had practised English every evening for a month before his university exams, forty-five minutes with an app and a notebook. Then exam week hit. Five days, no practice.
When exams ended, he looked at the notebook on his desk. He felt a tight, guilty knot. Thirty days, and now a hole in the middle.
"You could start again tonight," his sister Mina said.
"What's the point? The streak's broken."
He didn't start that night. Or the next. After two weeks, Mina found the notebook under a pile of exam papers.
"You didn't lose a month, Omar," she said. "You lost five days. Then you chose to lose the rest."

How long had Omar practised before exam week?
A month.
What was Omar feeling when he looked at the notebook after exams?
He felt guilty and defeated, a tight knot, seeing the missed days as ruining everything.
What went wrong in Omar's thinking, and what could fix it?
He read five missed days as total failure; restarting the same night with a short session would have kept the habit alive.
How does Mina see Omar's stopping?
Mina sees it as a choice driven by all-or-nothing thinking, and seems frustrated and caring.

The college gym was nearly empty on Monday morning. Naveen, the trainer, looked up as Gopika walked past without stopping.
"Gopika! You haven't been in for ten days."
"I had the flu. Then I just... didn't come back."
"You were here every day for two months."
"Exactly. And then I broke it." She pulled her bag strap tighter. "It feels pointless now. Like I've already failed."
Naveen shook his head. "Missing days because you were ill isn't failing. Deciding it's all ruined, that's what stops people."
Gopika looked at the treadmills, then at the clock. "Maybe just fifteen minutes today?"
"Fifteen minutes is a comeback."

Why did Gopika first miss the gym?
She had the flu.
What was Gopika feeling when she said "Like I've already failed"?
She felt guilty and discouraged, believing the break had ruined her two months of effort.
What turning point does Naveen's comment create?
He separates the illness from failure, and Gopika agrees to a small fifteen-minute restart instead of quitting.
What might Naveen be feeling when he sees Gopika walk past?
Naveen is probably concerned and encouraging, wanting her back after two good months.

Gopika,
You asked about my sketching challenge. Honest answer: it's dead. I was at 41 days straight, one drawing every night, posting them in our little group. Then Chachu's wedding in Lucknow happened. Four days of haldi, sangeet and relatives in every room. No table, no quiet. I told myself I'd catch up on the train back. I didn't.
When I got home and saw the empty days in my sketchbook, I felt so guilty I shut it. The streak was already broken, so what was the point of drawing that night, or the next? That was nearly three weeks ago. The sketchbook is still under a pile of wedding sweet boxes.
The stupid thing is, I miss it. I just can't face starting again from day one.
Alka

How many days in a row had Alka sketched before the wedding?
41 days straight, one drawing every night.
Why did Alka shut the sketchbook after coming home?
Alka felt guilty and defeated seeing the empty days, and decided the streak was ruined anyway.
What could Alka try instead of starting again from day one?
Alka could do one small sketch tonight and count it as picking up, not restarting, so one trip does not end the habit.

Gopika may feel sympathetic and see what Alka cannot yet: four days away did not undo 41 days of drawing.

Francis slammed the door so hard the calendar fell off the wall.
'Whoa,' his sister Ankita said from the sofa. 'What happened?'
'Neil happened.' Francis threw his bag down. 'I told him ONE thing. About liking Sara. He swore he'd never tell. And today he put it in the class group. With a heart emoji. Everyone saw.'
'Oh no.'
'Everyone laughed when I walked in. Sara wouldn't even look at me.' His voice cracked. 'I want to punch the wall.'
'Punch a cushion instead,' Ankita said, handing him one. 'And be as angry as you need. He broke a promise. That's a real thing to be furious about.'
Francis sat down, cushion crushed against his chest. 'I've trusted him since Class 3.'
'I know,' she said. 'That's why it hurts this much.'

What did Neil put in the class group?
He put in that Francis liked Sara, with a heart emoji.
What is Francis feeling when his voice cracks?
He feels humiliated and furious, and underneath deeply hurt that a friend since Class 3 broke his promise.
Why is Ankita's response helpful at this first stage?
She treats his anger as a fair reaction to a broken promise, offers a safe outlet, and doesn't rush him to calm down or forgive.
What might Sara be experiencing after the post?
Sara may feel embarrassed and put on the spot, which may be why she wouldn't look at Francis.

It's been a month now, and I can finally write about it without my hands shaking.
I had told Madhav, and only Madhav, that my parents were fighting a lot and might separate. We were on his terrace, and he said, 'Your secret's safe, Darshan.'
Two days later, at the bus stop, a boy from 10C asked me, all fake-sad, 'Is it true your parents are divorcing?' Madhav was standing right there. He didn't even look embarrassed.
I remember the heat rising up my neck. I wanted to scream. I walked home fast instead and threw my cricket bat across the room so hard it left a mark on the wall.
Back then I thought being that angry meant something was wrong with me. Now I think it just meant something real had been broken.

Where was Darshan when a boy from 10C asked about the divorce?
Darshan was at the bus stop.
What was Darshan feeling as the heat rose up the neck?
Darshan felt rage and humiliation at the secret being exposed, made worse by Madhav standing there unbothered.
What insight about anger does Darshan reach looking back?
That the anger wasn't a flaw but a sign that something real had been broken, a healthy first response to betrayal.
What would have changed if Madhav had kept the secret?
Darshan could have had a safe place to talk about the fights at home, instead of feeling exposed and alone.

Nirmala,
I'm writing this and I'm probably never sending it.
I told you about Papa losing his job because you're my best friend. I told you in your room with the door shut, and you promised. And today at lunch Rohit said, loudly, "Hey Asif, heard your dad's selling vegetables now?" and everyone laughed. You were sitting right there. You went red and looked at your plate. So I know it was you.
I've never been this angry. My hands are still shaking as I write. I wanted to throw my tiffin across the canteen. I wanted the ground to open up. I felt like everyone could see right through me.
Mummy says anger means someone crossed a line. Well, you crossed it. You took the thing I trusted you with and handed it round like a joke.
I don't know what I'll say to you tomorrow. Right now I just need you to know how much it hurt.
Asif

What did Rohit say loudly at lunch?
Hey Asif, heard your dad's selling vegetables now?
What does Asif feel writing this letter?
Asif feels furious and humiliated, hands shaking, betrayed by a best friend who shared the secret.
What could Asif do with this anger tomorrow?
Treat it as a sign a boundary was crossed, calm down first, then tell Nirmala honestly how much it hurt, or talk it through with Mummy.
What might Nirmala be feeling when she goes red at lunch?
Nirmala likely feels ashamed and guilty, knowing she broke Asif's trust.

Abhinav bhaiya, stop laughing, it's not funny. Okay, fine, you think I'm overreacting. I'm not.
Megha was my best friend. Was. In March I told her that I still sleep with Bholu, my old stuffed elephant, when I'm stressed. I told her because I trusted her. Today, in the class group chat, she posted a photo of an elephant with "guess who can't sleep without this?" Thirty-two laughing replies.
I've never felt so small. I wanted to disappear. And then, on the bus, I felt something else: this huge hot anger, as if my chest was on fire. I've been angry for three hours.
Mummy says the anger is telling me something. That Megha crossed a line, and it's okay that it hurts.
So don't tell me to calm down. I'm Usha, and today I'm allowed to be furious. Tomorrow I'll decide what to do.

What is the name of Usha's stuffed elephant?
Bholu.
What was Usha feeling on the bus?
Usha felt a huge hot anger after the humiliation, as if her chest was on fire.
What is wise about Usha deciding to wait till tomorrow?
It honours the anger as a sign a boundary was crossed while giving time to cool before choosing how to respond.
How might Abhinav be seeing his sister's anger?
Abhinav may have found it funny at first, but is coming to see how hurt and humiliated his sister is.

Monday. Yogesh told Shankar, his closest friend since Class 3, that he was scared of deep water and had faked a cold to skip swimming. "Don't tell anyone," he said. Shankar crossed his heart.
Tuesday. At the pool, the PE teacher called Yogesh forward. Before he could speak, Shankar shouted from the bench, "Sir, he's scared of water!" The whole class turned. Someone made chicken noises. Yogesh's ears burned so hot he thought they'd catch fire.
Wednesday. He didn't speak to Shankar at all. When Shankar tried to sit beside him in maths, Yogesh moved desks. Rage buzzed in him all day, loud and bright. At home he punched his pillow until his arms ached.
Thursday. His grandmother found him scowling at dinner. "Angry?" she asked. He nodded. "Good," she said, surprising him. "It means you know you deserved better. Now eat, and tomorrow we'll think about what to say to him."

What did Shankar shout from the bench?
Sir, he's scared of water!
What was Yogesh feeling when the class made chicken noises?
He felt humiliated and furious, his ears burning, betrayed by his closest friend.
Why is the grandmother's response helpful?
She treats his anger as a healthy sign that he deserved better, then helps him plan what to say instead of acting on it.
What might Shankar feel when Yogesh moves desks?
Shankar may feel rejected and guilty, realising how badly his shout hurt his friend.

"Tanuja, your face is exactly like mine was at fifteen. Sit with your Zubin Mama and listen. My best friend then was Behram. We shared everything. One evening I told him I was scared of the dark, still, at fifteen. The next morning, the whole class was making ghost noises at me. Behram was laughing with them. I remember my ears burning, my hands shaking. I wanted to throw my geometry box at him. I didn't; I walked out and sat behind the school water tank until the bell. My mother found me angry at dinner and said, 'Good. You should be angry. He broke your trust.' That surprised me. I thought anger was wrong. It wasn't. It was telling me something important had been crossed. What I did with it came later. But the anger itself, beta, that was honest."

By telling Zubin his anger was right, his mother helped him see it as a sign that trust had been broken, not as something wrong with him.
How might Behram have felt when Zubin walked out?
Behram may have felt a flash of guilt or awkwardness, realising his joke had deeply hurt his best friend.

At the bus stand in Nabha, Madhuri waited with a bundle of stitched blouses for a shop in Patiala. Gurpreet, her school friend, came hurrying over with news: Simran from their class had bought a house in Canada. 'And us? Still here, still twenty-six,' Gurpreet groaned. Madhuri smiled. Two years ago that line would have ruined her week. Now she thought of her mother, who learnt to read at forty, and of Harbans uncle, who opened his tailoring shop at fifty. 'Simran's life is Simran's,' she said. 'Mine is slower.' In a notebook at home was a plan in three parts: this year, a second sewing machine; next year, a short design course in Patiala; after that, an apprentice. Each month she ticked what she had done, not what others had. The bus came, dusty and late. She climbed on without hurry.

What is the first part of Madhuri's plan?
This year, a second sewing machine.
Why doesn't Simran's news ruin Madhuri's week now?
She has come to accept that lives move at different speeds, remembering her mother and Harbans uncle, so she feels steady rather than behind.
What habit keeps Madhuri measuring progress on her own terms?
Each month she ticks off what she has done rather than what others have, which keeps her attention on her own plan.
How might Gurpreet feel hearing Madhuri's calm answer?
Gurpreet, still stung by Simran's news, may be surprised and perhaps a little comforted that Madhuri isn't worried about being behind.

The bench by the harbour in Cape Town was cold, and Tariq had his hands deep in his jacket.

"My cousin just made partner at a law firm," he said. "He's twenty-seven."

Zanele laughed softly. "I started nursing at thirty-one. Before that I cleaned offices for eight years."

"Do you ever feel late?"

"All the time, at first. Then I noticed the people I admired most had strange, crooked roads."

Tariq was quiet. He was twenty-six, three years into a job he half liked, and he'd started a night course in marine biology. At his pace it would take four years.

"Four years is fine," Zanele said. "Ask whether you're closer to the person you want to be. Not closer to your cousin."

He watched a fishing boat come in slowly. For the first time that week, slow didn't sound like failure.

At what age did Zanele start nursing?
Zanele started nursing at thirty-one.
What was Tariq feeling at the end, watching the fishing boat?
He felt calmer and more at peace, as slowness stopped feeling like failure.
What could Tariq do to keep this steadier view?
He could keep measuring each year of the night course against the kind of person he wants to become, rather than against his cousin's promotions.
How does Zanele see Tariq's worry about being late?
Zanele sees it with warmth and recognition, having felt the same, and wants him to judge his progress by his own values.

The evening college library smelt of old paper and floor polish. Chandrika, twenty-five, sat at the long table with a blank page and a pencil.

Rekha, who sat beside her in accounts class and was forty-four, peered over. "Planning your wedding?"

"Planning five years." Chandrika wrote a line across the top: 2025 to 2030. "Everyone from school already has everything. I kept making one-month plans and hating myself on the first of every month."

"And now?"

"Now I'm trying this." Under 2025: finish the diploma. 2026: move to a proper accounts job. 2027: maybe my own flat. Beside each year she wrote one word: honest, steady, independent.

Rekha tapped the page. "I got my first real job at thirty-nine. Nobody gave me a medal for being late, and nobody took one away either."

Chandrika laughed, and kept writing.

How old was Rekha?
Rekha was forty-four.
How can you tell Chandrika felt calmer with the five-year plan?
She laughed and kept writing, instead of hating herself as she had on the first of every month with her one-month plans.
Why might the words beside each year help Chandrika?
Words like honest, steady and independent let her measure progress by what she values, not by what her schoolmates already have.
If you were Rekha, what would you want Chandrika to take from your story?
You would want her to see that late starts are normal and that her path is worth walking at her own pace.

Dear Rukmini,

You asked in your last letter how I stopped panicking about being "so behind." I don't think I stopped completely. But it's quieter, so here's what I did.

Camila, sixteen, didn't open the school portal for three days after the chemistry grades went up in Madrid. "It'll be fine," she told herself, scrolling videos until midnight. On Thursday, in the library, she finally clicked. A three out of ten. She shut the laptop so fast it banged. For an hour she did nothing. Then she texted Nour, the one friend who never made a joke of things: "I got a 3 in chemistry." Nour replied within a minute: "Thank you for telling me. Want to talk after class?" They sat on the wall outside the school. Saying it again, out loud, felt less heavy. Together they wrote three lines in her notebook: see Señora Ruiz on Monday, redo the test questions, tell Papá on Sunday at lunch.

What grade did Camila get in chemistry?
A three out of ten.
Why did Camila avoid the portal for three days?
Not looking softened the shock and kept her dread away, even though it couldn't change the result.
Which choice helped Camila move from avoiding to acting?
Texting one trusted friend, Nour, and then writing a short plan of three steps together.
How might Nour have felt receiving Camila's text?
Nour probably felt trusted and wanted to help, replying quickly and kindly instead of making a joke.

Twenty-three out of seventy. In the school library in Srinagar, Zainab sat with her chemistry pre-board paper folded in her bag. For a week she'd told everyone it was "fine" and hadn't opened it. Today Avni sat down next to her. "You've been weird since the results." Zainab took a breath and said it out loud for the first time: "I failed chemistry." Her voice shook. Avni didn't gasp. She nodded. "Okay. What went wrong?" "Organic. All of it." They sat with that. Then Avni said, "Want to go to Mrs Qadri with me after lunch? She did extra classes last year." Zainab unfolded the paper. The red ink looked less huge on the table than it had in her head. After lunch, they went.

What mark did Zainab get in chemistry?
Twenty-three out of seventy.
Why did Zainab's voice shake when she said it aloud?
She felt scared and ashamed, and saying it to someone made the result real after a week of avoiding it.

Saying the fact aloud to one trusted person, Avni, first, then planning together to see the teacher.
How might Avni feel when Zainab finally tells her?
Avni might feel relieved that Zainab opened up, and eager to help without making her feel worse.

Subject: I have to tell someone

Yamini didi,

I'm telling you first because you won't freak out. I got 11 out of 40 in the maths unit test. There. I wrote it.

11 out of 40.

Vishal, you asked how I got my weekends back. Okay. For two years my head said the same thing every Sunday: you should be more productive. You should be learning to code, you should be at the gym, you should be doing the side project. I'd say it and then lie on the bed feeling guilty and doing nothing. Then my cousin said something annoying and true: 'Rajni, nobody runs towards a should.' So I tried an experiment. Instead of 'I should be productive', I said, 'I'd like to get a bit more done, and today that means one thing: thirty minutes on the side project after lunch.' That's it. One sentence, one step. It felt almost too small. But I did the thirty minutes. Then I did it the next Sunday. The guilt got quieter. I finished the thing in March.

How long was the step Rajni set for the side project?
Thirty minutes on the side project after lunch.
Why did 'you should be more productive' leave Rajni doing nothing?
The should felt like a demand with blame attached, so Rajni felt guilty and stuck instead of motivated; the pressure used up the energy it was meant to create.
What made Rajni's new sentence work where the old one failed?
'I'd like to get a bit more done' invited instead of scolding, and pairing it with one small, timed step gave Rajni something doable, so action replaced guilt.
How might the cousin feel hearing the project was finished in March?
The cousin would likely feel pleased 😊 that one annoying but true line helped Rajni move from guilt to a finished project.

I'm Shankar. Madhav and I have shared a flat in Pune for two years, so I know his Sunday routine: a groan, then 'I should clean, I should study for the CA exam, I should call home,' and then four hours on his phone. Last month something changed, and I'm only guessing at why. He stuck a small card on the fridge. It said: 'I'd like to be on top of things. Today: one chapter, before lunch.' Just that. That Sunday he read one chapter at the dining table with his earphones in. The next week the card said: 'I'd like the flat to feel nice. Today: the kitchen only.' He did the kitchen. I don't know what's going on inside his head, but the groan has stopped, and last Sunday he asked if I wanted chai while he worked.

Where did Madhav stick the card?
Madhav stuck the card on the fridge.

It suggests Madhav feels less guilty and weighed down; a wish with one step may feel like an invitation, while the old list of shoulds felt like a pile of blame.

It is small, specific and timed, so Madhav can start and finish it, instead of facing a vague demand that makes him avoid everything.

Shankar has gone from watching four hours of phone after a groan to being offered chai while Madhav works, so the flat feels calmer for Shankar too, even without knowing exactly why.

Monday: Lakshmi's to-do list at the bank branch began with 'I MUST be more productive', underlined twice. By four she had answered emails, reorganised her drawer and done none of the loan files. She felt sick with guilt on the bus home.
Thursday: Sangeeta, at the next desk, glanced at the list. 'Must? Who's shouting at you?' Lakshmi laughed, then didn't. That night she rewrote the top line: 'I'd like to clear the Kulkarni file. First step: check the land papers, 10 a.m.'
The next Monday: By 10:40 the land papers were checked. The Kulkarni file went to the manager before lunch. Lakshmi crossed it out, wrote the next wish and its first step, and noticed she wasn't underlining anything any more.

'I MUST be more productive' was underlined twice.
Why did Lakshmi feel sick with guilt on the bus home on Monday?
The 'must' set a demand she hadn't met, so every avoided loan file felt like a personal failure, even though she had been busy all day.
What change to the list was the turning point?
Rewriting the demand as 'I'd like to clear the Kulkarni file' with a first step at 10 a.m. gave Lakshmi a clear place to start, and the file was done before lunch.
What did Sangeeta notice that prompted 'Who's shouting at you?'
Sangeeta saw that the capital MUST read like someone shouting orders, and may have guessed the pressure was hurting Lakshmi more than helping.

Yamini, I see you've written "SHOULD WORK HARDER" on your monitor in red. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age at this same office.

At twenty-five, Ramesh here was a skinny young man with a notebook that said, on every page: "You must be more productive." Every evening I read it and felt like a failure. The more I read it, the less I did. I'd sit at my desk feeling guilty and then go home having done nothing but feel guilty.

One day my old boss, Mrs D'Costa, read it over my shoulder. She said, "Who wants to work for someone who shouts at them all day? Not even you."

So I changed one line. "I'd like to be more productive. Today: finish the Kolhapur file before tea."

It sounds silly. But I finished the file. And the next day I wrote another small one.

So maybe, Yamini, take off the red note. Try "I'd like to" and one thing.

What did Ramesh change his notebook line to?
"I'd like to be more productive. Today: finish the Kolhapur file before tea."
Why did reading "You must be more productive" every evening make Ramesh do less?
The demand made him feel like a failure, and the guilt drained his energy instead of pushing him forward. It felt like being shouted at, which made starting harder.
Why did the new wording work better than the old one?
"I'd like to" invited rather than ordered, and the one concrete step before tea was easy to start. Finishing it lowered the guilt and led to another step the next day.
How might Yamini feel hearing Ramesh's story about the red note?
Yamini may feel a little embarrassed that the note was noticed, but also relieved that a senior once felt the same. The story offers a kinder way to push without shame.

The construction next door started at eight every morning, drilling through the wall of Sonali's one-room flat in Indore. She was a freelance translator with three pending jobs and a head that kept saying: You should be more productive. You should have finished these yesterday.

By noon on Monday she had done nothing but feel guilty and sweep the drill dust off her desk twice.

Saurabh, her husband, came home for lunch and found her staring at a blank screen. "Bad day?"

"I should be faster. I should be better at this."

He handed her a sticky note. "Try another word."

She thought, then wrote: "I'd like to be more productive. Next step: translate one page before the drilling stops at two."

With earplugs in and the note stuck on the laptop, she did one page. Then, while it was still quiet, half of another.

It wasn't three jobs. But it was a start, and the guilt was quieter than the drill.

When did the drilling stop?
At two.
How was Sonali feeling by noon on Monday, and what shows it?
She was stuck and guilty, which shows in her staring at a blank screen after sweeping the dust twice. The shoulds made her feel behind without helping her start.
What small change helped Sonali start working?
Swapping "I should" for "I'd like to" and naming one step, one page before two. The kinder wording plus a clear, small target made action easier than guilt.
What might Saurabh have noticed when he found Sonali staring at the blank screen?
Saurabh probably saw she was stuck, not lazy, and that the shoulds weren't helping. Offering a sticky note instead of advice let her find her own wording.

Every Sunday she looked at it, felt a wave of guilt, and then somehow spent the afternoon sorting her phone photos. Today Anjali, passing with a bucket of wet clothes, tapped it. It said I SHOULD BE MORE PRODUCTIVE.

It made her feel guilty and like rubbish every Sunday, and because it demanded without offering a step, the guilt led to avoiding work, not doing it.

It turned a demand into a wish plus one small, concrete step, 25 minutes on the introduction, which lowered the guilt and made starting easy.

Counsellor's note, employee support, 14 May.

Farhan, 25, came in exhausted and guilty. His notebook has a line he reads every morning: "I should be more productive." He says it makes him feel worse, not better; by noon he has usually decided he has failed again.

We worked on the wording. I asked what he wants, not what he should do. He said, "I'd like to finish the client report before lunch." Then we added one concrete step: "Open the report at 9.30 and write the first section."

He looked doubtful. "That's it? No should?"

We agreed he would try the new sentence for a week and note how he feels at noon.

Update, 21 May: he opened the report at 9.30 on five out of five days. He says the guilt is "quieter", and he finished the report on Thursday.

Sharmila

Farhan read, "I should be more productive."

Let's see how the week goes.

Yamini

Pradeep had twelve minutes before the night bus to the depot, and his dal was still too hot to eat fast. That was when Siddharth, fifteen, put down his spoon. 'Papa, why do we fast on Ekadashi? If God is everywhere, why would God want us hungry?' Pradeep's first thought was to snap that some things aren't questioned. His second was of his own father, who had never let him ask anything. He blew on the dal. 'What's made you think about it?' Siddharth talked fast: a book from the school library, a friend who fasts in Ramzan, a video about why people fast at all. Pradeep checked the clock and felt his chest tighten, and something else too, something like pride. 'I have to go. Sunday, you and me, tea and this question. Keep the book for me.'

How long did Pradeep have before the night bus?
Twelve minutes.
What mix of feelings did Pradeep have as Siddharth talked?
He felt uneasy, his chest tightening at a custom being questioned, but also proud of how Siddharth was thinking.
Why did asking 'What's made you think about it?' work better than snapping?
It let Siddharth explain his reasons and kept him talking, leaving the door open for Sunday instead of shutting the topic.
What is it like for Siddharth when Papa asks a question instead of snapping?
Siddharth feels safe enough to pour out what he has been reading, and may trust Papa more with hard questions.

Read this:

'Why is it a duty, though?' Varun asked, halfway through the rotis. 'You say I'll run the shop because Dada ran it. That's not a reason, it's a history.' Sumit felt the words land somewhere under his ribs. Thirty years behind that counter in Lajpat Nagar, and his son had just called it history. His wife glanced at him. He wanted to say, 'Because I said so.' Instead he put his roti down. 'All right. Tell me what you'd want instead.' Varun blinked, as if he'd been ready for a fight. He talked about design, about fabrics he'd seen online, about a course in Ahmedabad. Sumit listened, worried about the shop, and quietly astonished at how well the boy argued. 'Come to the shop after school tomorrow,' he said. 'Show me what you mean.'

Where is the family shop?
In Lajpat Nagar.
What was Sumit feeling when Varun called the shop 'a history'?
He felt hurt and unsettled, the words landing under his ribs, and worried about what would become of the shop.
What did Sumit's choice to listen first make possible?
Varun talked instead of fighting, Sumit heard about the design idea, and they agreed to meet at the shop the next day.
Why might Varun have blinked when Sumit asked what he'd want?
Varun expected an argument or a flat no, so being asked was surprising and probably a relief.

Read this:

'Papa, do you actually believe in rebirth?'
Kamal paused with the pickle jar. 'Why?'
'We learned how memory works in biology. If memories are in the brain, what's left to be reborn?'
'Your Dadi believed it all her life.'
'I know. I'm not saying she was wrong. I'm asking what you think.'
Kamal set the jar down. Nobody had asked him that. Not even himself, not in years.
'I can't argue it like your biology teacher,' he said slowly. 'But tell me the whole thing. Properly.'
'Seriously?'
'Seriously. Then I'll tell you why Dadi believed it, and you can argue with that too.'
Yash grinned. 'Deal.'
Kamal's stomach was still tight. But the boy was thinking. That, he had to admit, felt good.

What had Yash learned about in biology?
How memory works.
Why was Kamal's stomach still tight even as he agreed to listen?
He felt unsettled that a belief his mother held all her life was being questioned, while quietly proud that the boy was thinking.
What did Kamal's 'tell me the whole thing' do for their talk?
It turned a possible fight into an exchange, where Yash explains and then hears why Dadi believed, keeping the door open.
What might Yash feel when Papa says 'Seriously'?
Yash seems surprised and pleased, grinning, glad to be taken seriously instead of told off.

Read this:

Last Karva Chauth, my daughter Mehak, sixteen, put down her spoon and asked her mother, "Why do only women fast for their husbands? Why doesn't Papa fast for you?" I'm Yogesh, her father, and I felt the room tilt. My first urge was to say, "Because that's how it is." My chest felt tight; I worried she was throwing away everything we'd taught her. But I also felt a strange pride. It was a sharp question. So I didn't answer straight away. I asked, "What makes you ask?" She talked for twenty minutes about fairness. I listened. At the end I said, "I don't have a perfect answer. Maybe I'll fast next year too." She laughed. Now she brings her questions to me first.

On which occasion did Mehak ask her question?
On Karva Chauth, at dinner.
How did Yogesh feel when Mehak asked why only women fast?
He felt unsettled and anxious, his chest tight, but also proud of her sharp question.
What did Yogesh do that kept the door open?
He listened first by asking what made her ask, heard her out for twenty minutes and admitted he didn't have a perfect answer.
How might Mehak see her father now?
Mehak seems to see him as someone safe to question, since she now brings her questions to him first.

Read this:

"You're always watching," Tanuja said, bouncing the ball near the bench. "Want to play dodgeball?"
Jatin shrugged. "Nobody asked."
"I'm asking now."
"What if I get out first? What if I throw wrong and everyone laughs?"
"Then you get out first. I got out first yesterday. Nobody cared."
Jatin looked at the circle of shouting kids. "I don't know the rules properly."
"Stand next to me. I'll tell you as we go."
"Just one round?"
"Just one."
He stood, wiped his hands on his shorts and followed her. At the end of the round he was still in, grinning. "Again?"

What did Tanuja say happened to her yesterday?
She got out first yesterday.
What was Jatin worried about before joining?
He worried he'd get out first or throw wrong and everyone would laugh.
What bridge did Tanuja offer, and why did it work?
She invited him, let him stand next to her and promised to explain the rules, making the first step small and safe.
How might Tanuja feel when Jatin asks "Again?"
She may feel glad and a little proud that her invitation worked.

messages.content:
Read this:

All through Class 5, I watched the lane cricket from our gate. I knew every player's name and who bowled fast. I wanted to play so badly that I practised bowling against our wall at night. But I never asked. I was sure I'd say something stupid, or they'd say no, and then I'd have to walk past them every day. Then Vijay, who lived two houses down, came to the gate one evening. "You're the one who bowls against the wall, na? We need a bowler." I followed, heart thudding. My first ball was a wide. Nobody laughed. My third ball took a wicket. Now I'm in Class 6. I still get nervous sometimes, but I ask. "Can I bat next?" It gets easier every time.
Ramesh

Where did Ramesh practise bowling at night?
Against the wall at home, at night.
What worried Ramesh about asking to play?
Ramesh was sure of saying something stupid or being refused, and then having to walk past the players every day.
What turning point came when Vijay came to the gate?
Vijay invited Ramesh as a needed bowler, a friendly bridge; after that, with practice, asking got easier.
How might the other players have seen Ramesh after the wicket?
They may have seen a useful new bowler, not the quiet kid at the gate.

Monday. At recess Tenzin stood by the wall with a tennis ball in his pocket, watching the football game. He practised the words in his head: Can I play? He didn't say them.
Wednesday. Rehana, who sat beside him in class, jogged over. 'We need a goalkeeper. Want to?' Tenzin nodded before he could think. He saved one shot and laughed too loudly, then worried all afternoon that he'd looked silly.
The next Monday. Tenzin walked up to the game himself. His heart thumped. 'Can I play?' 'Obviously,' said Rehana. 'Goal's yours.'

What did Tenzin keep in his pocket?
A tennis ball.
What was Tenzin worried about on Wednesday afternoon?
He felt anxious that laughing too loudly had made him look silly.
What helped Tenzin ask to play by the next Monday?
Rehana's friendly invitation gave him a safe first go, and that practice made asking for himself feel possible.
Why might Rehana have invited Tenzin?
Rehana may have noticed him watching by the wall and guessed he wanted to join but was waiting to be asked.

metadata.subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Damini, you think you're the only one who waits at the edge? When your Sangeeta Mausi was ten, in Nashik, the girls played kho-kho every evening on the temple ground. I wanted to play so badly my feet itched. But I sat under the neem tree, pretending to read, waiting for someone to call me. I kept thinking, what if I run the wrong way, what if they laugh? A whole month of evenings. Then a girl called Kusum walked over and dropped her dupatta in my lap. 'Hold this for me, and then you're on my team.' I played badly that day. Nobody laughed. By Diwali I was the one calling the new girls in.

Where did Sangeeta sit while the girls played?
Under the neem tree, pretending to read.
What was young Sangeeta worried about?
She was anxious that she would run the wrong way and the girls would laugh.
What turning point let Sangeeta join the game?
Kusum walking over, handing her the dupatta and putting her on the team, a friendly bridge into the game.
Why might Kusum have walked over?
Kusum probably noticed Sangeeta watching every evening and guessed she wanted to play.

metadata.subtype: Wanting to join but holding back [Actor]

messages.content:
Read this:

Jaya had joined the school in November, halfway through the year, and on the first rainy day recess moved indoors. Four girls were playing carrom at the back table, laughing. Jaya wanted to play so much it ached. But all four seats were taken, and what would she even say? 'Can I have next game?' sounded pushy; 'I'm good at carrom' sounded like showing off. She sat at her desk sharpening a pencil that was already sharp. Irawati, striker in hand, looked up. 'You play?' Jaya's cheeks went hot. 'A little.' Irawati shifted her chair. 'Squeeze in, be my partner. I'm terrible at the red.' Jaya perched on the edge of the chair. By the end of recess she had pocketed the red twice, and said four whole sentences.

What was Jaya doing while the others played?
Sharpening a pencil that was already sharp.
What was Jaya worried about before Irawati spoke?
She was anxious that anything she said would sound pushy or like showing off.
What made Irawati's invitation work so well?
It was casual and made room without pressure, and asking Jaya to be her partner offered a friendly bridge into the game.
What might Irawati have noticed about Jaya?
Irawati may have noticed the new girl watching the game and guessed she wanted to join.

messages.content:
Read this:

Every evening the colony kids played seven stones in the lane behind Block C. Ganga watched from the steps with her chin on her knees.
She knew the rules by heart. She even knew Pinky always aimed too high. But what if she asked and they said no? What if she threw and missed everything?
On Thursday the ball rolled right to her feet. She held it, heart thumping.
Harish jogged over. "Good catch. You want to play? We need one more on our side."
Ganga nodded, cheeks hot. Her first throw missed. Harish just said, "Next one."
Her second throw knocked down three stones. Nobody made a big fuss. They just yelled, "Run!" and she ran.
The next evening, she walked straight down from the steps.

Where did the colony kids play seven stones?
In the lane behind Block C.
What was Ganga worried about while she watched?
She felt anxious that they would say no if she asked, or that she would throw and miss everything.
What did Harish do that made it easier for Ganga to join?
He invited her with a simple reason, "We need one more on our side," and when she missed he just said "Next one" instead of teasing.
What would change if nobody had invited Ganga?
She might have kept watching from the steps, longing to play but waiting, and her worry about saying or doing the wrong thing could have grown.
