messages.content:
Read this:

All day at school Preeti ran her lines: raise the eyebrows when Tanya talks, say "No way!" at the right pause, laugh a beat after the others. She had written them in the back of her rough book. By the time the auto dropped her at the colony gate, her jaw ached. Inside, she didn't say hello. She dropped her bag, lay on the cool floor under the dining table and pulled her dupatta over her face. Nirmala, her mother, came from the kitchen, saw her, and asked nothing. She switched off the tube light, stopped the mixer halfway through the chutney and set a glass of water by Preeti's hand. An hour later a small voice came from under the table. "Mummy, can I just be weird this evening?" "Be exactly you," Nirmala said.

Where had Preeti written her lines?
In the back of her rough book.
How did Preeti feel by the time she got home, and what shows it?
She was drained and overwhelmed; her jaw ached, she didn't say hello, and she lay under the table with her dupatta over her face.
Which choices by Nirmala gave Preeti a place to rest?
She asked nothing, switched off the light, stopped the noisy mixer and left water nearby, then told Preeti to be exactly herself.
How might the evening have gone if Nirmala had demanded to know what was wrong?
Preeti might have shut down further or broken down, because she had no energy left to explain.

Read this:

"You were great at the fest, man. Everyone laughed at your jokes." "They weren't my jokes, Hemant. I practised them from a video. Forty times." "Seriously?" "And I watched how Rishi laughs and copied the timing. Head back, two seconds." "Why would you do that?" "Because when I laugh my way, people stare." Farhan pulls his hood over his eyes. "I've got nothing left. My face hurts from making faces." Ammi's voice from the doorway: "Farhan, the room's dark, the fan's on low. No dinner talk tonight unless you want it." "Thanks, Ammi." "Should I go?" Hemant asks. "Stay. Just don't need me to talk." "Fine by me. I'll read. And you don't have to do the Rishi laugh here." A snort comes from under the hood: Farhan's own laugh, crooked and short.

How many times did Farhan practise the jokes?
Forty times.
Why does Farhan copy Rishi's laugh?
He is afraid of being stared at, because when he laughs his own way, people stare.
What choice helped Farhan rest after the fest?
Ammi kept the room dark and quiet with no dinner talk, and Hemant stayed without needing him to talk.
What is it like for Hemant to learn the jokes were practised?
Hemant is surprised, since the fest looked easy for Farhan, but then understands and offers him a place to be himself.

Read this:

Looking back at ninth grade, I can see how hard I worked just to seem normal. I studied the way Arohi laughed at lunch and copied the timing. I practised faces in the bathroom mirror: surprised, interested, bored. I had lines ready for every conversation, like "same, yaar" and "no way." Everybody said I was fun. Then I'd get home and could not speak at all. I'd lie on the floor of my room in the dark, and sometimes I cried for no reason I could name. My mother would put a glass of water by the door and say, "No questions today, Joseph." That door was the first place I could stop acting. I think it saved that whole year.

Where did Joseph practise faces?
Joseph practised faces in the bathroom mirror: surprised, interested, bored.
How did Joseph feel after school, and what shows it?
Joseph felt completely drained and exhausted from acting, unable to speak and lying on the floor in the dark, sometimes crying.
Why did the mother's approach help?
Joseph's mother left water and asked no questions, so home became a place where Joseph could rest without having to perform.
How might Arohi see Joseph at lunch?
Arohi probably saw Joseph as fun and easy company, without knowing how much effort the copied laughter took.

Read this:

Note for the school counsellor, from Anand's mother, Himani.
Anand, fifteen, comes home from school every day looking cheerful at the gate. His teachers say he jokes with everyone. But the moment he is inside he drops his bag, sits on the floor and rocks, sometimes for an hour. If I ask even one question, he shouts or goes silent. Yesterday he said, "I copy what the others do all day. I'm so tired of being someone else." I have set up a corner with a mat and dim light where no one talks to him until dinner. Could the school give him a quiet place at lunch too? I would like to meet you this week.

How long does Anand sometimes rock after coming home?
He sometimes rocks for an hour.
How does Anand feel about copying others all day?
He feels deeply tired and worn out by pretending, saying he is so tired of being someone else.
What did Himani do next that could help Anand?
She set up a quiet corner at home where no one talks to him until dinner, and asked the counsellor for a quiet place at lunch and a meeting.
How might the school counsellor see Anand after reading this note?
The counsellor may realise that the cheerful boy at school is using a lot of energy to fit in, and look for ways to lower that strain.

Read this:

Friday night.
Class party today. I had my lines ready: "Nice shirt." "Haha, true." I copied Tejas every time he laughed, a half-second late. I kept my face moving. Nobody noticed anything. I think I did it perfectly.
In the auto home my hands started shaking. At home I couldn't answer when Papa asked about dinner. I went into my room and sat inside the cupboard with the door half shut. Everything was too loud, even the fan.
Papa didn't push. He left a cup of tea on the desk and said through the door, "I'm just outside if you want." That's all.
I came out at ten. We watched cricket without talking. It was the first easy hour all day.
Saurabh

Where did Saurabh sit after coming home?
Saurabh sat inside the cupboard with the door half shut.
How did Saurabh feel after the party, and what are the signs?
Saurabh felt exhausted and overwhelmed; hands shook in the auto, answering Papa was impossible and even the fan felt too loud.
What did Papa get right after Saurabh came home?
He did not push or ask questions; he left tea and said he was just outside, which gave Saurabh room to rest.
What was the party like for Tejas, compared with Saurabh?
Tejas was probably just enjoying himself, unaware that Saurabh was copying his laughs and working hard all evening.

Read this:

Neelam: Didi, are you home?
Ishita: Yes, in the kitchen. How was school?
Neelam: I did Riya's laugh all day. Practised the "haha omg" face in the mirror at lunch.
Neelam: Said "same" to everything.
Ishita: That sounds tiring.
Neelam: I'm SO tired. I'm going to come home and I can't talk. Please don't ask me anything. Please.
Ishita: Okay. Your room is dark, fan's on, headphones are on the bed. No questions till you're ready.
Neelam: Mummy will ask about the test.
Ishita: I'll tell her later. You don't have to perform here.
Neelam: Thank you.
Neelam: Can we just watch the train videos after dinner? Without talking?
Ishita: Yes. Silent train videos. Our thing.

What did Neelam practise in the mirror at lunch?
The "haha omg" face.
How is Neelam feeling on the way home?
Neelam feels completely exhausted and anxious about being asked to talk after a whole day of copying others to fit in.
What did Ishita do that could help anyone in Neelam's place?
She prepared a quiet, dark room, kept questions away and made home a place where Neelam doesn't have to perform.
If you were Ishita, what might you want Neelam to know?
That it is safe to be natural at home, and that loving Neelam doesn't depend on the laughs and faces used at school.

Read this:

Home-visit notes, community nurse, Thursday.
Visited Mr Dave, bedridden since spring. His daughter Hansa has been the main carer. Last month she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks. Today there was a change. Her son Jagdish, who works in the city, has made a chart on the fridge: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines, with his sister and a cousin on it too. He asked me directly whether Hansa was eating properly and whether the bathroom was safe for her at night. He admitted he had skipped his own badminton for a month and was getting snappy. We agreed he would keep Wednesday evenings for himself.
What I did next: I gave the family the number of the carers' support group, and booked a doctor's check-up for Hansa next week.

What did Jagdish put on the fridge?
A chart: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines.
How had Hansa been feeling last month, and what showed it?
Exhausted; she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks.
Why was keeping Wednesday evenings for himself a wise choice for Jagdish?
He had skipped badminton and was getting snappy; protecting some time for himself guards against burnout so he can keep helping.
How might Hansa feel seeing her son's chart and questions?
She may feel relieved and cared for, no longer carrying every night turn alone.

Read this:

Saturday night.
Came home at seven and found Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove. I realised I couldn't remember the last time I'd seen her eat lunch. She keeps saying, "Thakuma needs me, I'm fine," but she's snapping at everyone and forgetting her own headache tablets.
So tonight I did three things. I heated the dal and sat with her until she'd eaten it. I called Mashi and asked her to take Sundays with Thakuma; she said yes straight away, sounding almost relieved to be asked. And I booked Ma an appointment with Dr Sen for Tuesday, for the headaches and the tiredness.
I also nearly cancelled my trek with Charu next month. Then I pictured both Ma and me burnt out. I'm keeping it.
Bidisha

What did Bidisha find when coming home at seven?
Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove.
What worried Bidisha about Ma?
Bidisha was worried because Ma was sleeping sitting up, skipping lunch, snapping at everyone and forgetting her own tablets.
Why was keeping the trek with Charu a wise choice?
Bidisha saw that giving up everything would lead to both Ma and Bidisha burning out, which would help nobody.
How might Mashi see being asked to take Sundays?
She sounded almost relieved, perhaps glad to be allowed to help instead of watching from the side.

Read this:

Vikas: Ma sounded so tired on the phone. Since Papa's stroke she's doing everything alone
Tenzin: is she sleeping?
Vikas: she says 4 hours. she eats standing up
Tenzin: that can't go on. she'll burn out
Vikas: I feel guilty I'm not there all the time
Tenzin: you can't be. but we can plan
Tenzin: what if you take weekends, and your cousin covers Wednesdays?
Vikas: and I'll ask Papa's doctor about a home nurse and a counsellor for Ma
Tenzin: yes. and you keep your Thursday badminton. you need it too
Vikas: feels selfish
Tenzin: it isn't. if you burn out, who helps her then?
Vikas: ok. calling Ma now to check she's eaten

How many hours does Ma say she sleeps?
Four hours.
How does Vikas feel about not being there all the time?
Vikas feels guilty, and even a little selfish about keeping badminton.
What makes the plan wise?
It checks on Ma's sleep and meals, shares tasks with a cousin, seeks a home nurse and counsellor, and protects Vikas's own time.
How might Tenzin see Vikas's badminton?
Tenzin sees it as necessary self-care, not selfishness, because burnout would help nobody.

Read this:

Avni, twenty-five, came home to the village for the weekend and found her mother, Manjula, asleep sitting up beside Dadi's bed at noon. Dadi now forgot names and wandered at night. Ma had grown thin and snappish. Avni checked the kitchen: no proper meal cooked in days. That evening she made rice and dal, sat Ma down and made sure she ate. "Ma, you can't do nights alone any more." She called her cousin Sunita, who agreed to stay two nights a week. She walked to the health centre and asked the doctor about help for Dadi and for Ma's exhaustion. On Monday morning Avni took the bus back to her job. "I'll call every evening, and come every second weekend," she promised. Ma hugged her hard.

What did Avni cook for her mother?
Rice and dal.
How did Avni feel seeing her mother asleep sitting up at noon?
She felt worried and concerned, seeing how exhausted Ma had become.
What did Avni do that cared for the caregiver wisely?
She made sure Ma ate, arranged her cousin to share nights, sought the health centre doctor's help and kept her own job with regular check-ins.
How might Manjula feel when Avni leaves on Monday?
Manjula may feel supported and less alone, knowing help is arranged and Avni will call every evening.

Read this:

In Lagos, Nkechi, twenty-six, noticed her father looked grey with tiredness. Since her mother's hip surgery, he had done everything: cooking, lifting, medicines at midnight. He said he was fine, but he'd lost his appetite and dozed at the table. Nkechi talked to her brother Omar. "We check on him, not just on Mum." They made a rota: Omar took mornings, Nkechi evenings. She asked the hospital social worker about a home nurse for two afternoons a week, and got Dad to see his own doctor about his sleep. And she didn't cancel her Saturday football. "If I collapse too, Dad has two patients," she told Omar. On Sunday, her father slept till nine for the first time in a month.

Who is Nkechi's brother?
Omar.
How did Nkechi feel noticing her father's tiredness?
She felt worried and protective, seeing he was grey, not eating and dozing.
What steps did Nkechi and Omar take to care for their father?
They made a rota, got help from the hospital social worker for a home nurse, took Dad to his doctor and Nkechi protected her own time.
How might Nkechi's father feel after sleeping till nine?
He likely feels rested and relieved that the load is finally shared.

Read this:

The visitors' room at the Ernakulam day-care centre for older people was quiet at four. Binita watched her father, Thomas, sign out Ammachi, his hands trembling. For two years he had cared for his mother alone since her memory began to fail.
"Pappa, when did you last sleep a full night?" Binita asked.
He laughed tiredly. "What is full?"
"Have you eaten today?"
"Tea."
Binita took the bag from him. She'd been noticing for weeks. That evening she made a list. She would take Ammachi on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Her brother would pay for a night helper twice a week. She asked the centre's social worker about a caregivers' support group and booked Pappa a check-up with his own doctor.
But she kept her Thursday evenings for her dance class. "If I burn out, Pappa, we both fall," she told him. He nodded, and for the first time didn't argue.

Which evenings did Binita keep for herself?
Her Thursday evenings, for her dance class.
How was Thomas feeling after two years of caring alone?
He felt exhausted and worn down, not sleeping properly and barely eating, with trembling hands.
What did Binita get right as a family member helping the caregiver?
She checked his sleep and meals, shared tasks with her brother, sought professional support and a check-up, and protected her own life to avoid burnout.
How might Ammachi's days change with Binita's plan?
She would still be cared for, but by a less exhausted son and a wider circle, which may make her days calmer and safer.

Read this:

"So then the senior grabbed my bag," Kiran said, "and I just stared him down."
"Last week you said you pushed him," said Madhav.
"I did push him. A bit. After staring."
"And yesterday there were three seniors."
The others laughed. Kiran's face went hot. "There were three. Two were just watching."
On the way to the bus Madhav said quietly, "Kiran, I was there. He asked for his bag strap back, you gave it, and we walked off. That's it."
"Everyone was listening," Kiran said. "If I tell it like that, it's boring."
"But you have to remember which version you told to who. Doesn't that get tiring?"
Kiran didn't answer, just kicked a stone all the way to the bus stop.

What did Madhav say really happened with the senior?
Madhav said the senior asked for his bag strap back, Kiran gave it, and they walked off.
How did Kiran feel when the others laughed, and why does the story keep growing?
Kiran felt embarrassed, face going hot, and keeps making the story bigger out of worry that the plain version would seem boring to everyone listening.
What could Kiran try the next time the group asks about the fight?
Kiran could tell the plain version with a joke, trusting that people like Madhav value an honest story over a dramatic one.
What is it like for Madhav to hear the story change each time?
Madhav, who was there, finds it awkward and tiring, and cares enough to point out the cost privately rather than in front of everyone.

Read this:

I'm Rajni, and in Class 10 I became someone who couldn't just say a number. In the prelims I got 78 in maths. When Pooja's group asked, I said 88. By lunch it had become 90, "but the teacher cut marks unfairly". On the group call that night, it was 92.
The worst part wasn't the lie. It was the remembering. I had to keep track of which person had heard which version, and once I caught myself saying 88 to someone who had heard 92. My stomach dropped.
When the real mark sheets were put up, Pooja saw mine. She didn't say anything cruel. She just said, "You didn't need to." Looking back, the 78 would have been fine. It was the 92 I couldn't carry.

What mark did Rajni actually get in maths in the prelims?
Rajni got 78 in maths in the prelims.
What does Rajni's stomach dropping suggest?
It suggests fear of being caught, because keeping track of different versions for different people had become stressful.
What went wrong, and what could Rajni have done differently?
Each retelling pushed the number higher until it couldn't be kept straight; saying 78 honestly at the start would have been far easier to carry.
How might Pooja have felt when she saw the real mark sheet?

When I was fifteen, a senior pushed me in the school corridor. I pushed him back. That's all. Two pushes.

Then, one afternoon, the senior himself walked up to our group and said, "Tell them what really happened." I couldn't even remember which version I'd told to whom. My mouth went dry. My friends slowly drifted away.
That flowerbed, beta, was the heaviest thing I ever carried.

The school bus back from the science exhibition was loud, hot, and stuck in traffic. Asif was squeezed next to Madhav in the back row with four other boys.
"So what did you get in the half-yearly?" one of them asked.
"Ninety-five in maths," Asif said. He had said ninety-two last week, to a different group. The real number was seventy-eight.
"Ninety-five? Show us," Madhav said, grinning. "Your mum sends the marks screenshot to everyone's parents anyway."

He tried to remember what else he'd said. Had he told Madhav ninety-two, or eighty-nine? The bus lurched. The other boys were waiting.
Asif took a breath. "Actually, it's seventy-eight," he said, too loudly over the horns. "I kept adding numbers."
There was a pause. Then Madhav shrugged. "Seventy-eight's fine, man. I got sixty-one."

At the Saturday sleepover in Aparna's flat in Andheri, the girls lay in a row on the mattress, and Sonali told the story again.

Baljeet

Mehak, you asked how I finally decided about the bakery. For three years I said, "Next season it'll pick up." Every season I said it. I'm Pema, Nazia's flatmate. For three weeks, Nazia came home saying the same thing: "My new manager hates me." He didn't say good morning. He gave the big client to someone else. He frowned at her report.

Indu, you think everyone at your office is against you? Sit. Your Ojas Mama believed the same thing once.
I was twenty-five, at my first design firm. I was sure the seniors laughed at my work. If two people whispered, it was about me. If my drawing was sent back, it proved it.

It's me, she thought. I'm just not good enough. I should work weekends.

Vinita replied fast: "If I told you my boss said 'sloppy' four times without ever saying what was wrong, what would you tell me?"
Simran stared at the screen. She'd tell Vinita to ask for specifics. She'd say one person's opinion isn't the whole truth. She'd ask whether the client had ever complained. The client hadn't. The client had sent a thank-you email on Monday.
The phone died. Simran sat in the dark bus, not happy, but steadier. Tomorrow she would ask her manager, calmly, which exact parts were sloppy. And she would read the thank-you email again.

On my second month as a trainee at the architecture firm, I sent the site the wrong ceiling height for a classroom. Three hundred millimetres too low. I found it myself on a Friday evening, rechecking a drawing for something else.
Nobody else had noticed. The contractor would start the framing on Monday.
I sat in the empty office for twenty minutes, sweating. I could quietly send a "revised" drawing and hope nobody compared. But if the framing started wrong, children would sit in that room for years.
I called Lakshmi Ma'am, my supervisor, at home.
She was sharp. "How did this happen? Did you not check against the section?" I said no, I hadn't, and that it was my mistake. She was quiet, then: "Send the corrected drawing now, copy me. I'll call the contractor."
It stung for a week. But since then, she gives me the checking of other people's drawings.
Chaitanya

Course note, Physics Lab II. Written by Uday, faculty in charge, 18 February.
Tanvir, one of our final-year teaching assistants, came to my office at 8 a.m. today, before class. He looked as if he hadn't slept.
He told me that while grading the circuits quiz last night, he had used last year's answer key for the first twenty papers. Six students had lost marks they had earned. No student had complained yet; the marks were not published.
I was not gentle. I told him that grading is a trust we give assistants, and that he should have checked the key before starting. He did not argue or make excuses. He said, "You're right. I've already regraded all twenty with the correct key. The changes are in this sheet."
Next steps: marks published correctly this afternoon. I have told Tanvir that I will continue to give him grading duties. Frankly, I trust him more after this morning, not less.

How many papers had Tanvir graded with last year's key?
Tanvir had graded the first twenty papers with last year's key.
What does Tanvir's look in the morning suggest he was feeling?
Tanvir looked as if he had not slept, suggesting he was anxious and afraid of how Uday would react to the mistake.
What did Tanvir do that turned a mistake into trust?
He reported the error before anyone found it, accepted the scolding without excuses, and had already regraded all twenty papers.
How might the six students have been affected if Tanvir had stayed silent?
They would have lost marks they had earned, possibly without ever knowing why, and the course's fairness would have been harmed.

Café manager's note, Saturday
At 3:40 pm Indu, our weekend trainee, came to me pale and said, "I wrote the wrong label on Mrs D'Souza's birthday cake. I wrote 'nut-free', but I used the almond sponge. The pickup is at five."

I'll be honest: I scolded her. I said allergy labels are the one thing we can never get wrong. She nodded and didn't argue, though her hands were shaking.
Then we fixed it. I called Mrs D'Souza, explained, and offered a fresh nut-free cake by six or a full refund. Indu and I baked the new sponge together. It went out at 5:55.
What I did next: I added a second check for allergy labels on every order, and I told Indu that because she spoke up, nobody got hurt. From next month I'm putting her in charge of the allergy checklist.

'Nut-free', though the almond sponge was used.

Called Mrs D'Souza, baked a fresh nut-free cake with Indu, added a second allergy check, and planned to put Indu in charge of the allergy checklist.

Mrs D'Souza might be annoyed about the delay but relieved and grateful the error was caught before the birthday.

The evening milk had been poured and the farmers had gone home when Ganga noticed it. In the register at the Rampur dairy collection centre she had written Shankar Kaka's cans as eight litres. The slip on the spike said eighteen.

Nobody would check before Saturday's payments. If anyone noticed later, she could blame the smudged slip.

Her fingers were cold. She carried the register to Sonali-didi, who was locking the cooling tank.

"Didi, I wrote eight instead of eighteen for Shankar Kaka. It's my mistake."

Sonali's voice rose so sharply that the helper boy looked over. "Do you know how that looks if he complains first? Twice you've been careless this month!"

Ganga stood and took it, face burning. They corrected the entry together, and Sonali signed beside it.

A month later, when Sonali went away for her sister's wedding, it was Ganga she left with the register and the keys.

What did the slip on the spike say?
The slip on the spike said eighteen.
How did Ganga feel as she carried the register to Sonali?
Ganga was scared, her fingers cold, yet determined to report her own mistake before anyone else found it.
What went wrong, and what fixed it?
Ganga made an entry error; reporting it at once and correcting it together, with Sonali's signature, fixed it before it could hurt Shankar Kaka's payment.
How does Sonali's view of Ganga change by a month later?
Though Sonali scolded her, she came to trust Ganga enough to leave her the register and the keys during the wedding.

On the terrace of the Andheri flat, someone had put on music, and Karan had a plate of samosas and a joke. "Women drivers," he said, spinning an imaginary steering wheel. "Left indicator, turns right." Two of the boys laughed. Pooja, holding a paper cup, gave the small tight smile Naveen had seen her use at the office when she didn't want a scene. Naveen felt the laugh sitting in his own throat. He put down his plate. "Karan, Pooja drove all four of us back from Lonavala in the rain last month, and I fell asleep in the front seat. Sounds like decent driving to me." His voice was steady. "That joke's old." Karan blinked, then shrugged. "Okay, okay." The music changed. Pooja looked at Naveen and mouthed, "Thanks."

Who drove the four of them back from Lonavala?
Pooja drove all four of them back from Lonavala in the rain.
What is Naveen feeling as the laugh sits in his throat?
Naveen feels uncomfortable and torn. He does not want to laugh along, yet he is also nervous about speaking.
What choice did Naveen make, and why might it have worked?
He put down his plate and spoke calmly, using a real memory of Pooja's driving, so it sounded like a fact and not a lecture.
How might Pooja feel when Naveen speaks?
Grateful and relieved. She had been putting up with the joke behind a tight smile, and she mouths "Thanks" afterwards.

"Did you see the news about that case?" Dev said, grinning. "Honestly, some rape jokes write themselves." A couple of people snickered. Swati looked down at her laptop. Rehan put his cup down. "Dev, I'm not laughing at that one." "Relax, it's just a joke." "Maybe. But it's about something that happens to real people. I'd rather not hear it." The room went quiet. Dev raised his hands. "Fine, fine. You've gone serious on us." "Maybe I have," Rehan said, and turned back to his screen. His heart was thumping. Ten minutes later Swati stopped by his desk. "Thanks for that." "I nearly kept quiet," he admitted. "I know. Nobody does it easily."

What did Rehan say when Dev made the joke?
Rehan said, "Dev, I'm not laughing at that one," and that he would rather not hear it.
What is Rehan feeling when he answers Dev, and how can you tell?
Rehan is nervous but resolved. His heart is thumping and he later admits he nearly kept quiet, yet he still speaks.
What does Rehan's choice to speak calmly, without insulting Dev, show about how to object?
He gave his reason briefly, said he would rather not hear it, and turned back to his screen, so the group heard it without a fight.
How might Swati have felt during the joke and afterwards?
Uncomfortable during it, since she looked down at her laptop, and grateful afterwards, since she thanked Rehan at his desk.

We were at Samir's birthday, six of us boys around a table of kebabs, when Samir told a joke about a woman who couldn't park. Everyone laughed. Then he told another one, a rape joke, the kind I'd heard a hundred times and laughed at to fit in.
This time I didn't laugh. I thought of my sister, who takes two buses home after dark.
The table went quiet around me. Samir said, "Arre, Kishore, it's a joke, yaar."
I kept my voice easy. "I know, bhai. It's just not funny to me. Tell the one about your driving test instead."
For a second nobody moved. Then someone laughed, at Samir's driving test, and the talk moved on.
Later, one of the others texted me: "Glad you said that. I didn't know how." Looking back, that text mattered more than the silence.

Whose birthday was it?
It was Samir's birthday.
What was Kishore feeling when he didn't laugh?
He felt uncomfortable and protective, thinking of his sister who takes two buses home after dark.
What made Kishore's response work?
He stayed calm and friendly, said the joke wasn't funny to him without lecturing, and offered a new topic so the group could move on.
How might Samir feel when the table goes quiet?
Samir may feel embarrassed and defensive, which is why he says it's just a joke, but he also learns the group won't simply laugh along.

Team lead's note, Thursday.
At lunch in the canteen today, one of the junior engineers made a joke about women and rape. Several people laughed. Shalini, who sits on that table, looked down at her plate.
Chinmay, 24, who joined in March, put his spoon down and said, calmly, "Not okay, man. Let's not." He didn't raise his voice. The one who told the joke said, "Relax, it's just a joke." Chinmay replied, "Still not okay." Then he asked Shalini about her project demo, as if nothing had happened.
I watched the table after that. Nobody told another joke of that kind.
Next step: I spoke privately with the engineer who told the joke, explained why it was harmful, and reminded him of our conduct policy. I also thanked Chinmay, and asked Shalini if she wanted to talk; she said she was fine but appreciated it.

What did Chinmay say when told to relax?
Chinmay replied, "Still not okay."
What might Chinmay have been feeling when he put his spoon down?
He was probably uncomfortable and determined, noticing Shalini look down, but calm enough to object without raising his voice.
Why was it helpful for Chinmay to then ask Shalini about her demo?
It moved the conversation on and treated Shalini as a colleague rather than a topic, without turning the moment into a big scene.
How might Shalini have experienced the lunch?
She seemed hurt and uncomfortable when the joke was told, and was likely relieved that someone objected so she didn't have to.

Friday
Office outing to the bowling alley. Rakesh and the boys from sales started on "women drivers" when Noor mentioned she'd driven in from Thane. Big laughs. She laughed too, but she stopped talking after that.
I laughed at the first one. I hate that I did.
At the second one I said, "Come on, she drove forty kilometres in traffic and got here before us. Maybe we're the bad drivers." A couple of people actually laughed at that instead. Rakesh rolled his eyes.
On the way out, Noor said quietly, "Thanks, Santosh bhai." That's all. But she was back to talking in the cab.
Note to self: next time, the first joke. Not the second. It's easier than I thought. My hands were shaking and nobody even noticed.
— Santosh

Where had Noor driven in from?
Noor had driven in from Thane.
How did Santosh feel after laughing at the first joke?
Santosh felt ashamed, writing that he hates that he laughed, and nervous when he did speak up, with his hands shaking.
What could Santosh do differently next time?
He could object at the first joke rather than the second, calmly and with humour, as he did when he pointed out Noor's drive.
How was Noor affected by the jokes and by Santosh speaking up?
She stopped talking after the jokes, which suggests she felt belittled, but after Santosh spoke she thanked him and was back to talking in the cab.

Boys' group chat, Friday night.
Divyansh: saw a lady take 5 mins to park outside the mall 😅 this is why women shouldn't get licences
Rohit: haha
Divyansh: Akash where's your laugh
Akash: Nah. My sister drives me to work every day and hasn't scraped once. I've scraped twice.
Divyansh: bro it's a joke
Akash: I know. Just not a funny one to me. The lady was probably just parking carefully.
(Three minutes of nothing.)
Sameer: honestly my mum is the best driver in our house
Rohit: ok fair, my brother failed his test twice
Divyansh: fine fine. Akash, you're driving to the match tomorrow then 🙂
Akash: Deal. Pick you up at 4.

Who drives Akash to work every day?
His sister drives him to work every day.
Why did Akash refuse to laugh, and what might he have felt typing his reply?
He was uncomfortable with a joke that mocked women and probably a little nervous about spoiling the mood, yet sure enough to say so calmly.
What made Akash's reply work in the group?
He stayed calm, used a real example and did not insult Divyansh, so Sameer and Rohit felt free to agree instead of taking sides.
How might Divyansh have felt when nobody replied for three minutes?
Divyansh likely felt awkward and a bit exposed, then eased the tension by joking that Akash should drive, a sign he had taken the point.

Damini opened the maths notebook and stared. In Coimbatore her class had done fractions last term, but here the children were already on ratios. At lunch the Hindi flew past too fast, and when she answered, two girls giggled at how she stretched her words. She carried her tiffin to the corner of the bench. Aditi, who sat in the row ahead, turned around. "Want me to show you how Ma'am does ratios? I'll do it at recess." Damini nodded, her throat tight. That evening Mummy set out the same routine as always: warm milk, one chapter of a storybook, lights off at nine. Damini told her about Aditi, and slept easily.

Where had Damini's class already done fractions last term?
In Coimbatore, her class had done fractions last term.
What was Damini feeling when two girls giggled at how she stretched her words?
She felt embarrassed and out of place, which is why she took her tiffin to the corner of the bench.
What made the biggest difference to Damini's day, and what steadied her at home?
Aditi's offer to explain ratios at recess turned the day around, and Mummy's usual routine of warm milk, a chapter and lights off at nine steadied her at home.
Why might Aditi have turned around to speak to Damini?
Aditi may have noticed Damini sitting alone in the corner and struggling with the maths, and wanted to help. 🙂

"You're sitting alone again," said Raghav, dropping his bag on the bench.
"I'm fine." Joseph pushed his rice around. "They laugh at how I say my words."
"Riya laughs at everything. She laughed at my glasses on the first day." Raghav grinned. "Which chapter are you stuck on?"
"All of it. In Kochi we did the water cycle last year. Here it's already the human body."
"Come to my desk. My brother's old notes are really neat."
"Really?"
"Really. And say that word again, I like it."
Joseph laughed for the first time all week. "Amma says I can call Kochi on Sunday evening if I keep my homework hour every day."
"Then keep it," said Raghav. "I'll save you a seat tomorrow."

From which city had Joseph come?
Joseph had come from Kochi.
What was Joseph feeling when he said the other children laugh at how he says his words?
He felt hurt and alone, which shows in how he pushed his rice around and sat by himself.
What could Joseph do next to feel settled in the new school?
He could go to Raghav's desk to use the neat notes and keep his daily homework hour, which Amma links to his Sunday call to Kochi.
Why might Raghav be quick to notice Joseph sitting alone?
Raghav mentions that Riya laughed at his glasses on the first day, so he seems to know how being laughed at feels. 🙂

When Nilesh, ten, moved from Mumbai to the small town of Satara, everything felt wrong. The boys spoke a village Marathi he could barely follow. The teacher wrote on a blackboard, not a smartboard. In maths, they were two chapters ahead.
In the first week, he ate lunch alone under the neem tree and told his mother he had a stomach ache every morning.
On Friday, a girl from his class, Alka, sat beside him. "You're from Mumbai? Is it true the trains are so crowded people hang out the door?"
Nilesh nodded. She laughed. "I'll teach you our Marathi if you tell me about the trains."
At home, his mother kept the same bedtime story and Sunday pancakes as in Mumbai. Slowly, the stomach aches stopped.

Where did Nilesh eat lunch in the first week?
He ate lunch alone under the neem tree.
What does Nilesh's morning stomach ache suggest?
It suggests he felt anxious and out of place at the new school.
What helped Nilesh most?
Alka's friendly offer to trade Marathi lessons for train stories, along with his mother keeping the same bedtime story and Sunday pancakes.
How might Alka see Nilesh at first?
Alka is curious about him and his big-city life, seeing him as interesting rather than strange.

In Amara's first week at the new school in Manchester, the teacher said, "Line up, pet," and she didn't know what "pet" meant. Her Lagos accent made one boy ask, "Can you say that again?" three times. The maths was different too: long division done in a strange new way.
Amara, nine, stopped talking in class. At home she told her dad she wasn't hungry.
On Thursday, at the lunch table, a girl named Ada sat down opposite her. "My mum's from Enugu," she said. "I had the 'pet' problem too. It means you're nice."
Amara laughed for the first time that week.
That night her dad made jollof like every Friday back home, one day early. "Same time, same pot, new kitchen," he said. Amara ate two plates.

Where is Ada's mum from?
Ada said, "My mum's from Enugu."
How was Amara feeling when she stopped talking in class?
Amara felt out of place and embarrassed about her accent and the new ways of doing things.
What made the biggest difference for Amara?
A kind classmate who understood her confusion and her dad keeping a familiar routine with jollof both helped her feel settled.
What might it be like for Amara's dad to watch her struggle?
He is probably worried and caring, which is why he makes jollof a day early to comfort her.

At his new school in Chennai, Anirban, eleven, sat in the front row trying to follow the Tamil class. He'd grown up in Kolkata with Bangla and English. Now the Tamil letters swam in front of him. At break, the boys played a game he didn't know the rules to.
He said "Achha" once, and someone laughed. He stopped saying anything.
The class monitor, Mahima, noticed him sitting on the steps. "You're from Kolkata? My uncle lives there. Do you like fish?"
"Very much."
"Then you'll like my mother's meen kuzhambu." She taught him the game's rules at the next break.
At home, his father still read him the Bangla newspaper comics every night, as before. By the end of the month, Anirban could write his name in Tamil, and Mahima wrote hers in Bangla.

What did Anirban say that made someone laugh?
He said "Achha" once, and someone laughed.
What was Anirban feeling when he stopped saying anything?
He felt embarrassed and out of place, unsure of the language and the game.
How did Mahima and his father help Anirban adjust?
Mahima befriended him, asked about his home and taught him the game, while his father kept their nightly comics routine.
How might Mahima feel about learning to write in Bangla?
Mahima probably feels proud and happy, enjoying the exchange with her new friend.

Monday. Farida's first day in Bengaluru. The maths class was two chapters ahead of her old school in Lucknow, and when the teacher said something in Kannada, everyone laughed except her. She ate her tiffin alone by the water tank.
Thursday. Nilesh, who sat behind her, pushed his notebook across. "We did fractions last month. Copy the examples, I'll explain at break." At home Ammi kept their Lucknow routine: tea at five, homework at the dining table, a story before bed. Farida fell asleep without crying for the first time.
The next Monday. Farida walked in and said "Namaskara" to the watchman, the one Kannada word Nilesh had taught her. He grinned from the gate. At break they shared her sheermal and his chakli.

What word did Farida say to the watchman?
She said "Namaskara" to the watchman.
What was Farida feeling on her first day, and what shows it?
She felt lonely and out of place, eating her tiffin alone by the water tank after missing the Kannada joke.
Which two things helped Farida settle, and why?
Nilesh's help with fractions gave her a friend at school, and Ammi's steady Lucknow routine made home feel safe.
What might Nilesh have noticed that made him offer his notebook?
Nilesh likely noticed she was behind in maths and alone, and was kind enough to help without making a fuss.

Ines stood on a small stool at the low table in Lisbon, her tongue between her teeth. She had a damp cloth and a serious face. Esther, her mother, sat with her tea and did not move. Ines wiped in big circles, and water ran over the edge onto the floor. She missed the crumbs near the edge. "Done!" she said. Esther looked at the wet table and the drip on the floor. She said, "Thank you, Ines, that helps. Shall we do the corner together?" Ines beamed and pushed the cloth over the last crumbs. Then she stood back and said proudly, "I am a helper."

What did Ines use to wipe the table?
Ines used a damp cloth.
How did Ines feel when she said "Done!"?
Ines felt proud and important, even though the table was still wet and had crumbs.
What did Esther do that made Ines want to keep helping?
Esther thanked Ines, did not take the cloth away and offered to do the corner together.
What might Esther be thinking as she looks at the wet table?
Esther can see it is messy, but she is patient and values Ines feeling useful more than a perfect table.

At snack time, Irawati, the nursery teacher, handed out the paper plates. "Who wants to be plate helper today?" Vasudha's hand shot up. She carried one plate at a time from the pile to each friend, slowly, with both hands, her lips pressed together. The third plate slipped and clattered on the mat. Vasudha froze and looked up. Irawati smiled. "Plates fall. Pick it up and carry on." Vasudha picked it up. When all the plates were down, she stood at the front, chest out. "I did the plates," she said. Irawati gave her a small sticker of a star.

Who was the plate helper at snack time?
Vasudha was the plate helper at snack time.
What was Vasudha feeling when the plate clattered on the mat?
Vasudha was startled and worried about being in trouble, which is why she froze and looked up.
What did Irawati do that helped Vasudha keep trying?
Irawati smiled, said plates fall and asked Vasudha to pick it up and carry on.
How might the other children feel as Vasudha hands out the plates?
The other children probably feel pleased to be served by a friend, and may want a turn as plate helper.

Uma: "Mumma, can I stir the kheer?"
Jasleen: "Yes, but slowly. Hold the handle, not the pot."
Uma: (stirring hard) "Like this?"
Jasleen: "A bit slower, beta. It's splashing."
Uma: "Oops. Some fell on the floor."
Jasleen: "That's okay. We'll wipe it after."
Uma: "Can I wipe it? I'm a good wiper."
Jasleen: "You are. Here's the cloth."
(Uma wipes the floor, leaving a wide sticky streak.)
Uma: "All clean!"
Jasleen: (smiling, wiping the streak later) "Thank you, my helper."
Uma: "Tomorrow can I carry the plates?"
Jasleen: "The steel ones, yes. One at a time."

What was Uma stirring?
Uma was stirring the kheer.
How did Uma feel about helping in the kitchen?
She felt proud and eager, calling herself a good wiper and asking to carry plates tomorrow.
What did Jasleen do well in accepting Uma's messy help?
She let Uma stir and wipe, praised her, gave simple safety tips and quietly finished the streak later without taking over.
How might Jasleen feel about the extra mess?
Jasleen seems patient and warm, smiling and accepting that the imperfect help matters more than a spotless floor.

Nursery teacher's note, Monday.
Today Sahil, five, asked if he could set out the plates for snack time. He carried them one by one from the shelf, very seriously, tongue between his teeth. It took him nearly ten minutes, twice as long as usual. One plate went on the floor; he picked it up and put it back on the table, and I swapped it for a clean one without fuss. When everyone sat down, he announced, "I did the plates!" and beamed. I thanked him in front of the class. I will give him the same job all this week, and let him choose a helper on Friday.
Vinita

How long did Sahil take to set out the plates?
It took him nearly ten minutes.
How did Sahil feel when everyone sat down?
He felt proud and happy, beaming as he announced that he did the plates.
Why was Vinita right to let Sahil keep the job?
Patiently accepting his slow, imperfect help lets him feel useful, which builds confidence more than doing it for him.
How might the other children see Sahil's job?
They might feel curious and want a turn, seeing how proud Sahil is and knowing he can choose a helper on Friday.

In their village near Mysuru, Devika, four, followed her grandfather Harsha to the cowshed every morning. Today she wanted to carry the small bucket of water. It sloshed with every step, and half spilled on her feet. She giggled. When they reached the cow, there was only a little water left. Dada didn't take the bucket. He held it steady while she poured it into the trough. "Good job, kutti." Then she tried to sweep the straw with his broom, which was taller than her. Straw went everywhere. Dada swept it again later without a word. At breakfast, Devika told Amma, "I fed the cow," puffing her chest out.

What did Devika want to carry?
She wanted to carry the small bucket of water.
How did Devika feel at breakfast?
She felt proud, puffing her chest out as she told Amma she fed the cow.
What did Dada do that helped Devika grow?
He let her carry and pour, praised her, and quietly swept again later instead of taking over.
How might Amma feel hearing Devika's news?
Amma would likely feel warm and amused, happy to see how proud Devika is of helping.

Marek pushed the stool to the kitchen sink in their Kraków flat. "I wash the potatoes!" His dad, Alejandro, handed him the brush and five muddy potatoes. Marek scrubbed each one very hard, tongue poking out. Water splashed on the floor and on the cat. One potato was still brown on one side. Alejandro's hand moved towards it, then stopped. "Good scrubbing. That one has a muddy spot. Can you find it?" Marek turned it round, found the spot and scrubbed again. "All clean!" he shouted, holding it up like a prize. At dinner Marek told everyone, "I made the soup."

How many potatoes did Alejandro give Marek?
Five muddy potatoes.
How did Marek feel holding up the clean potato?
Marek felt proud, shouting "All clean!" and holding it up like a prize.
What did Alejandro do instead of fixing the potato himself?
He praised the scrubbing and asked Marek to find the muddy spot, so Marek could finish the job himself.
What was it like for Alejandro to watch the splashing and the brown spot?
Alejandro was tempted to take over, since his hand moved towards the potato, but chose patience over a quick, neat job.

Dolma, sit down. I'm your uncle Tanvir, and I was twenty-four when a clerk at the ward office sent me from counter to counter for a copy of my birth certificate. At the third counter he said, without looking up, "Files move faster with a little tea money." My face went hot. I wanted to shout, and part of me wanted to just pay. Instead I kept my voice level and said, "Could you please show me the fee and the rule in writing?" He shrugged. I thanked him, noted his counter number and the date, and walked to the notice board where the grievance officer's name and helpline were printed. I filed a written complaint that afternoon and got a receipt number. Ten days later I had the certificate, no tea money paid, and a clerk who avoided my eyes.

What did the clerk say at the third counter?
He said files move faster with a little tea money.
What was Tanvir feeling when the clerk hinted at tea money?
Angry and torn: Tanvir's face went hot, wanting to shout and also to just pay.
What choices at the counter kept Tanvir safe and effective?
Tanvir stayed polite, asked for the fee and rule in writing, noted the counter number and date, and filed a written complaint.
How might the clerk have felt when Tanvir calmly asked for the rule in writing?
Probably uncomfortable and caught out, since the clerk only shrugged and later avoided Tanvir's eyes.

The office shut at four, and Ishita's job offer needed stamped address proof by morning. At half past two the clerk pointed her to window six, window six pointed back, and then a man in the corner leaned close. "Two hundred and it's done today." Her hands shook. Outside, her brother Sachin muttered, "Just pay it." Ishita took a breath. "Not today. I'll ask for the rule." At the window she said, "Could you write the fee and the steps on my form, please?" The officer on duty looked up, wrote both, and stamped it himself. Ishita also asked at the desk where complaints go and copied the number into her phone. She reached the car park with ten minutes to spare.

What amount did the man in the corner ask for?
He asked for two hundred to get it done today.
What was Ishita feeling when the man in the corner leaned close?
Shaken and angry, since her hands shook and she refused to simply pay.
What did Ishita do instead of paying, and what did it achieve?
She politely asked for the fee and steps in writing, and the officer wrote both and stamped the form; she also copied the complaint number.
Why might Sachin have said "Just pay it"?
Sachin was probably anxious about the four o'clock deadline and wanted the fastest way out for his sister.

messages.content:
Read this:

Kamal, you asked why I looked so tired last month. Let me, Francis, tell you the whole electricity story.
After Appa passed, I went to move the connection into my name. Counter A sent me to counter C. Counter C said a form was missing and sent me back to A. Third day, a man outside the building leaned in: "Give a little extra, it'll be done by evening." And the clerk at C said, "You can go through him, it's faster."
I was so angry my hands were shaking. I wanted to shout. I also, honestly, wanted to just pay and be done.
I did neither. I asked the clerk, politely, "Please write down which rule needs this form." He hesitated. Then I asked where the complaint register was. It was right there, on the side table. Suddenly the form wasn't missing anymore. The next week I filed the online grievance anyway, so the next person gets the list on day one.

What did the man outside the building say?
He said, "Give a little extra, it'll be done by evening."
What was Francis feeling when the clerk pointed to the man outside?
Francis felt angry, with his hands shaking, and also tempted to just pay and be done with it.
Which choice worked for Francis, and why?
Staying polite while asking for the rule in writing and for the complaint register worked, because it made the delay hard to keep up without a fight or a bribe.
How might the clerk have felt when Francis asked for the complaint register?
The clerk was probably uneasy and caught out, since he hesitated and then the missing form was suddenly not missing.

messages.content:
Read this:

Day one, a Monday. Rashmi reached the ration office at ten to add her new baby's name to the family card. Counter two sent her to counter five. Counter five said the officer was "on leave, come Thursday." Rashmi went home with the baby asleep on her shoulder and her jaw tight.
Thursday. The officer was in, but a man by the gate offered to "fast-track" it for an amount he whispered. Tenzin, her neighbour who had come along, raised his eyebrows. Rashmi felt her face burn. She walked away without answering.
The following Monday she came back with Tenzin and a notebook. At the counter she asked calmly, "Please write down which documents are needed and how many days it takes." The officer wrote it on the back of a form and signed it. Rashmi also noted the complaint number on the wall. Ten days later, the new card came.

Why did Rashmi go to the ration office?
She went to add her new baby's name to the family card.
How did Rashmi feel when the man at the gate made his offer?
Rashmi felt insulted and angry; her face burned, and she walked away without answering.
What made the third visit work?
Asking calmly for the documents and the timeline in writing, getting it signed and noting the complaint number, instead of arguing or paying.
How might Tenzin see the man's offer?
Tenzin seems uneasy and disapproving, raising his eyebrows, and he supports Rashmi by coming back with her.

metadata.subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Anjali, sit. Your Damini maasi will tell you about my first pension claim, the year after your nana retired.
I was twenty-five. The clerk at the district office kept my file under a stack of others for six weeks. Each time I went, he said, "Some paper is missing." Never which paper. Once he rubbed his thumb and finger together and smiled. I went home and cried in the bathroom, so angry I could not eat.
My friend Beena said, "Don't shout, and don't pay. Ask him to write down the rule." So next time I stood at his window and said, very politely, "Sir, kindly write which paper is missing and under which order." He stopped smiling. Then I asked where the grievance box was. The file moved in four days.
I was shaking the whole time, Anjali. Polite is not the same as weak.

How long did the clerk keep the file under a stack of others?
He kept it under a stack of others for six weeks.
What was young Damini feeling after the clerk's gesture?
She felt humiliated and furious, crying in the bathroom and too angry to eat.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
Asking politely for the missing paper and order in writing, and for the grievance box, worked because it made the clerk accountable without a fight or a payment.
How might Beena have felt watching her friend struggle?
Beena was probably concerned and protective, giving calm, practical advice so Damini would not either shout or pay.

messages.content:
