Rain came down in sheets, the ward office closed at five, and Sangeeta's mother waited outside in an auto, meter running. Sangeeta only needed her mother's name added to the property tax record. Counter three sent her to counter seven. Counter seven sent her back to three. Darshan, a man in a cream shirt, leaned on a pillar. "Madam, I can finish it today. Give me a little something for the babu, he'll sign." Her ears went hot. She wanted to shout, or just pay. Instead she said, "No, thank you," and went back to counter three. "Sir, could you write down which document is missing and the rule that asks for it? Then I'll bring it." The clerk looked up, surprised. Behind him hung a Citizen's Charter board listing time limits and a ground-floor complaint counter. She glanced at it, still polite. He pulled her file over, stamped two pages and said, "Come Friday for the copy."

What did Sangeeta need added to the property tax record?
Her mother's name.
What was Sangeeta feeling when Darshan made his offer?
She felt angry and helpless, her ears hot, tempted both to shout and to just pay.
Why did Sangeeta's request to the clerk work better than arguing or paying?
Asking politely for the missing document and the rule in writing, with the complaint counter on the wall, made it hard to keep sending her round without a reason.
How might the clerk have seen Sangeeta's written request?
The clerk seemed caught off guard, perhaps realising she knew her rights and would not pay or give up, and chose to process the file.

metadata.subtype: Ill-treated by a clerk or agent [Receiver]

messages.content:
Read this:

Note from Vishal, physics teacher. After the visiting scientist's talk on how galaxies form, Payal stayed in her seat after the bell, eyes on the empty stage. She is usually first out for lunch. When I asked if all was well, she said, "Sir, the scientist said half of it is still unknown and she has spent forty years on it. I want to be like that."
She copied a line from the board into her diary and left without her tiffin. Later I saw her asking the librarian for the astronomy shelf. I will pass her name to the science club and offer her a book. No concern about Payal today: she seemed lifted, not upset.

What did Payal leave behind when she walked out?
Her tiffin.
What was Payal feeling after the talk?
She was inspired and lifted. She stayed in her seat, wanted to be like the scientist, and forgot her lunch.
What could Vishal do next to support Payal's interest?
Vishal plans to pass her name to the science club and offer her a book, giving her a route to follow her curiosity.
How might the scientist's admission of not knowing half of it have affected Payal?
It seems to have impressed Payal, since she wants to be like someone who keeps working on what is unknown.

Read this:

Thursday night. I left my bag in an auto this morning with my exam hall ticket in it. I nearly cried at the school gate. At lunchtime the guard called me out: the driver, Samir Bhai, had come all the way back, and he put the bag in my hands. I tried to give him money. He folded my fingers over it and said, "Beta, study well. That's my payment." Then he was gone before I could thank him properly.
I've been thinking about it all evening. My worries about tomorrow's paper feel smaller, like somebody opened a window. I want to be a person who does that for someone one day.
Leela

What did Leela leave in the auto?
A bag with the exam hall ticket in it.
What is Leela feeling as Leela writes about Samir Bhai?
Moved and lifted. Leela's exam worries feel smaller, like somebody opened a window, and Leela wants to be like Samir Bhai.
What did Leela decide after Samir Bhai's kindness?
Leela decided to become a person who does something like that for someone else one day.
What might Samir Bhai have been thinking when he refused the money?
He seems to have wanted nothing in return, only for Leela to study well, which is why he folded Leela's fingers over the money and left.

Read this:

"You're quiet," Gautam said as they walked out of Ernakulam station.
"Did you see that man at the ticket counter?"
"The one in the old shirt?"
"The lady ahead of him was short twenty rupees and crying, and her train was leaving. He just paid it. Didn't say anything. Just waved her off."
"So?"
"So he didn't look like he had much himself." Jomon's voice wobbled. "I've been worrying about my marks all week. And then this."
"You're getting emotional about a ticket."
"Maybe." Jomon laughed, embarrassed. "But I feel bigger. Like the world's better than I thought an hour ago."
Gautam was quiet for a bit. "Yeah," he said finally. "Okay. It was nice."

How much was the lady short?
Twenty rupees.
How did Jomon feel after seeing the man pay?
Jomon felt moved and lifted, bigger, as if the world were better than he'd thought, and the marks worry shrank.
What might Jomon do with this feeling?
Jomon could hold onto it, perhaps by doing a small kindness himself, instead of brushing it off as silly.
How does Gautam react to Jomon's feelings?
Gautam first teases, then quietly agrees that it was nice.

Read this:

Last winter, in an ordinary physics class, Usha Ma'am said something I still can't shake. She was explaining the elements, and she stopped and said, "The iron in your blood was made inside a star that exploded billions of years ago."
The room went quiet. I looked at my hands. My hands were made of old stars. I'd been so anxious that week about a fight with my best friend, replaying every word. Suddenly it felt tiny, and I felt huge and tiny at the same time.
After class I asked Ma'am how anyone had figured that out. She lent me a book. I read it on the bus, twice. I'm Zeenat, and whenever I'm stuck in my own head now, I look at my hands.

What did Usha Ma'am say about the iron in our blood?
It was made inside a star that exploded billions of years ago.
How did Zeenat feel after hearing the idea?
Zeenat felt awe, huge and tiny at once, and the anxious replaying of the fight suddenly felt small.
What did Zeenat do to keep the feeling going?
Zeenat asked Ma'am how it was worked out, borrowed a book and read it twice, and now looks at those hands when stuck.
How might Usha Ma'am have felt when Zeenat asked after class?
Usha Ma'am was probably pleased and encouraged that an idea had moved a student enough to ask.

Read this:

Music teacher's note, Friday.
Our choir visited the old age home today. An elderly resident, Mrs Fernandes, asked to sing for us: a hymn from her childhood, in a thin, shaking voice. Nobody moved.
I watched Sharmila, who usually jokes through everything. She stood completely still, hands pressed together, eyes wet. On the bus back she didn't touch her phone. When I asked if she was all right, she said, "I don't even believe in much, Ma'am. But it felt like the whole room lifted."
She asked if the choir could learn the hymn to sing with Mrs Fernandes next month. I said yes.
Jahnavi

Who sang for the choir?
An elderly resident, Mrs Fernandes.
What does Sharmila standing still with wet eyes suggest?
It suggests she felt deeply moved and lifted, a kind of awe, even though she doesn't believe in much.
What step did Sharmila ask for, and why is it a good one?
To learn the hymn and sing it with Mrs Fernandes next month, turning the moment into a way to give something back.
What might the visit have meant to Mrs Fernandes?
Mrs Fernandes likely felt valued and happy to share a hymn from her childhood with young listeners.

Read this:

Tuesday
Today was supposed to be terrible. Maths test, and I'd fought with Mummy about the phone, and I was angry all the way to the bus stop.
Then something happened. There was a little boy at the stop, shivering, no sweater, crying because he'd missed his school bus. An old lady, Kalyani Aunty from the flower stall, came out, took off her own shawl, wrapped him in it, and gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask. She didn't even know him. She waited with him until his father came.
I just stood there. Something in my chest went huge and quiet. Like when I heard the gurdwara kirtan at dawn last Gurpurab. My maths test, the fight, everything, suddenly looked so small.
In the test I was calm. I think I did okay.
Tonight I said sorry to Mummy.
Jasleen

What did Kalyani Aunty give the boy from her flask?
She gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask.
What was Jasleen feeling while watching Kalyani Aunty?
Jasleen felt awe and deep quiet, moved by the stranger's kindness, as the anger and worry shrank.
What could Jasleen carry forward from this morning?
Remembering moments of kindness or beauty, like Kalyani Aunty's shawl, can lift daily worries and help Jasleen stay calm.
How might the little boy have felt when Kalyani Aunty wrapped him up?
The boy likely felt comforted and safe after feeling cold, scared and alone.

Read this:

Tenzin sat in the high chair, banging a spoon on the tray.
"Ba-ba-ba!" Then Tenzin stopped and looked at Mama Sharmila, mouth open, waiting.
"Ba-ba? Is that so?" said Sharmila.
Tenzin grinned. "Da! Ba-da-da." Pause. Eyes on Mama's face.
"Da-da-da! You are telling me a story."
"Bah!" Tenzin slapped the tray, laughed, and waited again.

What did Tenzin do after saying "Ba-ba-ba!"?
Tenzin stopped and looked at Sharmila, mouth open, waiting.
What does Tenzin's waiting, with eyes on Mama's face, suggest Tenzin wants?
An answer. The pause and the steady look show Tenzin expects a reply and enjoys getting one.
What could Sharmila do to keep the exchange going?
Answer each sound in a warm voice and then wait for the next one, as Sharmila did by saying "You are telling me a story."
What is it like for Sharmila when Tenzin pauses and looks up?
Sharmila is invited to take a turn. The pause shows it is time to reply, and each reply gets Tenzin laughing and babbling again.

Read this:

Daily note from the crèche, Ramesh.
Shankar sat by the window with the toy phone and said, "Hallo? Hallo?" Then Shankar tilted the head, waiting. I said, "Hello! Where are you going?" Shankar said, "Bus!" and paused again. I replied, "The bus goes to the market." Shankar giggled, babbled a string of sounds, and waited. We went back and forth until snack time.
Next: I told Shankar's grandmother that bath time can be the same. Answer each sound, then wait.

What did Shankar say into the toy phone?
"Hallo? Hallo?"
What might Shankar be expecting when pausing after saying "Bus!"?
A reply from Ramesh. The tilted head and the waiting show Shankar expects the other person to take a turn, and the giggling shows delight when it comes.
What simple habit does Ramesh suggest for home?
To answer each sound Shankar makes and then wait, during ordinary times like bath time and meals.
How might Ramesh's note help Shankar's grandmother?
It shows that no special lessons are needed: answering each sound and waiting is already the kind of conversation that helps Shankar.

Read this:

On the balcony of the Jangpura flat, Noor, fourteen months, sat on her grandmother Hansa's lap. "Ba-ba-ba," said Noor, then stopped and looked up. "Ba-ba? Is that so?" said Hansa. Noor kicked her feet. "Da!" She waited again, eyes on Hansa's face. "Da! Really? Tell me more." Noor laughed, patted Hansa's cheek, and babbled a long string. Then she paused. Hansa nodded. "Mm-hmm." Noor babbled again, happily.

How old was Noor?
Fourteen months.
What does Noor waiting and watching Hansa's face suggest?
It suggests she felt excited and expectant, eager for her grandmother's reply.
What did Hansa do that helped the conversation?
She answered each babble with words and waited, turning Noor's sounds into a back-and-forth.
How might Hansa feel during this game?
She probably feels warm and delighted, enjoying Noor's laughter and cheek pats.

Read this:

"Pa-pa!" said Sonali, holding up a spoon.
"Yes, Sonali! Papa's here!" said Kashish.
Sonali banged the spoon. "Ba!"
"Ba? A ball?"
"Ba!" She stopped, watching his face.
"Ball! Where's the ball?"
Sonali pointed at the sofa. "Da!"
"There it is! You found it!"
Sonali squealed and threw her arms up. "Pa-pa!"
"Yes, Papa."
She waited. He waited. Then she laughed and started again.

What was Sonali holding up?
A spoon.
How did Sonali seem to feel when Kashish said 'You found it'?
She seemed delighted and proud, squealing and throwing her arms up.
What could Kashish keep doing to help Sonali's early talking?
Keep replying to each sound, naming things like the ball, and pausing so Sonali gets her turn.
What is this back-and-forth like for Kashish?
He seems happy and engaged, enjoying their little conversation.

Read this:

Toddler room note, Monday.
Mahima (18 months) sat with Pallavi, our new carer, during water play. She splashed and said, "Ah!" then stopped and looked at Pallavi. Pallavi said, "Ah! Splash!" Mahima grinned, splashed again, "Ah-da!" and waited. This went on for nearly ten minutes, Mahima waiting each time for her turn to come back.
Mahima is usually quiet in the mornings, so this was lovely to see. I told her father at pickup, and suggested bath-time splash talk at home. I'll pair Pallavi with Mahima again on Wednesday.

How old is Mahima?
18 months.
How can you tell Mahima felt happy during water play?
She grinned, kept splashing and waited eagerly for Pallavi's reply for nearly ten minutes.
What did the note-writer suggest for home, and why?
Bath-time splash talk, so Mahima's father can continue the same back-and-forth that builds early conversation.
How might Pallavi feel after this morning?
Pallavi, as a new carer, probably feels pleased and more connected to Mahima.

Read this:

On the charpai under the neem tree, baby Kishore looked up at his father. "Ba-ba-da!" Then he stopped and stared, waiting. Jatin put down the rope he was twisting. "Ba-ba-da? Is that so?" Kishore kicked his feet and squealed, then said, "Da! Da-goo!" and waited again, eyes wide. "Da-goo," Jatin agreed seriously. A goat bleated by the well. Kishore turned to look, then back to his father, and babbled a long, happy answer.

What was Jatin doing before he answered Kishore?
He was twisting rope.
What does Kishore's waiting and staring suggest?
He seems eager and expectant 😊 wanting his father to answer before he goes on.
How could Jatin keep these exchanges going through the day?
He could keep pausing for Kishore's sounds and answering them while feeding, bathing or walking to the well.
What is it like for Jatin when Kishore babbles back?
Jatin likely feels warm and amused, enjoying a real little conversation with his baby.

Read this:

On the hostel terrace, the party was loud with music, and Dolma had been talking with Vaibhav about a trekking trip for a good quarter of an hour. It had been fun. Dolma noticed the plate of samosas across the room and the conversation slowing. "It was great talking to you," Dolma said, smiling. "I'm off to get something to eat before it disappears. Send me the trek photos?" Vaibhav grinned. "Sure! Save me a samosa." Dolma waved and walked over, not feeling awkward or as if anything had been dropped.

What did Dolma and Vaibhav talk about?
A trekking trip.
What was Dolma feeling when leaving the conversation?
Warm and comfortable. Dolma enjoyed the chat and left smiling, without any awkwardness.
What made Dolma's exit graceful?
Dolma said the chat was great, gave a clear reason for leaving, and asked for the trek photos, which kept the door open.
How might Vaibhav feel about Dolma leaving?
Good and not dismissed. Vaibhav grinned, joked "Save me a samosa" and may look forward to sending the photos.

Read this:

"...and that's why I switched from engineering," said Thomas.
"That makes so much sense," said Farida. "It was really great talking, honestly. I'm going to grab a drink from the kitchen."
"Sure, go."
"Are you coming to the film society thing on Friday? We can continue there."
"Yes, I'll be there."
"Good. Then I'll find you," said Farida. "Thanks for telling me about the switch."
Thomas smiled. "Thanks for asking."
Farida left toward the kitchen, and Thomas turned to the next person, feeling as if the chat had been a good one.

Where did Farida suggest they continue the chat?
At the film society thing on Friday.
What did Thomas feel as Farida walked away?
Pleased and satisfied, as if the chat had gone well, and ready to talk to the next person.
What did Farida do that made leaving warm?
Farida said it was great talking, gave a reason for going, suggested continuing at the film society on Friday, and thanked Thomas.
How might Farida have felt on leaving toward the kitchen?
Probably warm about the chat, since Farida said it was really great talking, thanked Thomas and planned to find Thomas on Friday.

Read this:

At Sangeeta's birthday party last month, I got stuck near the balcony with her, talking about the college canteen. It was a nice chat, but I was starving and the biryani was disappearing.
Earlier that evening, I'd seen someone just walk away from a person mid-sentence, and that person looked hurt. I didn't want to do that.
So when there was a natural pause, I smiled and said, "It was really great talking about this. I'm off to get some food before it's gone. Catch you later?" Sangeeta laughed. "Go, go! Save me a kebab." I brought her one, actually.
The next week she messaged me first, asking if I wanted to join her study group. I think that small, warm exit mattered more than I realised. I'm Deepak, by the way, still bad at parties but getting better.

What was disappearing at the party?
The biryani.
What was Deepak feeling before leaving the conversation?
Deepak was hungry and a little worried about leaving rudely, having seen someone look hurt after an abrupt exit.
What made Deepak's exit graceful?
Deepak waited for a pause, said it was great talking, named the reason for leaving and added 'Catch you later?', keeping it warm.
How did Sangeeta respond to the exit?
She laughed, asked for a kebab and later messaged Deepak first, showing she felt good about the chat.

Read this:

Hostel warden's note, freshers' social, Saturday.
I watched Bhupen, a first-year, doing something many students find hard. He'd been chatting with Vasudha from the second year for about fifteen minutes near the tea counter. I could see he wanted to meet the others from his course, who were waving at him.
He waited for a pause and said, "Vasudha, this was really great. I'm going to say hi to my course people, but let's talk again at the library?" She smiled and said, "Definitely." He left warmly, and she went back to her friends looking pleased.
Later I saw them sitting together at breakfast. I'll mention this at the next freshers' talk as a good example of ending a conversation well.

Where were Bhupen and Vasudha chatting?
Near the tea counter.
How did Vasudha seem to feel after Bhupen left?
She looked pleased, as the warm ending made her feel valued.
Which parts of Bhupen's exit made it work?
He waited for a pause, said it was great, gave a reason and suggested meeting again, which kept the door open.
What would change if Bhupen had just walked off?
Vasudha might have felt dismissed, and they might not have sat together at breakfast later.

Read this:

Saturday night
Cousin's engagement party. Trisha, my cousin's friend, found me by the dessert table and talked for a long time about her law exams. She's lovely! But my feet hurt and Mummy was signalling me to help with the gifts.
I used to just mumble "okay, bye" and vanish. Tonight I tried something new. When Trisha paused, I said, "It was so nice talking to you, I really hope the exams go well. I have to go help Mummy with the gifts now, but let's catch up at the wedding?" Trisha said, "Yes! Save me a seat!"
I walked off feeling light, not guilty. She waved at me twice later.
Sarita

What was Trisha talking about?
Her law exams.
How did Sarita feel walking away?
Sarita felt light and not guilty after ending the chat warmly.
What made Sarita's exit graceful?
It said the talk was nice, wished Trisha luck, gave a clear reason and suggested catching up at the wedding.
How did Trisha react to the exit?
She was happy, asking Sarita to save her a seat and waving twice later.

Read this:

Madhav: how was the farewell party? you were with Nishant's cousin for ages
Parul: 20 mins lol. He's nice but I wanted to see Ishita before she left
Madhav: so how'd you escape 😅
Parul: I just said "It was really great hearing about your trek. I'm off to get some food before it's gone. Catch up at the next meet?"
Parul: and smiled and went
Madhav: and he was ok??
Parul: he said "Totally, go before the samosas vanish" 😄
Parul: and just now he sent me the trek photos he was talking about
Madhav: wow. when I leave conversations I just say "ok bye" and disappear
Parul: yeah that's why people think you're angry 🙂

Who did Parul want to see before she left?
She wanted to see Ishita.
How did Parul feel about ending the chat with Nishant's cousin?
She seemed relaxed and confident, liking him but eager to see Ishita, so leaving didn't make her anxious.
What could Madhav try instead of "ok bye"?
He could thank the person for something specific, say where he's going and suggest catching up later, the way Parul did.
How did Nishant's cousin seem to feel about Parul leaving?
He took it well and felt friendly enough to send her the trek photos afterwards.

Read this:

I am Bidisha, and I am nine. Last Sunday I asked Dadu why we could not eat before the puja, because I was very hungry. Dadu frowned. "Don't answer back. Go and sit down."
I did not answer back. I only asked why. But my face went hot and I ran to my room.
My cousin Kashish came in. "Dadu doesn't mind questions. He minds questions in front of everyone. Write it down, and ask after tea when he's happy."
I wrote it in my notebook and asked after tea. Dadu put down his cup and said, "Come here." He told me a long story about why fasting is done. It was my first time hearing it.

How old is Bidisha?
Bidisha is nine.
What was Bidisha feeling when Dadu said "Don't answer back"?
Bidisha felt hurt and confused, since the question was only a "why". The hot face and running to the room show the sting of not being heard.
What did Kashish suggest that helped Bidisha get an answer?
Kashish suggested writing the question down and asking after tea when Dadu was happy. That gave Bidisha a calm way to be curious without the shame of asking in front of everyone.
How might Dadu have felt about the question the first time?
Dadu may have felt challenged in front of everyone, since Kashish says he minds questions in front of others. Later, over tea, he was glad to explain.

Read this:

Guest visit note, Tuesday. Nandini, class 4, put up her hand in the assembly when our guest, a retired railway inspector, was speaking. "Sir, why do trains not fall off the bridge when it shakes?" The guest, who prizes discipline, said sternly, "Sit down. Children do not interrupt." Nandini sat, looking at her hands, and her lip trembled.
After assembly I sat beside her. I said, "That was a good question, and there is a time to ask it." We wrote it on a slip and put it in the "Ask the Guest" box. The guest answered it kindly on Friday, with a drawing. Nandini smiled the whole afternoon.
Hansa, class teacher

What did Nandini ask the guest?
Nandini asked why trains do not fall off the bridge when it shakes.
What was Nandini feeling as she sat with her lip trembling?
Nandini felt embarrassed and hurt. Sitting down and looking at her hands with a trembling lip shows she felt scolded for being curious.
What did Hansa do to protect Nandini's curiosity while respecting the guest?
Hansa praised the question, wrote it on a slip and put it in the "Ask the Guest" box. That gave Nandini a respectful route to be heard.
How might the guest have seen the interruption at first?
The guest, who prizes discipline, probably saw it as a break in respect. When the question came by slip, the guest could answer kindly.

Read this:

"Jasleen, you ask so many questions. Good. Let me tell you about your Sangeeta Nani when she was nine.
"We lived in Amritsar with my Taya ji, who was very strict. One evening he chased away a stray puppy from our gate with a stick. I asked, 'Taya ji, why can't we keep it? It's so small.' He said, 'Don't answer back to elders,' and walked off. I wasn't answering back. I was asking.
"I cried on the stairs. I thought my questions were bad.
"My Bua found me there. She didn't argue with Taya ji. She gave me an old notebook and said, 'Write your questions here. Every Sunday, bring it to me, and we'll find answers.'
"I filled three notebooks that year. And, Jasleen, the puppy? Bua fed it behind the house. Taya ji pretended not to see.

What did Taya ji say when young Sangeeta asked her question?
He said, "Don't answer back to elders," and walked off.
What was young Sangeeta feeling on the stairs?
She felt hurt and confused, crying because she thought her questions were bad when she had only been asking.
What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
Bua gave young Sangeeta a notebook for questions and a Sunday time to discuss them, which kept respect for Taya ji and still gave her curiosity a way to be heard.
How might Taya ji have seen the question about the puppy?
Taya ji likely saw it as a child challenging his decision, since he valued deference, though later he quietly let the puppy be fed.

Read this:

At the crowded family function in Indore, the drums were so loud that Avni had to lean close to shout. All the children were sitting on a mat on the floor while the adults sat on chairs.
Avni tugged Minakshi Mami's sleeve. "Mami, why do children always sit on the floor? The chairs are empty at the back."
Mami frowned. "Don't answer back, Avni. Go sit."
Avni's face burned. She hadn't meant to be rude. She sat down, arms folded, and didn't eat her gulab jamun.
Later, when the music stopped for dinner, her Nani found her in the corner. "What happened, gudiya?"
Avni told her.
Nani nodded. "It was a fair question, asked at a busy time. Mami was rushing. Ask me anything, anytime." Then she walked Avni to the back and they sat on two of the empty chairs together.

What were the children sitting on?
All the children were sitting on a mat on the floor.
What was Avni feeling after Mami told her not to answer back?
Avni felt embarrassed and hurt, her face burning, because she hadn't meant to be rude and had only asked a question.
How did Nani help Avni, and what could others learn from it?
Nani listened, called it a fair question, explained Mami was rushing, and invited Avni to ask anytime, giving her a place to be heard.
How might Minakshi Mami have seen the question?
Minakshi Mami, busy and rushed at the loud function, likely heard it as a challenge to the elders' rules rather than simple curiosity.

Read this:

In their Kolkata flat, Bidisha watched Mohit Jethu finish a packet of biscuits on the balcony and toss the wrapper over the railing into the lane.
"Jethu, why do you throw plastic outside? Our teacher says it blocks the drains."
Jethu's face darkened. "Don't answer back to your elders. Your teacher doesn't pay the bills here."
Bidisha went quiet, then went to her room and sat on the bed, hugging her knees.
Her mother came in. "I heard. You weren't rude. You asked a real question."
"Then why did he get angry?"
"Jethu grew up when children didn't ask. It feels strange to him." Ma thought. "Tonight at dinner, let's ask it as a question for everyone: where should our rubbish go?"
At dinner, Bidisha asked. Jethu grumbled, but the next morning a small dustbin appeared on the balcony.

What did Jethu throw over the railing?
Jethu tossed the biscuit wrapper over the railing into the lane.
Why did Bidisha sit hugging her knees?
Bidisha felt hurt and confused after being told off for asking a real question she thought was reasonable.
What small step did Ma suggest, and why did it help?
Ma suggested asking the question at dinner for the whole family, so Bidisha could be heard without seeming to challenge Jethu alone.
How did Jethu likely feel when Bidisha asked her question?
Jethu likely felt challenged and a little embarrassed, since he grew up when children did not question elders.

Read this:

"Bade Papa, why did you cut the neem tree? It shaded the whole courtyard."
Darshan lowered his newspaper. "Sachin. Children don't answer back to elders."
"I wasn't answering back. I only asked—"
"Enough."
Sachin's ears went red. He went inside and kicked the doorstop.
Mummy was rolling rotis. "What happened?"
"I asked a question! Now I can't ask anything?"
"You can. Bade Papa grew up where children stayed quiet before elders. On his evening walk, say you've been wondering about the neem, and ask him to tell you."
At dusk Sachin fell into step beside him. "Bade Papa, I keep wondering about the neem. Will you tell me?"
Darshan walked a while. "Its roots were cracking the wall, beta. Your Dada planted it. Cutting it was hard for me too."

What was cracking the wall?
The neem tree's roots were cracking the wall.
How was Sachin feeling when his ears went red?
Sachin felt embarrassed and angry, hurt that a real question was treated as rudeness.
What helped Sachin get a real answer?
Mummy suggested asking on the evening walk, framed as wondering and asking to be told, which gave Sachin a respectful route to be curious.
Why might Darshan have snapped "Enough"?
Darshan grew up where children stayed quiet before elders, and the neem was painful for him, since cutting a tree Dada planted was hard.

Read this:

Every Sunday at four, my grandfather Omkar tells me about the day the river flooded his village. I'm Deepak, and I've heard it maybe thirty times: the boat, the tin trunk, his mother carrying the brass lamp. When I was fifteen I would say, "Nana, I know." Now I just settle into the chair and ask something new.
Last week I asked, "What did the water smell like?" He stopped, looked at the ceiling, and said, "Like wet earth and burnt wood." He had never said that before. His eyes went shiny. I think he wants the story remembered more than he wants me to learn from it.

What does Omkar tell Deepak about every Sunday at four?
Omkar tells Deepak about the day the river flooded his village.
What does Omkar's shiny-eyed reaction suggest Omkar was feeling?
It suggests Omkar felt moved and glad to be asked something new. Recalling a smell no one had asked about brought the memory closer.
What does Deepak do each time the story is told again, and what does it lead to?
Deepak settles in and asks a new question each time. Asking what the water smelled like drew out a detail Omkar had never told before.
How might Omkar have felt when Deepak said "Nana, I know" at fifteen?
Omkar might have felt a little dismissed, as if the story mattered less to the listener than to the teller. Now the new question shows the story is being kept.

Read this:

I watch from my balcony, since Yamini's family sits in the courtyard below every evening. Yamini's Nani was on the cot, telling the flood story again. I've heard it drift up at least four times. She always starts: "That year the river came at midnight."
Yamini, elbows on knees, listened as if it were new. Then Yamini asked, "Nani, who carried the little ones?" The old woman lit up, her hands started moving, and she named two names I'd not heard before.
Yamini didn't correct or hurry her. When it was done Nani patted Yamini's cheek. I don't know what Yamini thinks each time, but Yamini never looks bored.
— Zainab, neighbour

Where does Yamini sit while Nani tells the flood story?
Yamini sits in the courtyard, with elbows on knees, near the cot.
What might Nani have felt when Yamini asked "who carried the little ones?"
Nani seems to have felt delighted and eager, since Nani lit up and started moving hands. Zainab can only judge from what shows outwardly.
What does Yamini do each time the story is repeated?
Yamini listens as if it were new, asks a fresh question and does not correct or hurry Nani. That draws out details that Nani names.
What does Zainab see in Yamini's way of listening?
Zainab sees patient interest, since Yamini never looks bored. Zainab does not claim to know Yamini's thoughts, only what the listening looks like.

Read this:

Friday. Dadu started the story of the 1988 flood again at dinner. Bhupen's cousin Sahil rolled his eyes; they'd heard it maybe forty times. Bhupen put down his phone. "Dadu, what did the water smell like?"
Dadu stopped, surprised. "Like mud and diesel. And fear."
Tuesday. The flood story came again. This time Bhupen asked, "Who rowed the boat?"
"A fisherman called Pobitro. He never took a single rupee." Dadu's voice went soft. "I never thanked him properly."
The next Sunday, Dadu told it once more. Sahil stayed at the table this time and asked, "Did you ever find Pobitro again?"
Dadu looked at both of them for a long moment. "No. But you two know his name now."
Afterward, Bhupen wrote the name, Pobitro, and the smell of mud and diesel in a notebook he'd started keeping.

What did Dadu say the flood water smelled like?
Dadu said it smelled like mud and diesel, and fear.
What was Dadu feeling when he spoke about Pobitro?
Dadu felt tender and regretful, his voice going soft because he never thanked Pobitro properly.
What did Bhupen do that changed how the story felt?
He put down his phone and asked a new question each time, so Dadu felt heard and remembered new details instead of just repeating.
How did Sahil's view change over the week?
Sahil went from bored and eye-rolling to curious enough to stay and ask his own question.

Read this:

"Mehak, you asked how I got so patient with old people. Sit, let me tell you.
"When I was twenty, home from engineering college, my Ammachi would tell the same story every evening: how she came to Kottayam by boat as a bride, with one tin trunk. I knew it by heart. I used to finish her sentences to hurry her along.
"One evening I saw her face fall when I did it. She stopped mid-story and went to bed early.
"Next day, I tried something. When she started, I asked, 'Ammachi, what was in the trunk?' Her eyes lit up. Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother. She'd never told anyone about the pickle.
"After that, I asked one new question each time. She didn't want to teach me anything, Mehak. She wanted to be listened to.
"When she died, Jomon, the one who finished her sentences, knew the most stories of all.

What was in Ammachi's tin trunk?
Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother.
What did Ammachi feel when young Jomon finished her sentences?
Ammachi felt hurt and dismissed, her face falling so much that she stopped mid-story and went to bed early.
What was the turning point in Jomon's story, and why did it work?
Young Jomon asked what was in the trunk instead of hurrying her, and the new question made Ammachi feel heard and share a detail she had never told.
How did the change affect Ammachi?
Ammachi felt listened to and happy, her eyes lighting up as she shared new details.

Read this:

The power had been out for an hour in the Jaipur lane, and Kavitha sat with Lalit Uncle, her eighty-year-old neighbour, on his verandah with a candle and a hand fan. Her own phone was at five percent; her exam notes were waiting.
"Did I tell you about my tailoring shop near Johari Bazaar?" he asked.
He had, many times. The wedding sherwani, the rush before Diwali, the customer who never paid.
Kavitha glanced at her phone, then put it face down. "Tell me again. But this time, who was your first customer?"
Lalit Uncle blinked. "My first? A schoolteacher, Sharma ji. He wanted a kurta with pockets big enough for chalk." He laughed and laughed.
For forty minutes he talked. When the lights came back, he said, "You're a good listener, beti. My own sons only ask about my medicines."
Kavitha studied late that night, and didn't mind.

How long had the power been out?
The power had been out for an hour.
What was Lalit Uncle feeling when he talked about Sharma ji?
Lalit Uncle felt delighted and happy, laughing and laughing as he remembered his first customer.
What choice did Kavitha make, and why did it help?
She put her phone face down and asked a new question about the first customer, which made the old story fresh and made him feel heard.
What would change if Kavitha had excused herself to study?
Lalit Uncle would likely feel lonely and unheard, since he says even his sons only ask about his medicines.

Read this:

Every Sunday after church, Francis climbed to the third floor of the Bandra building with a packet of Indu Aunty's favourite rusks. And every Sunday, between the first cup of tea and the second, she told the story again: her first day at the telephone exchange, the huge board of wires, the supervisor who shouted, the call she put through to the wrong city. Francis knew it by heart. His cousin had once asked, "You've heard it fifty times, why sit there?" But Francis had noticed that Indu Aunty's hands moved differently as she told it, quick and sure, as if plugging in wires. So each week he asked one new thing. Today: "What did you do with your first salary?" She stopped, then laughed. "I bought my mother a steel tiffin. She used it for twenty years." Her eyes were wet. "Nobody ever asked me that."

What did Indu Aunty buy with her first salary?
She bought her mother a steel tiffin.
Why did Francis keep asking one new question each week?
Francis felt fond of Indu Aunty and curious about her life; the way her hands came alive told him the story mattered to her.
What small practice could someone borrow from Francis?
When an elder repeats a story, stay and ask one fresh question, like the first-salary one, instead of saying "you told me already".
What was it like for Indu Aunty to be asked about her first salary?
She was surprised and moved, eyes wet, because nobody had ever asked, and it let her remember her mother and the tiffin.

Read this:

"Asif Bhai, can you ask Abbu for the rolling bag? The blue one with wheels." Irawati dropped onto the sofa beside her brother.
"You said rolling bags were silly."
"That was before. Now twenty-two people in my class have it. Twenty-two!"
"So? Do you like it?"
Irawati paused. "It… rolls."
Asif grinned. "Wow. Strong review."
"If everyone bought it, it must be good. Twenty-two people can't all be wrong."
"Twenty-two people can all see the same advert."
"Bhai!" She hugged her old red backpack to her chest. "I just don't want to be the only one."
"Ah," Asif said, softer. "That's the real reason, na?"
Irawati picked at the zip and didn't answer.

How many people in Irawati's class have the rolling bag?
Twenty-two people.
What does Irawati's pause before saying "It… rolls" suggest?
Irawati doesn't really love the bag itself; the number of classmates who own it is what makes it feel right.
Asif's question "Do you like it?" was a turning point. What could Irawati decide after answering it honestly?
Irawati could decide whether the bag is worth asking for on its own, or talk openly about the fear of being the only one with a different bag.
How does Asif see the reason behind Irawati's request by the end?
Asif realises it is less about the bag and more about not wanting to stand out, so the teasing turns gentle.

Read this:

My name is Francis, and last term I begged for a spinning-top battle set. Everyone in Class 5 had one. At break they crashed tops in a tin tray and shouted. I didn't even like it much. The tops were loud and my fingers hurt from pulling the string. But thirty kids can't all be wrong, I thought. Ankita, who sits next to me, didn't have one either. "I'd rather draw," she said. When Mum finally bought me a set, I played for two weeks. Now it's in my cupboard. Ankita still draws. I kind of wish I'd asked myself what I liked first.

Where did the children crash their tops at break?
In a tin tray.
Why did Francis want the set even though pulling the string hurt?
Francis thought that if thirty kids all had it, it had to be good, even without really enjoying it.
Looking back, what does Francis wish had come first, and how could that help next time?
Francis wishes they had asked what they liked before begging; next time, Francis could try a friend's set for a while before asking for one.
How might Ankita see the whole trend from the next seat?
Ankita seems calm about not having one and happy drawing, so the craze probably looks like something that will pass. 🙂

Read this:

Class 4 observation, Devika, age 9. Today Devika asked if she could 'please, please' get the scented gel pens by Monday. When I asked why, she said, 'Ma'am, the whole class has them. If everyone chose them, they must be the best pens.' I asked which colour she liked. She shrugged: 'Whichever the others have.' Later I saw her borrow a friend's pen, write one line, and hand it back without much interest. I did not lecture. At circle time I asked each child to share one thing they liked that nobody else did. Devika talked about her grandfather's fountain pen for five minutes, smiling. I will mention this to her mother. — Manjula Rao, class teacher

Which pens did Devika want by Monday?
The scented gel pens.
What does Devika's shrug about the colour suggest?
It suggests Devika feels little real interest in the pens themselves; the wish comes from everyone else having them.
What did Manjula Rao choose to do instead of lecturing, and what did it bring out?
Manjula Rao asked each child to share something only they liked, and Devika happily talked about the grandfather's fountain pen, a liking that was truly Devika's own.
How might Devika's mother use this note when the pens come up at home?
Devika's mother could ask what Devika really enjoys, like the fountain pen, instead of simply buying what the class has.

Read this:

Wednesday

Dear Diary,
Everybody in 5C has a squishy on their bag now. A peach one, a cloud one, a strawberry with a face. Today I counted: nineteen. NINETEEN. I asked Ammi for one after school and she asked what I like about them. I said they're squishy. She waited. I said everyone has one, so they must be good, right? Nineteen people can't all be making a mistake.
Farida doesn't have one. She says they smell like an eraser and she'd rather save for the drawing book. I squeezed Mahnoor's squishy at lunch and honestly it was just okay.
But I still want one. A cloud one.
Deepika

How many squishies did Deepika count on bags in 5C?
She counted nineteen.
How does Deepika seem to feel about not having a squishy yet?
Deepika seems left out and a little envious, since nineteen classmates have one, even though Mahnoor's squishy felt just okay.
What question could help Deepika decide whether to spend on a squishy?
Deepika could ask what to choose if no one in 5C had one, the way Farida thinks about the drawing book.
How might Farida feel being one of the few in 5C without a squishy?
She seems settled in her own choice, though she might sometimes feel left out when the others compare theirs.

The weekly haat set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur every Thursday. Nikita dragged her aunt Tanuja straight past the vegetables to the stall with the light-up pens. "This one, Maushi. The one with the blinking tip." "Do you need a new pen?" Nikita counted on her fingers. "Rupa has it, Salma has it, both Patil boys, the whole back bench. The whole of Class 6 bought it last week." "And what does it write like?" Nikita paused. "Blue." Tanuja laughed. "So many people bought it," Nikita insisted. "They must know something." Tanuja picked up a pen, clicked it, and scribbled on her palm. The ink skipped. She held it out without a word.

Where was the weekly haat set up?
It was set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur.
Why did Nikita insist that the pen was good?
She was eager to have what the whole of Class 6 had and felt confident they must know something, even though she couldn't say how it wrote.
What turning point could help Nikita choose for herself here?
Testing the pen on Tanuja's palm showed the ink skipping, which gives Nikita a real fact to weigh against the crowd.
What was Tanuja hoping Nikita would notice when she held out the pen without a word?
Tanuja seemed to want Nikita to see for herself that the pen skipped, rather than being told not to buy it.

Monday. Two boys in Farhan's class came with shiny blue space-rocket bags. Farhan looked at them and shrugged. His old green bag was fine.
Wednesday. Now six children had rocket bags. Hrithik said, "Everyone has one. It's the best bag." Farhan looked down at his green bag. It suddenly looked babyish.
Friday. Farhan begged Ammi for a rocket bag. "Why? You love your green one," she said.
"Because everyone has it. Twelve people, Ammi! They can't all be wrong."
Ammi asked what he liked about it. Farhan thought hard. "It's… blue?" He wasn't really sure.

How many children had rocket bags by Wednesday?
Six children had rocket bags by Wednesday.
Why does Farhan suddenly want the rocket bag?
He feels left out and uneasy, because so many classmates have it that it seems it must be best, not because he likes it.
What question from Ammi helped Farhan think?
Asking what he liked about the bag showed Farhan he wasn't really sure, apart from everyone having it.
How might Hrithik feel about the rocket-bag trend?
Hrithik seems excited and sure it's the best bag, maybe enjoying being part of the group.

You want those sneakers with the lights, beta? Everyone has them? Sit with your Ujjwal Nana. Let me tell you about the spinning tops.
When I was ten, one boy brought a red wooden top to school. By the next week, every boy had one. I had a marble set I loved, but suddenly I felt like a fool with it.
I nagged my mother for three days. "Why do you want it?" she asked. I said, "Everyone has one! Twenty boys can't be wrong!"
She bought it. I spun it for a week, then it went in a drawer. I went back to marbles with my friend Faizan, who never cared about tops at all.
The top wasn't bad. I just never wanted it. I wanted what everyone had.

What toy did young Ujjwal love before the tops came?
He had a marble set he loved.
Why did young Ujjwal suddenly feel like a fool with his marbles?
He felt embarrassed and left out, because every boy had a top, and so many people seemed to prove tops were better.
What turning point in the story showed young Ujjwal what he really wanted?
After spinning the top for a week and putting it in a drawer, he went back to marbles, showing he had only wanted what everyone had.
How might Faizan have seen the spinning-top craze?
Faizan never cared about tops, so he probably felt calm and unbothered while everyone else rushed to get one.

Every child in Dhruv's class seemed to have the new football card album. At break they traded stickers loudly. Dhruv stood at the edge.
At home he asked his sister Kalyani to help him ask Papa. "But you don't even watch football," Kalyani said.
"Everyone has it. Twenty-five kids. It must be good."
There was a problem: the album cost more than the pocket money he had left that month, and Papa had said no extra money until his birthday.
Dhruv sat on his bed feeling miserable. Kalyani sat beside him. "What would you actually do with it?"
He thought. "Trade stickers… so I can be in the circle at break."
"So it's the circle you want, not the album."
Dhruv was quiet for a long time.

How many kids did Dhruv say had the album?
He said twenty-five kids had it.
What was Dhruv feeling as he sat on his bed?
He felt miserable and left out, sure the album must be good because so many had it.
What could Dhruv do instead of buying the album?
He could find other ways to join the break-time group, like asking to watch the trading or sharing a game he enjoys.
How does Kalyani see Dhruv's wish?
Kalyani sees that Dhruv doesn't like football and wants to belong more than he wants the album itself.

By December, nearly every girl in Class 4B at Shalini's Bengaluru school had the same purple backpack with a unicorn zip. Shalini's own blue bag was only a year old and had never torn. But every morning she counted: twelve purple bags yesterday, fourteen today.
"Amma, I need the purple one," she told Minakshi at the market.
"Do you like it?" Minakshi asked.
Shalini hesitated. The unicorn looked a bit silly. "Everyone has it. So it must be the best."
Minakshi turned the price tag over. "Tell me one thing it does better than your blue bag."
Shalini thought hard, frowning at the unicorn.

How many purple bags did Shalini count today?
Fourteen.
Why does Shalini want the purple bag even though the unicorn looks silly?
She feels left out and eager to fit in, sure that if so many girls have it, it must be the best.
Why is Minakshi's question a good one?
It asks Shalini to judge the bag by what it does, not by how many classmates own it.
How might Minakshi see Shalini's reason?
Minakshi likely sees that Shalini wants to belong more than she wants the bag itself.

Read this:

"Didi, I need a battle top."
"A what?"
"The spinning tops with the launcher. Everyone in 5C has one."
"Do you like them?"
"I haven't played. But thirty people have them, Didi."
"So?"
"So thirty people can't all be wrong."
"Remember the slime craze?"
"...Yes."
"You begged for slime. You used it twice."
"That was different."
"How?"
"Everyone had slime too... oh."
"What do you actually like playing at recess, Ganga?"
"Hopscotch with Minu."
"Does Minu have a top?"
"No."
"Borrow one first and see if you even like it," Ishita said.
"Okay. But if I like it, you'll buy one?"
"We'll see."

How many people have tops, according to Ganga?
Thirty people.
What does "thirty people can't all be wrong" suggest about Ganga's feelings?
Ganga feels a strong pull to fit in and trusts the crowd more than any real liking for the tops.
What small step did Ishita suggest?
Borrowing a top first to see whether Ganga actually likes it.
How does Ishita see the craze?
Ishita sees it like the slime craze: wanted because everyone had it, then quickly forgotten.

Looking back, I'm a bit embarrassed. I'm Imran, and in Class 6 everybody was playing that football card game, the one with the shiny player cards. Yusuf had forty cards. The whole back bench traded at lunch.
I didn't even like football much; I liked drawing. But when twenty kids all want the same thing, it feels like they must know something you don't. So I saved my pocket money for three weeks and bought two packs. I traded for exactly one lunch break. Then the craze moved to marbles.
The cards are still in a shoebox under my bed. What I really wanted, I think, was to sit on that back bench.

How many cards did Yusuf have?
Forty cards.
What was Imran really feeling in Class 6, looking back?
Imran felt left out and wanted to belong, so buying the cards felt like a ticket to the back bench.
What could Imran have asked before saving for three weeks?
Whether Imran actually liked the game, or only wanted it because so many classmates had it.
How might Yusuf have seen Imran joining the trades?
Yusuf probably welcomed another trader, not knowing Imran didn't care much for football.

Class teacher's note to Shankar's parents, after the monsoon break

Shankar seemed unsettled this week. Since school reopened, about fifteen children have come with the same blue astronaut bag. On Tuesday Shankar kept his old bag under the desk instead of on the hook. On Wednesday he asked me, 'Everyone has it, so it must be the best one, no?' When I asked what he liked about it, he thought, then said, 'The zip? I don't know. Everyone has it.' His own bag is in good condition, and I told him I like the patch on it. I am writing so you know where the requests at home may be coming from. Perhaps ask him what he would like about the new bag, not just who has it.

Kishore, Class 4B

How many children came with the blue astronaut bag?
About fifteen children.
Why did Shankar keep his old bag under the desk?
He probably felt embarrassed and left out, because so many classmates had the new astronaut bag.
What does Kishore suggest the parents try, and why might it help?
Asking Shankar what he would like about the bag, not just who has it, so he can notice whether he wants it or just wants to match.
How might Shankar's parents feel reading the note?
They may feel relieved to understand where his requests are coming from and better able to talk with him calmly.

Read this:

25 December

Merry Christmas! Lalremsiami came over with plum cake and showed me the farm game on her mum's phone. EVERYONE in 5C plays it. Riya, Tanmay, both Sharma twins, even Kabir, who hates games. Lalremsiami says 32 people in our class have a farm. 32! That's nearly all of us. So it has to be super fun, right? I watched her play for a while. You plant carrots and wait. And wait. Honestly it was kind of boring. But I still want it so much. If 32 people like it, maybe I just didn't get it yet? I asked Papa. He said, 'Tell me one thing you liked while you watched.' I couldn't say one. I'm still asking again tomorrow.

Devika

How many people in the class have a farm, according to Lalremsiami?
32 people in the class have a farm.
What is Devika feeling about the farm game by the end of the entry?
Devika feels torn: a bit bored by what was seen, yet still wanting the game badly because so many classmates play it.
How could Papa build on his question?
Papa could let Devika try the game a few times and then talk about whether it is actually fun, rather than how many people play it.
How might Lalremsiami see Devika's interest?
Lalremsiami probably sees it as a chance to share a favourite game with a friend, not as pressure.

During the week of the temple fair at Sirsi, every child in Class 3 seemed to own the same metal spinning top with a red light inside. They spun them on the school verandah at every break. Aditi's wooden top, the one Ajja had carved, stayed in her bag. 'Why don't you get the light-top?' asked Charu. 'Everyone has it.' That evening at the fair, Aditi tugged Amma's sari at the toy stall. 'That one. Please. Everyone has it.' Amma held it out to her. 'What do you like about it?' Aditi frowned. It was heavy. The light hurt her eyes a little. 'Everyone...' she began, then stopped. 'So many kids can't be wrong, na?' Amma waited. Aditi looked down at her bag, where the wooden top was.

Who had carved Aditi's wooden top?
Ajja had carved it.
Why did Aditi stop in the middle of saying 'Everyone...'?
Aditi felt unsure and a little confused, noticing she didn't actually like the heavy top and had wanted it mainly because everyone had one.
What did Amma do that helped Aditi think?
Amma asked what she liked about the top and then waited, giving Aditi space to notice her real reasons.
How might Charu see Aditi's wooden top?
Charu seems to see it as odd or out of date, simply because it is different from what everyone else has.

In the New Year holidays in Kyoto, Hiroshi went shopping with his mother for the new school term. At the stationery shop, he pointed at the blue robot pencil case. "That one." "You liked the green one last week," his mother said. "Everyone in my class has the robot one. Tariq has it. Even the teacher said it's nice." "Do you like it?" Hiroshi hesitated. The robot's eyes were a bit strange. But twenty-six people couldn't all be wrong about it. "Yes," he said. His mother bought it. At home, he put it next to his old green one and looked at them for a while. He wasn't sure which he liked. He only knew which one everyone had.

Who in Hiroshi's class has the robot pencil case?
Tariq has it, and everyone in his class.
Why did Hiroshi hesitate when his mother asked if he liked it?
He felt unsure, because he thought the robot's eyes were a bit strange but wanted what everyone else had.
What question could help Hiroshi choose next time?
He could ask himself which one he would pick if nobody in class had either, to find his own preference.
How does Hiroshi's mother see his choice?
She seems doubtful, remembering he liked the green one and asking whether he really likes the robot case.

At every family gathering in the village that winter, someone said it: the new mobile tower behind the temple was making the cows give less milk. Chacha said it at the engagement. Sarita Bhabhi said it while serving kheer. By the wedding, nobody even said "maybe" any more; heads just nodded. Vijay, home from the city for the week, listened and chewed slowly. He didn't want to be the know-it-all nephew. So when the talk turned to cows again, he asked with real curiosity, "Where did we first hear that? I keep trying to remember." There was a pause. Chacha scratched his head. "Ramdin said it at the dairy, I think." Sarita laughed. "And Ramdin heard it from his brother-in-law." Someone mentioned the dry monsoon, and how poor the fodder had been. Nobody felt caught out. The talk simply grew a little more careful.

What did everyone at the gatherings say about the mobile tower?
It was making the cows give less milk.
Why did Vijay ask his question with real curiosity instead of correcting the family?
He didn't want to be the know-it-all nephew; he hoped to get his elders thinking without making them feel caught out.
How did Vijay's question change the conversation, and why did it work?
It traced the claim back to Ramdin at the dairy and led others to mention the dry monsoon and poor fodder. Because nobody was shamed, people grew more careful instead of defensive.
How might Chacha have felt answering Vijay?
Chacha paused and scratched his head, perhaps a little puzzled to find the claim came from a chat at the dairy, but not insulted, since Vijay asked rather than accused.

Read this:

At the Thursday board-game nights in Lars's flat in Gothenburg, the old windows always came up. The panes were wavy, thicker at the bottom, and every few weeks someone explained why: glass is secretly a slow liquid, and over a hundred years it had sagged. Daniel said it first, back in the autumn. Then Maja repeated it to a new guest, and by spring it was simply part of the flat, like the creaky floor. Lars had nodded along a dozen times. One evening, while Daniel was telling it again to his cousin, Lars asked, "Where did we first hear that? I honestly can't remember." Daniel grinned. "A teacher, maybe? A quiz show?" Nobody was sure. Lars looked it up while the dice rolled: old glass was often made uneven, and builders tended to set the thick edge at the bottom. "Huh," said Daniel. "Better story, actually."

What explanation did the group give for the wavy windows?
Glass is secretly a slow liquid, and over a hundred years it had sagged.
Why might Lars have asked "Where did we first hear that?" rather than saying the idea was wrong?
Lars wasn't sure either and wanted to wonder about it together, not make Daniel look foolish in front of a guest.
What did Lars do after asking, and how did it help the group?
Looked it up while the dice rolled and shared that old glass was made uneven with the thick edge set at the bottom, which settled it without an argument.
How did Daniel take the correction?
Daniel grinned and called it a better story, which suggests he felt curious rather than embarrassed, because nobody shamed him.

On night shifts at the district hospital, it came up whenever the ward got busy: "Full moon. Always crazy on a full moon." Sister Preeti said it, the ward boys said it, even the guard at the gate said it. Jagdish, eight months into the job, had started saying it too, and one night noticed he didn't know why. At the 2 am tea break he asked carefully, "Sister, where did we first hear the full-moon thing? From training?" Preeti blew on her tea. "From my seniors, I suppose. Everyone just knows." "Should we look at our admissions register? Just for fun?" She laughed, but she pulled it out. Over three months, the full-moon nights weren't any busier than the others. Preeti tapped the page. "Hm. The busy nights just stick in the mind more." She didn't seem offended, only curious.

What did the admissions register show?
Over three months, the full-moon nights weren't any busier than the others.

It was the kabaddi team's evening practice in a Nagpur school ground. Tushar, the senior captain, pointed at the new junior who had come late. "Pankaj, make him do ten push-ups."
Ten was fine. Pankaj counted.
"Now twenty. Discipline matters." Tushar's voice was calm, almost bored.
The junior's arms were shaking. Pankaj's throat went tight. Should he say something? But he had already done ten. Stopping now would look like saying Tushar was wrong.
"Keep going," Tushar said. "Just continue."
Pankaj kept counting. His voice cracked on fourteen. The junior's face was red and wet.
At seventeen, the PE teacher came across the ground. "Stop. Now." She knelt by the junior. Pankaj sat down on the grass, his hands trembling.

How many push-ups did Tushar first ask for?
He first asked for ten push-ups.
What was Pankaj feeling as his voice cracked on fourteen?
He felt tense and distressed, doubting it was right, but stopping felt harder than going on because he had already started.
What could Pankaj have done at the first doubt?
He could have stopped counting and said the junior had done enough, or gone to find the PE teacher himself.
How might the junior have felt doing push-ups while two seniors watched?
The junior would have felt humiliated and exhausted, with no way to refuse two seniors.

Read this:

"Disha, just pin this one photo on the board."
"Vaibhav, that's the Class 9 boy asleep in the library. Why?"
"It's a council joke. Harmless. We do one every year."
"...Okay. One."
"Good. Now this one. Him with his mouth open."
"Vaibhav, I don't like this."
"You already pinned the first. The second's the same thing."
"It feels mean."
"Relax. I'm the council head. If anyone asks, I told you to."
"My hands are sweating."
"Just continue. Two more and we're done."
Disha picked up the third photo. Her fingers shook so much the pin fell. She stared at it on the floor.
"I'm not doing the rest," she said quietly, and began taking the first two down.

Who was in the photos?
The Class 9 boy was in the photos.
What was Disha feeling when her hands were sweating?
She felt tense and guilty, sensing it was mean, while Vaibhav's calm authority made stopping feel hard.
What helped Disha stop, and what could make it easier next time?
Noticing her own shaking gave her the moment to refuse; next time she could stop at the first photo, when saying no is easiest.
How might the Class 9 boy feel if he saw the photos on the board?
He would likely feel embarrassed and exposed, laughed at by the whole school for being asleep.

Read this:

I was fifteen when Coach Jeevan picked me for the district football final. I'm Darshan. Before the match he took me aside. "Their number 9 is their best. Just a small bump early. Make him nervous."
A bump. That seemed okay. In the first ten minutes I bumped him.
At half-time Coach said, "Good. Now a harder one. Leave a mark. Just continue what you started."
I felt sick. I remember my knees shaking in the tunnel. But I'd already done the first one. Stopping felt like admitting the first was wrong too.
In the second half I tackled number 9 from behind. He went down holding his ankle.
We won. I've never felt worse after a win.

What did Coach Jeevan first ask for?
He asked for just a small bump early.
What was Darshan feeling in the tunnel at half-time?
Darshan felt sick and afraid, knowing a harder tackle was wrong but feeling trapped by having already done the first.
What could Darshan have done at the first doubt?
Darshan could have refused the first bump, when saying no was easiest, or told the coach the plan felt unfair.
How might number 9 have felt going down holding his ankle?
He would have felt pain and shock, and maybe anger at being targeted on purpose.

Read this:

Assistant coach's note, athletics camp, day 3.
The head coach told Sharmila, the team captain, to 'toughen up' Kiran, a new runner who had missed a morning session. It started small: one extra lap. Then another. The coach kept saying, calmly, 'Continue. It's for his own good.' By the sixth lap in the midday heat, Kiran was stumbling and asking to stop. Sharmila was biting her lip, glancing at the coach, clearly upset, but she kept counting laps aloud. When I stepped in and stopped it, she burst into tears. 'I wanted to stop after two. But he was so calm, and I'd already done two.' I sat Kiran in the shade with water and called the camp doctor. I reported the instruction to the camp director immediately, and spoke with Sharmila, who asked to talk to Kiran herself tonight.

How many laps had Kiran run when the assistant coach stepped in?
Six laps, in the midday heat.
What was Sharmila feeling as she kept counting laps?
Sharmila felt distressed and torn, biting her lip and wanting to stop, but the coach's calm orders made going on feel easier.
What protective steps did the assistant coach take?
Stopped the laps, gave Kiran shade and water, called the camp doctor and reported the instruction to the camp director at once.
What was the punishment like for Kiran?
Kiran was exhausted and frightened, stumbling and asking to stop while no one listened.

Thursday night.
I can't stop thinking about rehearsal. Rhea Didi, the drama club head, told me to 'coach' Asif from Class 8 because he stammers on his lines. First she said, make him repeat the line. Fine. Then, make him say it louder. Then, in front of everyone, make him say it until he gets it right. Asif's face went red, then white. I kept looking at Rhea Didi, and she just nodded and said, calmly, 'Continue, he needs this.' And I did. Four more times. My hands were shaking. I felt like two people: one saying 'again', one screaming stop. It felt harder to stop than to go on, because I'd already started. After, Asif ran out. I told Ms Fernandes before I left school, and she found Asif and called his parents. Tomorrow I'm apologising.
Keerthana

What did Rhea Didi say when Asif went red?
'Continue, he needs this.'
What was Keerthana feeling while making Asif repeat the line?
Keerthana felt torn and distressed, hands shaking, one part saying 'again' and another screaming to stop.
What made it hard to stop, and what could help next time?
The calm authority and having already started; next time Keerthana could stop at the first doubt, say no, or go straight to a teacher.
How was the rehearsal for Asif?
Asif felt humiliated and frightened, going red then white before running out.

Disha: i did something awful
Chandrika: what

Disha: first she said just remove her. then 'post the meme, it's team discipline'. then 'reply to the comments, keep it going'

What was the first thing the captain told Disha to do?
Remove Tanya from the team group.
How did Disha feel while following the captain's orders?
Disha felt distressed and uneasy, hands shaking, but each step made stopping feel harder.
What did Chandrika urge, and why was it right?
Delete the posts and tell the coach right away, so an adult could protect Tanya the same day.
How is Tanya affected?
Tanya is hurt and humiliated, crying in the washroom after being removed and mocked.

The monsoon camp for the district kho-kho team was held in the school hall because the ground had flooded. On Saturday, Coach Tiwari handed Nirmala, the captain, a sheet. "Read out the fitness scores. Everyone should hear." Easy enough. Nirmala read them. Then the coach tapped the last line. "Now read my comment on Himani." It said: Weak link. Drags the team down. Himani, fourteen and the youngest, was staring at her shoes. Nirmala's voice stopped. "Sir, maybe I could just..." "Just continue, captain. It's for her own good." His voice was calm, as if this were ordinary. Nirmala's hands were shaking. Stopping now felt harder than going on. She read it. Himani's eyes filled. That night Nirmala couldn't sleep, replaying the moment her voice had stopped and then started again.

What did the coach's comment on Himani say?
Weak link. Drags the team down.
What was Nirmala feeling when her voice stopped?
She felt tense and full of doubt, knowing it would hurt Himani, but the coach's calm "just continue" made stopping feel harder than going on.
What could Nirmala do now?
She could apologise to Himani, tell her the words were unfair, and tell a trusted teacher or her parents about the coach's instruction.
What was it like for Himani to hear the comment read aloud?
It was humiliating; as the youngest, Himani stared at her shoes and her eyes filled in front of the whole team.

Nursery note, Friday. Trisha called across the room from the story corner while I was helping another child with a zip. I did not hear at first. After a few calls with no answer, Trisha stopped, walked over, put both hands on my knee and looked up. I turned straight away. I wrote down that Trisha's fix was to move closer once calling had failed. Next time I will thank Trisha for coming over and look up sooner. Dhruv

Where did Trisha call from?
Trisha called across the room from the story corner.
What was Trisha feeling when calling brought no answer?
Trisha was probably a little frustrated and determined to be seen, which is why Trisha walked over and put both hands on the knee.
What could Trisha try if walking over does not get noticed, and why?
Trisha could say the name aloud while touching an arm, because touch plus voice is clear even in a busy room.
How does the plan look to Dhruv?
Dhruv was busy with another child and missed the calls, and sees that Trisha's step of moving closer worked and plans to notice sooner next time.

Read this:

In the farmhouse near Nashik, Vijay sat by the grain sacks. "Dada! Dada!" he called across the room. His dada, Tarun, was mending a rope and didn't look up. Vijay tried again, quieter. Nothing. He got up, walked the long way past the goat pen, and put both hands flat on Dada's knee. He tipped his head back and looked up. Tarun put the rope down. "Ah, Vijay."

What was Tarun mending?
He was mending a rope.
What was Vijay feeling after his calls got no answer?
He was probably disappointed but determined, so he walked over instead of giving up.
Which step made the difference, and why?
Putting his hands on Dada's knee and looking up, because being close is much harder to miss than calling across a room.
How does Vijay's touch feel to Tarun?
It gently pulls Tarun out of his work, and he responds warmly by putting the rope down.

Read this:

"Baba?" Rania called from the rug in the Amman flat. Her father, Kwame, was at the sink, radio on. "Baba!" No turn. Rania pushed up, toddled across the tiles and pressed both palms against his knee. Then she looked up at him, chin tilted. Kwame looked down and switched off the tap. "Hello, my sweet. You came to find me?"

What was on while Kwame was at the sink?
The radio was on.
What was Rania feeling when she pressed her palms on his knee?
She wanted him badly and felt determined after her calls went unheard.
What could Kwame change so Rania's first call works?
He could keep the radio lower or glance round now and then, so her voice reaches him from across the room.
How does Kwame see Rania's walk over?
He sees she has come looking for him and responds warmly, switching off the tap.

Dinner was on the table in the sixth-floor flat, and Vijay stared at his bowl of spinach and beans. He tapped the spoon twice. "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" His father Suraj raised an eyebrow. "All of them?" "All. Even the green ones." "Then two stories." Vijay made a face at the first bite, ate steadily after that, and showed the empty bowl. Then he ran to pick two books from the shelf.

How many stories did Vijay ask for?
He asked for two stories tonight.
What might Vijay be feeling as he looks at his bowl and makes his offer?
He is probably a little reluctant about the spinach but eager for the second story, so he is willing to trade one for the other.
What other approach could Vijay use to get the extra story, and why?
He could ask for a smaller helping and finish that first. A goal that feels smaller is easier to reach, and he would still earn the story.
How does Suraj see Vijay's offer?
Suraj hears a clear deal and gets the vegetables eaten. He also sees his son planning instead of refusing.

Read this:

"Beans again?" Varun poked the plate.
"Beans and carrots," said Amma. "Eat up."
Varun looked at the green pile, then at Deepika, who was reading a comic.
"Amma. If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?"
Amma raised her eyebrows. "All of them? The carrots too?"
"All. Carrots too."
"Two stories, then. Deepika reads one, I read one."
"Hey!" said Deepika. Then she shrugged. "Fine. But I pick mine."
Varun ate the beans in big fast bites, making faces, and held up his clean plate. "Two stories!"

Which vegetables were on Varun's plate?
Beans and carrots.
What was Varun feeling as he ate in big, fast bites?
His faces show he didn't enjoy the beans, but he felt determined and excited about getting two stories.
What might make Varun's deal fairer for everyone?
He could ask Deepika too, since she is one of the readers; naming the price and the prize worked because everyone knew the terms.
How does Deepika see the deal?
Deepika is surprised to be pulled into it, but agrees as long as she gets to pick her own story.

Note for Gopika's parents, Wednesday evening. Dinner went well today, which surprised me. Gopika saw the palak and started to push the bowl away, then stopped and asked, "If I eat all my vegetables, can I have two stories tonight?" I said yes, if the bowl was empty. It took a while, with a few sighs, but it was empty. Madhav wanted the same deal for his peas, so I agreed for him too. We read two stories each on the big bed. Both were asleep by nine. You may want to keep using this; both of them seemed proud of their clean bowls.

What vegetable did Gopika start to push away?
Gopika started to push away the palak.
What do Gopika's sighs over the bowl suggest?
They suggest Gopika found the palak hard going and felt reluctant, but stayed determined because two stories were promised.
Which other approach could the note-writer try on nights when Gopika doesn't bargain?
State a simple rule up front, like 'vegetables first, then stories', so the deal is clear without Gopika having to ask.
How does the note-writer see the deal?
The note-writer was surprised it worked so well and suggests the parents keep using it, since both children seemed proud.

Note to Rashmi's mother, Thursday. Rashmi came to the playgroup with one shoe on. I did not point to where it might be. I asked, "What did you do first today?" She thought, then went step by step in order. First the bedroom, where she looked under the cot. Then the verandah. Then the front gate, where she had played with the swing. The shoe was behind the flowerpot there. She held it up and put it on herself. Going through her day in order helped more than running about. Manoj, playgroup teacher

Where was Rashmi's missing shoe found?
It was behind the flowerpot at the front gate.
How was Rashmi feeling as she went from place to place?
She seems calm and focused, working through her morning in order. The note says she went step by step instead of running about.
What else could Rashmi do next time so the shoe does not go missing?
She could put both shoes on the same spot each time after playing. Then the first place she looks is the right one.
How might Rashmi's mother feel when she reads the note?
She would probably feel reassured. She learns Rashmi managed to find it herself, with only one question from the teacher.

Read this:

It was almost time for the temple fair, and Trisha had only one sandal. "Go back through the day," Ajji always said. So she did. First the bedroom: under the cot, only a lizard. Then the verandah, where she had shelled peas with Keerthana that morning: a pea pod, no sandal. Then the gate, where they had played hopscotch in the dust. There, half buried beside the gatepost, was the pink strap. Trisha pulled it out, banged the dust off, and ran to catch up with Keerthana on the road.

Where did Trisha find the sandal?
Half buried beside the gatepost.
What does Trisha's run down the road suggest she was feeling?
She seemed relieved and happy, eager to reach Keerthana and the fair with both sandals on.
What else could Trisha do so she doesn't lose a sandal before an outing?
She could keep both sandals together by the door; going back through the day in order worked because it narrowed the search to three places.
How might Keerthana see the search?
Keerthana had been part of Trisha's day, so Keerthana may have waited on the road, glad the fair wasn't missed.

Ulla had one red rain boot on and one sock foot, and the kindergarten bus came at eight. Papa Liam checked the clock. "Think back," he said. Ulla closed her eyes. "Bedroom. Then the porch. Then the gate, where I jumped in the puddle." She padded to the bedroom first. Nothing under the bed. Then the porch, where the rain jackets hung. Only a wet umbrella. Then the garden gate, and there it was, lying on its side in the big puddle, full of water. Ulla tipped it out, squelched her foot in, and made the bus just in time.

Where did Ulla find the boot?
By the garden gate, lying on its side in the big puddle, full of water.
What might Ulla have felt as she squelched her foot into the wet boot?
She probably felt relieved to have found it and to catch the bus, even if the wet boot was uncomfortable.
What else could Ulla do so this doesn't happen before the bus?
Put both boots by the door straight after playing outside; retracing worked, but it only just beat the bus.
How might Papa Liam experience the morning?
Watching the clock, Papa Liam was probably tense, and then relieved that thinking back found the boot so quickly.
