The little grocery shop near the bus stand would shut at eight, and the clock said twenty to. Bidisha's mother had given her a long list in a hurry: apples, bananas, spinach, tomatoes, onions, milk, curd, paneer. Her brother Ojas hopped beside her. "That's so many!" Bidisha stopped outside the door. "Three groups," she said. "Fruits first: apples, bananas. Vegetables: spinach, tomatoes, onions. Then milk, curd, paneer." She repeated it in the queue, and went through the shop one shelf at a time. Nothing was missed, and Ojas carried the bag home, proud to be useful.

When would the grocery shop shut?
The shop would shut at eight.
What was Bidisha feeling outside the shop, and how did the grouping help?
Bidisha felt pressed for time and a little overwhelmed by the long list, but three groups turned one big list into three small ones she could hold.
What alternative approach could Bidisha use, and why?
Bidisha could ask her mother to write the list down or take a picture of the list to check in the shop. That would keep the items in front of her even when rushed.
How does the shopping trip look to Ojas?
Ojas hopped along, said there were so many items and later carried the bag proudly, so Ojas felt part of the job and pleased to help.

Read this:

Outside the vegetable market in Lajpat Nagar, Gargi's father, Jeevan, read out the list on his phone: "Apples, milk, onions, bananas, curd, tomatoes, paneer, oranges, potatoes." Gargi held up a hand. "Stop. Nine things jumping around. Let me fix it." She tapped her fingers. "Fruits: apples, bananas, oranges. That's one. Vegetables: onions, tomatoes, potatoes. Two. Milk things: milk, curd, paneer. Three." "And?" "And now it's three little lists of three, not one big list of nine. The fruit man, the vegetable woman, the dairy." Jeevan put his phone away as a test. Gargi led him from stall to stall and they came out with every item, and one packet of peanuts that was not on any list.

How many things were on the list Jeevan read out?
There were nine things on the list.
How did Gargi feel about the long list before she sorted it?
She felt overwhelmed by nine things "jumping around", and then confident once the groups made sense.
What else could help Gargi if the list had twenty items?
She could still group them but also jot the groups on paper, because even small groups add up when a list is very long.
How does Gargi's plan look to her father?
Jeevan is curious and a little impressed, trusting her enough to put his phone away as a test.

Read this:

"Yogesh, get the shopping, na? My hands are full of dough."
"How much?"
"Rice flour, bananas, carrots, butter, peas, papaya, cheese, lemons, beans, yoghurt. Can you remember that?"
"Wait, Mumma. Say it again slowly."
Tanuja said it again. Yogesh closed his eyes.
"Okay, fruits: bananas, papaya, lemons."
"Lemons are fruits?"
"In my list they are. Vegetables: carrots, peas, beans. Dairy: butter, cheese, yoghurt."
"And rice flour?"
"Rice flour is alone. It's a one-thing group."
Tanuja laughed. "Say it back without looking."
"Three fruits, three vegetables, three dairy, one flour. Ten."
"Off you go then."

Which items did Yogesh put in the dairy group?
Butter, cheese and yoghurt.
What does Yogesh asking to hear the list slowly suggest about how he felt?
He felt a little worried the list was too long, and wanted time to sort it before trusting himself.
What else could Yogesh do at the shop to be sure he has everything?
He could count the items in each group as he pays, so a missing one shows up right away.
How does Yogesh's grouping look to Tanuja?
Tanuja is amused by the "one-thing group" and pleased that he can say it all back, so she trusts him to go.

Read this:

If I say nothing, Kasper will get bored, Omar told himself on the walk to school in Rotterdam. Nobody wants to be boring, not even a bully. On Monday Kasper flicked his ear and called him "Sleepy Omar". Omar kept his eyes on his sums and said nothing. On Tuesday Kasper gave up after two tries and went back to his lunch. Omar felt lighter, almost proud. But by Friday the nickname had reached two other boys, and Kasper was back, louder, waiting at the gate. Omar's stomach tightened. Maybe saying nothing was only the first step, he thought, and not the whole plan.

What nickname did Kasper give Omar?
Kasper called him "Sleepy Omar".
What was Omar feeling on Friday when Kasper was waiting at the gate?
Worried, because his stomach tightened as he realised that saying nothing was not enough on its own.
What other approach could Omar add to ignoring, and why?
He could tell a teacher what has been happening, because the nickname is spreading and an adult can act where silence alone cannot.
How might Kasper have read Omar's silence on Monday and Tuesday?
At first it may have felt dull, which fits Kasper giving up after two tries, but later Kasper may have taken the silence as a sign that Omar would not answer back.

Read this:

Every day at the water cooler, two boys from 7B called Jomon a name about his accent and knocked his bottle aside. Jomon had a plan. "If I don't react, they'll get bored." So he stared at the wall and filled his bottle slowly. On Monday they said it twice and left. On Tuesday, only once. He thought it was working. On Thursday they followed him to the stairs, saying it louder, and one of them yanked his bag strap. His classmate Charu saw it. "Ignoring isn't stopping them," Charu said. Jomon's jaw was tight. "It worked a bit." "A bit isn't enough. Come on." They went to the class teacher before the next period. She listened to both of them, told Jomon it was not his fault, and walked straight to the 7B teacher's room while they waited.

Where did the boys tease Jomon each day?
At the water cooler.
What did Jomon hope would happen, and how did he feel, as he stared at the wall?
He hoped they would get bored if he didn't react; he felt tense but hopeful that staying calm would end it.
What else could Jomon do besides ignoring?
Tell a teacher early, as he finally did with Charu, because adults can stop teasing that ignoring only slows down.
How does Charu see the ignoring plan?
Charu thinks 'a bit' isn't enough and pushes Jomon to tell the teacher straight away.

Read this:

I'm Arnab, and I sit behind Lalit. Since the start of term, a boy in our class has been flicking Lalit's ear in the line and calling him "Specs". Lalit told me his plan was to act as if he couldn't hear. For a week it sort of worked: the boy did it less, maybe got bored. Then on Monday he snatched Lalit's glasses and passed them round the room. Lalit still said nothing. His hands were shaking when he got them back. I don't know what he was feeling, but I knew ignoring had stopped working. At lunch I asked him to come with me to Mrs Pinto. He came. She listened, told him it wasn't his fault, and moved the other boy's seat that afternoon. She also said she would call Lalit's parents that evening.

What did the boy do on Monday?
He snatched Lalit's glasses and passed them round the room.
What might Lalit's shaking hands suggest?
He was frightened and upset, even though he stayed silent.
What else could Lalit have done when the teasing started?
Told a teacher early; ignoring can be a first step, but once it continues an adult needs to step in.
How does Arnab see the ignoring plan?
Arnab saw it work a little at first, but realised after the glasses that it had stopped working.

Read this:

Voice note for Rafiq, from Pema. You asked how I even started on boards, so listen. First I counted backwards starting from the exam in March, week by week, and found I had about twenty-two weeks. Then I wrote every chapter of every subject beside its marks weightage from the syllabus sheet. That was the surprise: Science and Maths hold the biggest share, and I had been giving Social Science the same time as them. So I gave the early mornings, when my head is clear, to Science and Maths, and moved the lighter subjects to the evening. I taped the count of weeks over my desk. It does not make the syllabus smaller, but now it looks like a mountain with steps.

How many weeks did Pema count before the March exam?
Pema counted about twenty-two weeks.
What did Pema feel on discovering the marks weightage?
Surprised, and probably a little worried, because time had been spread evenly while the marks were not.
What could Pema do if early mornings stop working?
Review after a week and move the hard subjects to another clear-headed time, because the plan should follow energy.
How might Rafiq see Pema's plan?
As clear and useful because it turns a big syllabus into steps, though Rafiq may wonder whether early mornings would suit everyone.

Jyoti shares a desk lamp with me in the hostel, so I watched the whole thing on Sunday night. She pinned a calendar to the wall and drew a red circle round 3 March, the first board paper. Then she counted backward, tapping each week with her pen. "Sixteen weeks. Not twenty. Sixteen." Next she opened the marking scheme and wrote every chapter on a sheet with its marks beside it. Nazia from the next room leaned in the doorway and asked why she was wasting time on lists. "Look," Jyoti said, pointing. "Science and Maths have the heaviest chapters, and they're my weakest. English I'm fine in. So those two get my mornings, five to seven, when my head's clear." I don't know if she was calm or scared underneath. Her pen was very steady, though. On Monday her alarm went off at a quarter to five.

What date did Jyoti circle in red?
She circled 3 March, the first board paper.
What does Jyoti's steady pen suggest?
It suggests she felt focused and in control while planning, though the narrator cannot tell whether she was calm or anxious underneath.
What else could Jyoti add to the plan, and why?
A spare week or two before March for revision or sick days, because a plan with no slack breaks at the first delay.
Why might Nazia see the lists as a waste of time?
Nazia may feel that only studying counts as progress, not yet seeing how the lists show where the hours matter most.

Read this:

10 November. Manoj sits on the floor with the exam datesheet and a school calendar. Maths on 11 March, Science on 18 March. He counts the weeks back from the first paper. Seventeen. Then he goes through the syllabus and writes the marks for each chapter beside it. "Chemistry and algebra carry the most, and they're my worst," he mutters. Leela Chechi, home from college, watches him circle them. "Then those get the mornings," he decides. "Five-thirty to seven-thirty, before anyone's awake."
14 January. The mornings are still dark and he still hates the alarm. But the chemistry chapter on acids is done, and he can explain it to Leela Chechi without the book.
11 March. Before leaving for the Maths paper he turns the plan over. On the back, in November handwriting: "Hardest first. Most marks first."

When was the Maths paper?
The Maths paper was on 11 March.
How did Manoj seem to feel about the early alarm by January?
He still hated it and felt tired in the dark mornings, but he was probably quietly proud once he could explain acids without the book.
What would you change first if Manoj fell behind in February?
Redo the count from the new date, still putting the heaviest weak chapters first, instead of dropping the mornings altogether.
What might Leela Chechi think while watching him circle the chapters?
Leela Chechi may be impressed that he planned from the dates and marks, and later glad to see it working when he explains acids without the book.

messages.content:
Read this:

Rehana, you say you spend an hour every evening deciding when to start? Let me tell you about my board year. I am Nikita, and I used to negotiate with myself daily: after a snack, after a call, after the news. The evening would slip away. Then one night I wrote a single sentence on a card: "When it is six o'clock and my chai is finished, I open Physics at my desk." No decision, only a cue. The first evening felt silly. By the third, my hand reached for the book as soon as the cup was empty, and Amma, who brought the chai, found it already open when she came to collect the cup. The debate ended because there was nothing left to debate.

What sentence did Nikita write on the card?
Nikita wrote "When it is six o'clock and my chai is finished, I open Physics at my desk."
What was Nikita feeling about the daily debate over starting?
Frustrated, since the evening kept slipping away while Nikita bargained.
What other cue could Nikita have used?
Right after washing the dinner plates, because any fixed daily event can act as a starter.
How might Amma have seen the change in the evenings?
Probably with relief and curiosity, since the book was already open when Amma came to collect the cup.

Every evening Usha lost an hour to the same argument with herself: start now, or after one more video, or after Ojas stops practising the harmonium in the next room. The Physics paper was five weeks away and the argument was winning. On Sunday she sat on the balcony and thought it through. Deciding every day is the problem. So I decide once. If it's six and my chai cup is empty, Physics comes out on the desk. Harmonium or no harmonium. She wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it on the cup. On Monday at six, Ojas was halfway through a very loud scale. Usha drained her chai, looked at the note and walked to the desk. Earplugs in. Book open, chapter four. No debate.

What was Ojas doing at six on Monday?
He was halfway through a very loud scale on the harmonium.
Why did Usha decide to decide only once?
She was frustrated at losing an hour every evening to the start-now-or-later argument, and wanted a rule that ended it.
What could Usha do if the six o'clock chai sometimes runs late?
Keep the cue but add a backup, such as opening the book at quarter past six even without chai, so the plan doesn't hang on one detail.
How might Ojas see Usha's new routine?
Ojas may barely notice, or feel a little guilty about the noise, but the plan works whether or not the practice goes on.

For two weeks, Ramesh's evenings in the Hyderabad flat went the same way. Home at half past five, chai, phone, then "I'll start at seven." Seven became eight. Eight became dinner. On Friday he caught himself arguing with the clock again and stopped. The deciding is what eats the time, he thought. What if I don't decide? What if the chai decides? He tore a page from his rough book and wrote: When it's 6 and the chai is finished, Physics opens at the desk. He stuck it on the fridge, where Pallavi Akka read it aloud in a newsreader voice. Saturday, 6:02, cup empty. He felt the old five-more-minutes tug, looked at the fridge and went. By 6:05 he was drawing ray diagrams.

What was Ramesh doing by 6:05 on Saturday?
He was drawing ray diagrams.
What did Ramesh feel at 6:02 on Saturday?
He felt the old reluctant tug of wanting five more minutes, but the note on the fridge helped him past it.
Why might a fixed cue work better for Ramesh than "I'll start at seven"?
The cue removes the daily decision: a vague start time invites endless delay, while an empty cup at six is a clear signal to move.
How might Pallavi Akka see the note on the fridge?
Pallavi Akka finds it funny enough to read in a newsreader voice, but may be impressed when it actually gets him to the desk 🙂.

In their small town in Maharashtra, all six of Ojas's friends were taking Science, so Ojas ticked the Science box too, without much thought. On the first day Santosh cracked a joke on the back bench, and it felt like the best decision of his life. But by the first term's Physics test the picture looked different. Ojas stared at a page of forces and lenses that the other boys followed easily. His marks came in low. Friends still gathered at the tea stall after school, and being there felt warm, but Santosh was at ease with Physics and Ojas was not. "Do you actually like it?" Santosh asked once. Ojas did not know what to say.

Why did Ojas choose Science?
Ojas chose Science because all six of his friends were taking it.
What was Ojas feeling when Santosh asked whether he liked Science?
Uncertain and uneasy, since he did not know what to say.
What could Ojas do now?
Talk to a teacher or counsellor about his strengths and get help in Physics, because friendship is a comfort but not evidence of aptitude.
How might Santosh see Ojas's struggles?
With some concern, since Santosh asked whether Ojas actually liked it, which suggests Santosh noticed.

When the subject-choice forms went round at Xin's school in Singapore, his whole lunch table ticked the triple-science box. Yuki didn't even look up. "Obviously science, right? We'll all be in the same class." Xin had spent the holidays drawing comics and helping his aunt at her design studio, but he ticked the box too. The first term was fun: the same jokes, the same table, lab partners who were already friends. Then Physics moved on to kinematics. The others groaned and got it. Xin stared at the equations until they blurred. By the second term he was copying Yuki's homework and staying back for extra classes alone, while his friends went for bubble tea without him. Being together, he realised, hadn't made the Physics any easier.

Which box did Xin's lunch table tick?
The triple-science box.
How did Xin feel by the second term?
He felt lonely and discouraged, struggling with Physics and staying back alone while his friends went out.
What else could Xin have weighed when choosing?
His own interests, like comics and design, and how he found Physics, since his friends' choices said nothing about his fit for the subject.
How might Yuki see Xin copying homework?
Yuki may be happy to help at first but also uneasy, realising the choice that kept them together is costing Xin.

The Physics lab at Harish's school in Bhopal smelled of dust and metal, and on the last day of the first term Ira Ma'am handed back the test papers. Harish got 19 out of 70. Around him, Nikhil, Sameer and Aditya, the friends he had followed into Science because none of them could imagine separate classes, were comparing scores in the fifties. Ira Ma'am asked him to stay back. "You write beautifully in your lab reports," she said, "but the numericals are blank. Why Science, Harish?" He opened his mouth, then shut it. "The others were taking it." "And what did you want?" He looked at the History book in his bag, borrowed from his cousin. He didn't answer. His friends were waiting outside, laughing about something, and for once he didn't want to join them.

What did Harish get in the Physics test?
19 out of 70.
Why didn't Harish want to join his friends outside?
He felt embarrassed and low, realising he had chosen Science to stay with them rather than for himself.
What could Harish do next?
Talk honestly with Ira Ma'am and his parents about his interest in History, and ask what options exist to change course or get support.
How does Ira Ma'am see Harish's struggle?
She sees a capable writer lost in numericals and suspects the choice didn't fit him, so she asks why he chose Science.

Keerthana, your Tanuja Nani once had a brother, Mahesh, and this is about the canal. He was fifteen. After the first rains, four friends said, "Let's swim at the sluice." Mahesh's stomach turned over, because he had seen how the water ran that week. But everyone was nodding and Ravi was already pulling off his shirt, so Mahesh thought, they all want this, and said nothing. Ravi slipped at the edge and the current took him ten feet before a fisherman waded in and dragged him out, coughing. They ran home in silence. Years later at a wedding, Mahesh said, "I never wanted to go." Kishan said, "Neither did I." And Ravi said, "I was only showing off because I thought you all wanted to." Three of them, one belief nobody had checked.

Where did the friends want to swim?
The friends wanted to swim at the sluice.
What did Mahesh believe about the others, and what did he feel?
Mahesh believed everyone wanted to go, though his stomach turned over, so he felt uneasy but stayed silent.
At what moment could Mahesh have changed the outcome, and how?
When his stomach turned over, he could have said 'I'm not sure about this,' because others who felt uneasy might have agreed.
What was Ravi's view of what the group wanted?
Ravi believed the others wanted to swim and was showing off for them, when in fact they felt uneasy too.

On the second night of the school trip to Nainital, someone whispered that the whole dorm was sneaking out to the lake at midnight. Siddharth lay on his bunk, stomach tight. The lake was dark, the road was steep, and the teachers would be furious. But everyone else seemed so keen. So when the torches came on at midnight, he pulled on his shoes and followed without a word. It was cold, a boy slipped on the wet steps and grazed his knee, and a teacher's torch found them by the jetty. All eight were marched back, and their parents were phoned in the morning. On the bus home Anand, who had walked beside him the whole way, said quietly, "I hated every second of that." Two more boys nodded. Siddharth stared at him. "Me too. Why didn't anyone say?"

Where was the dorm sneaking out to?
To the lake, at midnight.
How did Siddharth feel lying on his bunk?
He felt anxious, stomach tight, worried about the dark lake, the steep road and the teachers' anger.
What might have happened if Siddharth had spoken up?
Anand and the others who also hated it might have joined him, and the group could have stayed in, since several already felt the same.
What was the walk like for Anand?
Anand hated every second but stayed silent too, believing the others wanted to go.

Behind the tuition building in Pune, Rishi pulled out a packet of cigarettes he had taken from his cousin. "Everyone's trying one. Right?" Nilesh felt his throat tighten. He didn't want to. But Anand was already nodding, the others were crowding in, and nobody said anything, so Nilesh assumed he was the only one who minded. He took one, coughed until his eyes watered, and went home smelling of smoke. His mother noticed at dinner, and they talked for a long time. The next day, waiting for the bus, Anand said, "Honestly, I only nodded because everyone else looked fine with it." Farid added, "I almost threw up." Nilesh laughed, then stopped. Five of them had stood there, and at least three had wanted to say no.

Where did Rishi get the cigarettes?
From his cousin.
Why did Nilesh go along even though he didn't want to?
He felt uneasy and alone, assuming he was the only one who minded because nobody else spoke.
What could Nilesh do the next time he feels this way?
Say a simple "I'm out" early, since others who feel the same will often join once one person speaks.
How did Anand see the moment behind the building?
Anand only nodded because everyone else looked fine, so Anand felt uneasy too but hid it.

In the school design lab, Lavanya looked at the tasks on the board for the model bridge: paint, wire the lights, test, build the frame. Vijay was ready to paint. "Not yet," said Lavanya. "Paint needs a dry frame, and the test can't happen until the wiring is done. Those two start the chain." She drew arrows: frame, then dry, then paint; circuit, then test. "Frame glue first, today, because it needs a whole day to dry. Circuit tomorrow. Meanwhile, Vijay, you can do the signboard and the poster. Nothing waits on those." Vijay shrugged, then began cutting card, his tongue between his teeth. By Friday the frame was dry and painted, and the little lights blinked on the first try.

Why could Vijay not start painting at once?
Painting needs a dry frame, and the frame glue needed a whole day to dry.
How does Vijay feel when told not to paint yet?
Vijay is a little reluctant and shrugs, but settles into the signboard work with concentration.
What could Lavanya do if the glue takes longer than a day to dry, and why?
Lavanya could move other tasks such as the poster and the wiring ahead while waiting, because independent jobs can run in parallel.
How might Lavanya see Vijay being ready to paint?
Lavanya sees the painting as coming too early, since paint needs a dry frame, so she gives Vijay the signboard and poster, which nothing waits on.

Read this:

Dear Dilnaz,

Our model of a village bridge is finally on track, and I think I cracked why the last one wasn't.

Last time we all started with the fun bits. Someone painted, someone wired the lights, and then we found the painted parts had to be sanded off to glue the frame. Wasted a week.

This time I sat down on Sunday and asked: what has to wait for what? The frame needs two days to dry. Painting can't start till then. The LED lights can't be tested till the circuit works. But the poster and the written report don't need anything.

So on Monday, the very first thing, Faisal and I glued the frame. Rhea started the circuit the same day. Meanwhile Om wrote the report. By Thursday the frame was dry and painting began.

Nothing is waiting anymore. It feels almost too easy.

Love,
Nikita

How long does the frame need to dry?
The frame needs two days to dry.
How does Nikita feel about the project now?
Nikita feels relieved and quietly proud, even a bit surprised that it feels almost too easy.
What else could Nikita plan for, now that the order is clear?
Nikita could add a spare day before the deadline in case the paint or glue takes longer, since the whole chain depends on drying.
How might Om see the new plan?
Om likely feels less stressed, because the report could start on Monday without waiting for anyone else.

People think I was just bossy, Vinita, but no, there was a reason. Let me tell it properly.

I'm Irawati. Our Class 10 group had to build a working model of a water pump for the district exhibition in three weeks. Everyone wanted to start with the painting, because that's the fun part.

I drew the steps on a paper plate in the canteen. The wooden base had to be glued and left to set before anything went on it. The pump couldn't be tested until the motor circuit worked. The chart and the explanation card didn't depend on anything.

So I said: base and circuit start today, first. Chart people, start whenever. Painting waits.

Two of the girls sulked. But on day nine, the base was solid, the circuit ran, and we tested water flow. The group that started with paint was still waiting for glue at the exhibition.

What did Irawati draw the steps on?
Irawati drew the steps on a paper plate in the canteen.
How did two of the girls feel when painting had to wait?
They felt annoyed and sulky, because painting was the fun part and they had to hold off.
What could Irawati say to make the order feel less bossy?
Irawati could show the group the paper plate and explain the chain, so they see why painting waits instead of just being told.
How might the girls who sulked see the plan by the exhibition?
They would likely feel grateful and a bit sheepish, seeing their model tested while another group was still waiting for glue.

At the back of a classroom in Madrid, Dalia watched three girls copy Ines's way of speaking and giggle whenever Ines answered a question. It had been going on for weeks. Dalia opened her mouth once and closed it again. What if they started on her? She had seen what happened to the last person who spoke up. So she looked down at her worksheet. At break Ines ate alone by the wall, and Dalia, two benches away, chewed slowly and said nothing. The mocking got louder on Thursday. On Friday Ines did not come to class. Dalia told herself it was not her fault and that she could not have changed anything, and she hated how well that sounded.

Who did Dalia see being mocked?
Dalia saw Ines being mocked by three girls.
What is Dalia afraid of, and how does it show?
Dalia is afraid of becoming the next target, shown by opening and closing her mouth and looking down at her worksheet.
What could Dalia do next, and why?
Dalia could sit with Ines at break and tell a teacher what she has seen, because company and an adult report are lower-risk ways to help.
How might Ines see Dalia's silence?
Ines likely feels isolated, eating alone by the wall while a classmate who sees everything says nothing.

In the Class 8 room at the start of every lunch break, the same thing happened. Three boys took Samir's water bottle, poured it on his chair, and called him "baby" when he stood up wet.

Naveen sat two rows away. Every day he thought about saying something. And every day he thought: last year it was Dhruv, and whoever stood up for Dhruv got it next. So he kept his eyes on his book.

By October, Samir was eating lunch alone in the library. His seat in class had moved to the corner. He barely spoke.

One afternoon Naveen saw him wiping his chair with his sleeve, not even looking up, and felt sick at himself.

After school he went to the class teacher, Miss Rego, and told her everything, including that he had watched for weeks. She thanked him, spoke to Samir privately that afternoon, and called the counsellor.

What did the boys pour on Samir's chair?
They poured his water bottle on his chair.
Why did Naveen stay silent for weeks?
Naveen was afraid of becoming the next target, remembering that whoever stood up for Dhruv got bullied next.
What else could Naveen have done early on that felt safer?
He could have told Miss Rego privately in the first week, so the boys would not know who reported it and Samir would not be left alone for weeks.
How might Samir have experienced the weeks when nobody spoke up?
Samir likely felt isolated and ashamed, which shows in eating alone, moving to the corner and hardly speaking.

Dear Sonali,

You asked why I've been so quiet lately. It's about Kunal from my tuition batch.

Since August, two boys have been taking his notes, drawing on them and passing them round. Everyone saw. I saw. I told myself it wasn't my business, and honestly, I was scared. Last year one of those boys spread rumours about a guy who complained, and he left the batch.

So I did nothing for two months. Kunal stopped coming for a week. When he came back he sat by the door and left the minute class ended.

Yesterday I finally told Sharma Sir after class, including that I'd stayed quiet. He thanked me, said I wasn't in trouble, and called Kunal's parents that evening. Today the boys were moved to another batch.

I keep thinking I could have done this in August.

Pranav

Since August.

Pranav feels guilty and regretful, thinking it could have been done in August.

Pranav could have spoken to Sharma Sir privately after class in August, since telling a teacher quietly carries less risk than confronting the boys.

Dear Lakshmi Masi, you asked me what an ordinary Tuesday should look like in ten years, so I tried it. I want to wake up in a city of medium size like Nagpur, within a bus ride of Mummy and Papa, and sometimes work from home. Then I worked backwards: which jobs make that likely? Teaching, accounts in a local firm, software services with a nearby office. And which push it far away? Jobs that post you anywhere in the country, or firms in big cities with twelve-hour days. I've made a chart: field, qualification, cities where the work exists. Software and accounts look promising, and I can ask your friend at the software firm what it is really like. I'd been asking what to be. Now I'm asking how to live. — Vikas

What kind of city does Vikas picture living in?
A mid-sized city near family, where work can sometimes be done from home.
What is Vikas feeling as the ordinary Tuesday takes shape on paper?
Hopeful and clearer in mind: the picture of living near family with flexible hours gives the choice a direction.
What else could Vikas do to check the chart, and why?
Talk to someone who already lives that kind of life, because a real person can say whether flexible hours and local jobs actually exist.
How might Lakshmi Masi see the letter?
Lakshmi Masi, who asked the question, sees Vikas thinking about a way of life before job titles, and may be glad and offer to connect Vikas with the friend at the software firm.

You asked why I'm not applying to the big-city colleges, Lalit? Let me explain it the way I figured it out.

I'm Ayesha. Most people start with a job and see what life comes with it. I did it the other way. I sat on our terrace in Nashik and pictured myself at twenty-eight. A home in a city that isn't huge, maybe Pune or Nashik itself. Near Ammi and Abbu, because I'm their only daughter and Abbu's health isn't great. Flexible hours, so I can take a day off without begging.

Then I worked backwards. Which jobs allow that? Pharmacist: possible, but fixed hours. Data analyst: can work remotely, flexible, exists in cities that size. Civil services: I'd be posted anywhere, far away. Crossed out.

So what qualifications does a data analyst need? Maths, statistics, some coding. So: science with maths in Class 11. That's where I am now.

Which career did Ayesha cross out, and why?
Civil services, because Ayesha would be posted anywhere, far away.
How did Ayesha seem to feel about staying near Ammi and Abbu?
She felt caring and a bit worried, wanting to stay close because Abbu's health isn't great.
What else could Ayesha check about the data analyst path?
Ayesha could speak to someone working as a data analyst in a similar city to confirm the flexible hours are real.
How might Ammi and Abbu see Ayesha's plan?
They might feel touched and relieved that Ayesha is planning to stay close, and pleased by how carefully it was thought through.

I'm Asif, Rehana's cousin, and I watched her plan her future in a way that confused me at first.

Everyone else in our family started with a job title. Doctor. Engineer. Rehana started with a picture. One evening she drew it on the back of a notebook: a small house in a city like Mysuru, twenty minutes from her parents, a job that ended by five, weekends free for her painting.

Then she worked backwards from it. She asked me which jobs exist in smaller cities. She made a list: school teacher, bank officer, graphic designer working from home. She crossed out anything that would send her to Mumbai or abroad.

By the end of the month, she'd chosen commerce with computer applications. I don't know how sure she felt. But when our uncle pushed medicine at Eid, she said calmly, "That life doesn't look like mine," and didn't seem upset.

What city did Rehana picture living in?
A city like Mysuru, twenty minutes from her parents.
What might Rehana have been feeling when she answered their uncle at Eid?
She seemed calm and settled, confident enough in her picture of life to turn down the suggestion without getting upset.
What else could Rehana do to test her plan?
She could talk to someone working as a teacher or bank officer in a smaller city, to check that the hours and life match her picture.
How did Rehana's method look to Asif?
It confused Asif at first, since everyone else started with job titles, but Asif came to see it as a clear way to choose.

Ridhi set two sheets on the staffroom table: three years of cutoffs for Computer Science at the state college, and her own mock scores. “Sir, be honest. Is this branch realistic?”
Madhav Sir, the teacher who had coached earlier batches, ran a finger down the columns. “You've scored 118, 124 and 121. Last year's cutoff was around 145.”
“So it's a stretch?”
“A big one. But look here.” He tapped another row. “Information Technology at the same college, around 120. You're close to that.”
“So I could aim for both?”
“List both, keep working on your weak topics, and put the one you're likely to get where you can see it.”
Ridhi wrote two lines on a card. She had come in expecting a no, and left with a plan.

What were Ridhi's three mock scores?

Disappointed but practical: she keeps asking about other options and leaves with a plan.

Keep raising her mock scores while ranking branches by how likely they are, since her real chances can then change as her scores improve.
How does the conversation look to Madhav Sir?
Madhav Sir uses what he saw with earlier batches to give honest ranges, so he may want to protect a student from false hope while still keeping her options open.

In January of Class 12, I was sure I'd get computer science at the top engineering college in our state. I'm Minakshi, and I'd never actually checked.

My friend Farida said, "Show your mocks to Mrs. Rao. She's coached students for fifteen years."

So I printed my last four mock scores and the college's closing ranks for the past three years. Mrs. Rao spread them out on the staffroom table and was quiet for a while.

"Computer science there is a stretch," she said. "Not impossible, but a stretch. Your mocks put you around here." She pointed. "But look: electronics and computer engineering at the same college closed here last year. That's realistic."

I felt disappointed for a minute. Then relieved. I had a real target instead of a wish. I kept computer science as my reach option and put the other branch right below it.

Fifteen years.

Minakshi felt disappointed for a minute, then relieved to have a realistic target.

Minakshi could ask which topics would lift the mock scores most, to keep the reach option alive.

Sudha came to the guidance hour with her father, Samir, and a folder: her six mock scores and the last three years' closing ranks for civil engineering at the university she wanted. She asked me directly, "Is this realistic?"

I also showed her that environmental engineering at the same university usually closed lower, and suited the interest in water systems she had mentioned.

Six mock scores.

The rule: each person solves one problem during the week and presents the solution to the other two. Week three was a dull one, with exams and heat, and I saw Samir skip. The others didn't scold. Friday
Third Friday of the plan and I nearly skipped it. The deal Maria, Sunny and I made: one problem a week from the practice site, everyone solves it alone, and on Friday after school we each show our solution on Maria's tablet in the library, five minutes each.
This week's problem was about reversing words. I left it till Thursday night and got stuck. I was going to text them that I was ill. Then Maria messaged, “Tejas, you alive? Friday! 🙂” Annoying. But it worked.
I showed my half-solution anyway. Sunny had done it a totally different way, with a loop running backwards. Maria's was the shortest. I felt a bit resentful that both of them finished, but seeing three ways to solve one thing taught me more than a whole video.
Next week's problem is already copied into my notebook.

It was about reversing words.
How did Tejas feel on seeing that Maria and Sunny had both finished?
Tejas felt a bit resentful, yet found that seeing three different solutions taught more than a whole video.
What could the three add so a stuck member doesn't think of pretending to be ill?

Gurleen was angry and then confused, until seeing what was different.
What else could Gurleen do to plan a promotion, and why?
Gurleen could ask the manager what senior posts might open in this team and build a plan from that, because the path has to fit where the team is heading.
How might Yogesh have seen his own promotion?
Yogesh probably saw it as the result of his own effort and did not think about how much the growing team helped.

I sat next to Nikita at the insurance firm for three years, so I saw her plan from the outside.
When Farid was promoted to manager in just two years, Nikita wrote his steps on a sticky note: lead a migration, present at the all-hands, get a certification. She pinned it to her screen.
She did all three within eighteen months. I watched her present at the all-hands, hands shaking a bit but clear.
What neither of us thought about was that Farid had been in the digital team, which doubled in size that year and needed new managers. Nikita's claims team hadn't grown at all. There was simply no manager seat.
When the promotion list came out without her name, she took the sticky note down and folded it very small. I don't know exactly what she felt. She didn't talk much that week.
— Vinita

Which three steps did Nikita copy from Farid?
Lead a migration, present at the all-hands, and get a certification.
What might Nikita have been feeling when she folded the sticky note very small?
She was probably disappointed and hurt, since she followed Farid's path exactly and still found no manager seat in her team.
What would you change first in Nikita's approach?
Before copying Farid's steps, she could ask her manager whether her own team would have a senior opening, and plan around that context or a move.
How might Farid see Nikita copying his path?
Farid might feel flattered but uneasy, knowing his promotion came partly from his team's growth, which she could not copy.

Week one. At lunch, Darshan told Nikita how he'd become team lead in two years: run the internal tools project, mentor two juniors, speak at the tech meet. Nikita wrote it on a napkin. If it worked for him, it would work for her.
Month six. Nikita had finished all three. She was proud of the tech-meet talk. But her manager kept saying, "There's no lead opening on our side right now." Darshan's team had doubled that year; hers had lost two people.
Month ten. The promotion list came out. Darshan's teammate got the new lead role. Nikita wasn't on it.
She found the napkin in her drawer and stared at it. Same steps, different team. She felt foolish for not asking the obvious question at the start: was there even a seat?

How much had Darshan's team grown that year?
Darshan's team had doubled that year.
How did Nikita feel when she found the napkin in her drawer?
She felt foolish and disappointed, seeing that the same steps could not work in a team with no lead opening.
What else could Nikita have tried at the start instead of copying Darshan?
She could have asked her manager about openings in her own team and read the promotion criteria, then built a plan that fit her situation.
How does Nikita's experience look from Darshan's side?
Darshan meant to help, but his advice left out the context of his fast-growing team, so he may feel awkward when her plan doesn't work.

On the terrace above his family's hardware shop in a small town, Chetan had one online post open on his phone: a stranger claiming to have joined a company at triple the usual pay. Phone to his ear, he told Nirmala, the recruiter, "I want three times what you offered." A pause. "That's far beyond what this role pays," Nirmala said politely. "I don't think we can go further. Thank you for your time." The line clicked. Chetan sat among the rolls of wire, stunned. Two weeks passed and no other offer came. He wrote back to ask about the original figure. Nirmala replied that the role was still open, but the number on offer now was lower than before.

What was Chetan's demand based on?
Chetan based his demand on one online post.
How did Chetan feel after the call ended?
Chetan was stunned and probably embarrassed, sitting among the rolls of wire.
What could Chetan have done instead of relying on the post, and why?
Chetan could have checked several sources and asked peers about typical pay for the role, because one unusual case is a poor guide to the market.
How might Nirmala have seen Chetan's demand?
Nirmala probably saw it as unrealistic and ended the talk politely, and the goodwill was harder to regain afterwards.

Tuan had read a post on a forum the night before: someone claimed a junior data engineer in Melbourne had been offered almost double the usual pay. He screenshotted it.
The next afternoon, on a video call, Wanjiru, the start-up's recruiter, asked about his expectations.
"I'm looking for this," Tuan said, naming a figure far above what the job ad had suggested.
Wanjiru's eyebrows rose. "That's well above the market for this level. Where does that number come from?"
"I've seen it offered elsewhere."
"I see." She was polite, but her voice cooled. "I don't think we're a match on this. Thank you for your time."
The call ended in under ten minutes.
A week later, after two other rejections, Tuan emailed Wanjiru to ask if the role was still open at the advertised range. He felt his cheeks burn as he pressed send.

Where did Tuan get the idea for his figure?
From a post on a forum claiming a junior data engineer in Melbourne had been offered almost double the usual pay.
How did Tuan feel when pressing send on the email to Wanjiru?
He felt embarrassed and humbled, cheeks burning, because he now had to ask for less after overreaching.
What else could Tuan have done before the call?
He could have checked several sources and talked to peers to find a realistic range, then asked slightly above his target with reasons.
How does Tuan's demand look from Wanjiru's side?
To Wanjiru the number seems unrealistic and based on nothing solid, so she loses confidence and ends the talk politely.

The HR office at the private hospital in Siliguri had a calendar of the Kanchenjunga and a fan that wobbled.
Dolma, the HR manager, smiled at Jomon. "We'd like you as our biomedical technician. This is the offer."
Jomon didn't look at the paper. He'd seen a post in a group chat the night before: someone claiming a technician in a big city hospital got triple the normal pay.
"I'm expecting this," he said, and named a figure far higher.
Dolma's smile faded a little. "That's what we pay senior engineers with ten years' experience. Where have you seen it for this level?"
"Online."
"I'm sorry, Jomon. We can't go anywhere near that. I think we should stop here."
Two weeks later, with no other offer, Jomon came back to the same office. "Is the post still available? At the first figure is fine." Dolma was polite, but she said she'd need to check again.

What did Dolma say the figure Jomon named was normally paid for?
She said it is what they pay senior engineers with ten years' experience.
Why didn't Jomon look at the offer paper, and what does that suggest about his feelings?
He was so set on the number from the group chat that he felt overconfident and sure he deserved more, so he didn't even read what was offered.
What would you change first in Jomon's approach?
Check the offer and compare it with several realistic sources, then ask for a slightly higher figure with reasons, instead of relying on one post.
How is Dolma affected by Jomon's demand?
Dolma loses some goodwill toward him, so even when he returns and accepts the first figure, she is cautious and needs to check again.

Pradeep, you look tense about your guest list, so let me tell you what my husband and I did. I'm Shreya. Ten days before our wedding we had a shouting match over it. He wanted a hundred and fifty, and I had found myself adding relatives until it reached three hundred. I walked out to the balcony, he stayed in the kitchen, and we didn't speak for an hour. Then he came out with two cups of tea. We set a cap of two hundred and a rule: exceptions only if both of us agreed. The next day we sat with each set of parents and said why: "We want to be able to talk with everyone who comes." Both families listened. It hurt less because we had both stopped fighting first.

What cap did the couple set for the guests?
They set a cap of two hundred.
How did Shreya feel on walking out to the balcony?
Shreya was upset and frustrated after the shouting match, and needed a pause before speaking again.
Which choice in the story helped end the fight, and why?
Stopping for an hour and then agreeing a cap with a rule for exceptions helped, because it replaced arguing about numbers with a shared limit.
How might Shreya's husband have felt when he brought out the two cups of tea?
He probably felt regret and a wish to make peace, offering tea as a way to reopen the conversation.

The printer needed the final guest count by nine the next morning, and at eleven at night Ishita and Karthik were shouting in the kitchen of their rented flat in Chennai.
"Your mother added thirty people today!"
"And your father added twenty-five last week!"
Karthik slammed the list on the counter. Then he stopped, breathed, and sat on the floor. "This isn't working."
Ishita sat next to him. After a minute, she said, "Let's stop adding and make a rule. A cap. Two hundred and fifty."
"And exceptions?"
"Only if someone we'd actually miss would be hurt. And we both have to agree."
They went through the list quietly with that rule. Two exceptions made it; the rest didn't.
At midnight they wrote a message to both families: the cap, the reason (the hall size and their savings), and a thank-you. They sent the count to the printer at eight fifty.

What was the guest cap Ishita suggested?
Two hundred and fifty.
What was Karthik feeling when he sat down on the floor?
He was frustrated and exhausted from the fight, and stepping back showed he wanted to stop hurting each other.
What else could the couple have done if the families had objected to the message?
They could have called each family, listened to their concerns, and explained the rule again with the same kind reasons.
How might Karthik's mother see the couple's message?
She may feel disappointed that some of her thirty names were cut, but a clear reason and a thank-you make it easier to accept.

The fight in Darshan and Aditi's Pune flat started over a single name: Aditi's college friend's parents.
"You don't even know them!"
"You invited your entire gym!"
Aditi grabbed her keys and walked out. Darshan sat on the balcony, angry and then just tired.
She came back an hour later with two cups of tea. "Can we start again? Not the list. The rules."
They agreed on a cap of two hundred. Then an exception rule: someone outside the cap comes only if both of them would feel the person's absence at the wedding. Not one, both.
Suddenly the list was easy. The gym friends were out. The college friend's parents, who had once fed Aditi for a month, were in; Darshan agreed after hearing that.
On Sunday they visited both sets of parents together and explained: the cap, the rule, the reasons. Aditi's mother grumbled, then said, "Fine. At least it's fair."

What was the cap Darshan and Aditi agreed on?
A cap of two hundred.
How did Darshan feel on the balcony after Aditi walked out?
Darshan felt angry at first, then just tired and drained by the fight.
What else could the couple do if new requests arrived after the list was sent?
They could apply the same exception rule to each request, and explain it kindly each time rather than reopening the whole list.
How might Aditi's mother see the new rule?
Aditi's mother grumbled at first but found the rule fair, which made it easier to accept even without every name she wanted.

On Monday, Uday told the team on the group thread, "I'm offline after six from now on." He got three thumbs-up. On Tuesday at ten past six, with a client demo two days away, the manager, Shreya, sent a message: "Quick one, can you check slide twelve?" Uday's thumb hovered. He answered within a minute. On Wednesday a teammate sent a "small" question at twenty to seven. On Thursday someone tagged him at half past seven. Nobody was rude. They had simply learned that six meant "unless someone asks". By Friday Uday was back to replying at nine at night, and felt worse than before, because he had said out loud that he would not.

Who sent the first message after six?
The manager, Shreya, sent it.

Uday felt discouraged and guilty, because he had broken the limit he had announced.
What could Uday do differently next time?
Uday could hold the boundary the first time and offer an answer the next morning, and give the manager a phone route for real emergencies.
How did the teammates read Uday's behaviour?
They learned that the boundary bends when asked, so they kept messaging, without meaning any harm.

On Monday Tushar sent a cheerful message to his team group at the Hyderabad office: "From today I'm logging off at six. Family time! Please plan around it." Three hearts appeared.
At 8.15 that night, while he was helping his niece with fractions, his phone buzzed. Lalit, his manager: "Quick one, where's the vendor sheet?"
Tushar hesitated. It was just one question. He answered in thirty seconds.
Lalit replied, "Thanks! Also, can you check row 40?" That took an hour.
By Thursday, three different teammates had messaged him after nine, each starting with "I know you're offline, but..." On Saturday his sister asked why he had missed dinner again. Tushar scrolled back through the week and saw that the first person to break the six o'clock rule had been him.

What time did Lalit's first message arrive?
It arrived at 8.15 that night.
What might Tushar have been feeling when he hesitated before replying?
He was torn between his new limit and not wanting to seem unhelpful to his manager; telling himself it was just one question eased his unease.
What could Tushar have done differently when Lalit messaged?
He could have replied the next morning, or agreed beforehand that real emergencies come as a call, so the first test of the limit held.
How do Tushar's teammates see his six o'clock rule by Thursday?
They have learned it bends: they still say "I know you're offline, but..." and message anyway.

Kiran slumped into the pantry, where Vinita was stirring her coffee.
"Didn't you post 'offline after six' on Monday?" she asked.
"I did," Kiran said, rubbing his eyes. "And then Sanjay called at 7.30 on Monday about the demo."
"And you picked up."
"He's the manager! It was one time."
"Kiran, I messaged you at ten last night about the test plan. You answered in two minutes."
"Because I'd already answered Sanjay."
"Right. So the whole team saw that six o'clock means maybe."
He was quiet. "I guess I just didn't want him thinking I'm not serious."
"Everyone knows you're serious. Now they also know your 'offline' isn't real. Honestly, I'll probably ping you tonight too."
"Please don't."

Sanjay called at 7.30 on Monday about the demo.

Kiran was anxious that the manager would think he wasn't serious, so the fear of looking uncommitted won over the limit.
What could Kiran do now to rebuild the limit?
He could restate the six o'clock rule, ask Sanjay how true emergencies should reach him, and then stop answering non-urgent pings every time.

Vinita reads it as a sign his evenings are open, so she keeps messaging late, while also nudging him to stop answering.

On Monday morning Uday pulled the whole team into the meeting room and put a sheet on the wall screen: monthly users, money in, money out, the line going the wrong way. "This is where we are," Uday said. "And this is what I want to change."
Then came a slide for each role. The mobile work would move to a clinic dashboard. Support and sales would sit together. Parul's testing job would grow to cover the new product, with the same pay and a new review date.
Parul asked three questions about the numbers and then nodded slowly. By Friday two engineers had handed in notice, politely and with thanks. Everyone else stayed and started on Monday's plan.

What did Uday put on the wall screen at the start of the meeting?
Uday put up a sheet of monthly users, money in and money out.

Parul was wary at first and then steadier: asking three questions about the numbers and then nodding slowly shows the doubts were being answered.

Uday could offer a fair handover period and a reference, so the departure is respectful and the team's work continues smoothly.

"Everyone, I'll show you the numbers first, then the decision." Damini clicked to the chart. "Four hundred schools tried the parent app. Eleven pay. But sixty schools use the fee-reminder feature every week, and forty have asked if they can pay for just that."
"So we're switching to fee reminders?" Rehana asked from the back.
"Yes. Here's what that means for each of you. Rehana, design stays, but you'll simplify, not add. Backend team: most of you move onto reminders. Two of the mobile roles will shrink, because the parent app goes into maintenance. I'll talk to those two of you today, one to one."
"Why not give the parent app another quarter?"
"Because we've given it three. I'd rather tell you the truth now than in six months."
Two weeks later, two mobile engineers had taken jobs elsewhere. Rehana stayed. "At least I knew exactly why," she said.

Forty.
Why did Rehana stay?
Rehana felt respected and reassured, because she knew exactly why the change was happening.
What else could Damini do for the two engineers whose roles shrank?
Offer references and help with their job search, and keep them informed so they leave on good terms.
How might the two mobile engineers have experienced the meeting?
They likely felt disappointed and uncertain, but at least heard the news openly before the one-to-one talks.

I put off the all-hands for two weeks because I was scared of the faces. When I finally stood in front of our nine people, Urmila, my co-founder, stood next to me with the laptop.
I didn't soften it. I showed them the churn chart for the consumer app, down every month since October, and then the one bright line: small shops using our stock alerts every single day. I said, "We're pivoting to stock alerts for shops. Here's why." Then I went role by role. Support would stay. Two marketing roles would end, with six weeks' notice and help finding new jobs. Engineering would shrink the app to one feature.
Two engineers left within a month; one told me they'd hoped to build consumer products. The other seven stayed. Later Urmila told me what one of them said in the kitchen: "I don't love it, but I can see the reasoning. That's enough."

Small shops using the stock alerts every single day.

Devika was scared of seeing the team's faces and dreaded delivering hard news.

Devika showed the real numbers, explained the reasons and went role by role, so people could see the reasoning.

That engineer probably felt disappointed that the work they cared about was ending, which is why they left.

"Uncle Ramesh was going to organise everything," Avni said. But Ramesh's phone had been out of network since dusk and nobody had decided on a place to meet. Hours had gone.
I gave the children dry blankets first, then wrote every name on the board and phoned the ward office and the temple hall. By dawn four more relatives had been found. Avni's voice shook. "We should have named a place."

Nandini was writing in the school relief centre at 4 a.m.

12 August, 11 p.m., Mama's house, Kolhapur
I'm writing this on a borrowed mattress because my hands won't stop shaking. The alert came at five. We all said the same thing: Akash Kaka will tell us what to do. He always does. He has the car, he knows the relief office people. So we waited for his call. At six his phone was out of network. We kept calling. Aaji asked where we were meeting. Nobody knew. Papa thought the temple hall, I thought Akash Kaka's building. We lost three hours going between the two in the rain, with Aaji on the back of the scooter. We finally found each other here at nine, soaked. Tomorrow I'm writing a family meeting point on paper for every single one of us, and a second number to call.
Tanuja

How long did the family lose going between the temple hall and Akash Kaka's building?
Three hours, in the rain, with Aaji on the back of the scooter.

Tanuja was frightened and exhausted, still shaken by hours of not knowing where the family was meeting.
What other approach could the family use instead of relying on Akash Kaka?
They could agree a written meeting point and a second contact for everyone, so one phone out of network doesn't stop the plan.
How might Akash Kaka feel when he learns what happened?
He may feel guilty and upset that everyone waited on his phone, even though the network failure wasn't his fault.

Dear Noor,

You asked how the product is going, and I owe you an honest answer. Every time the sales head raised his voice in a review, I changed the plan. When the operations head pushed just as hard the next week, I changed it back. The support and design teams said little, so I assumed they were fine. Last Friday two of the designers told me they've stopped bringing ideas because nothing they say ever sticks. The app has three priorities now and nobody can say what it is for. I kept telling myself I was keeping the peace, but really I was avoiding the discomfort of saying no. I'm going to write the goal on one page and check every request against it.

Anirban

What did the two designers tell Anirban last Friday?
They said they've stopped bringing ideas because nothing they say ever sticks.
What does Anirban seem to feel about the changes of plan, and what shows it?
Anirban sounds regretful: the letter admits that keeping the peace was really avoiding the discomfort of saying no.
What other approach could Anirban use in reviews, and why?
Anirban could ask each team to state its need in turn and test each request against the one-page goal, so decisions follow the goal instead of the loudest voice.
How do the designers experience these reviews?
They feel ignored, since ideas never stick when louder voices decide, so they stopped offering them.

Shalini, you asked why the product I manage feels like a mess. I can tell you exactly. It's me. I'm Uma, and for a year I gave in to whoever shouted loudest. The sales director would storm into my cabin, and I'd move his feature to the top. Then the CEO's office would call, and I'd move theirs. The support team kept sending polite emails about customers who couldn't reset passwords. Polite emails don't storm into cabins. So they waited. Eight months. Last week the support lead resigned. Her exit note said, 'We were never heard.' And when I look at the product now, it's twelve half-finished features for three loud people, and a password reset that still doesn't work. Nobody would call that a direction.

How long did the support team's password issue wait?
Eight months.
How does Uma feel about the support lead's exit note?
Uma feels guilty and ashamed, seeing that the quieter team was never heard.
What approach could Uma use instead to set priorities?
Uma could agree criteria like customer impact with all teams and score requests openly, so the loudest voice doesn't decide.

They felt ignored while customers struggled with password resets, so much that their lead resigned.

I'm Farida, and I've been on Sahil's team for two years. He's kind, and he hates conflict. I noticed it most in planning meetings. When Mr Bhatia from sales raised his voice, his request went on the board in red. When our design lead, who speaks softly, said the checkout was confusing customers, Sahil nodded and wrote it at the bottom. In March the finance head sent an angry email; the next day her report jumped the queue. By June we had shipped three features for sales, two for finance, and nothing the designers or the call centre had asked for. The call centre stopped attending planning. Checkout complaints doubled. Sahil looked exhausted in every meeting. I don't know what he was thinking, but the product no longer seemed to be going anywhere.

What happened when Mr Bhatia raised his voice?
His request went on the board in red.

He was probably anxious to avoid conflict and exhausted, pulled by whoever pushed hardest.

He could agree shared goals and a scoring method before the meeting, so quiet teams' requests are weighed on facts, not volume.
How might the call centre staff see the planning meetings?
They feel their input doesn't matter, which is why they stopped attending while complaints piled up.

On Wednesday the fest committee chalked out the stalls in the school hall. Minakshi, who was running the lemonade and snacks stall, sat on the steps with Vasudha and a notebook. 'Imagine it's Saturday night and the stall flopped,' she said. 'Why?' She wrote as they talked: not enough change ready, so people walk off; rain, and the stall is in the open courtyard; a poor spot behind the science block. Vasudha added, 'And the sugar might run out by noon.' Minakshi hadn't thought of any of that when she had only planned how many people would come. Beside each item she wrote a small fix: coins from the shop counter at home, a tarp from the caretaker, asking the committee to swap the spot, and double the sugar.

Which reasons for a flop did Minakshi write herself?
Minakshi wrote not enough change ready, rain in the open courtyard, and a poor spot behind the science block.
What does the notebook suggest about how Minakshi now feels about the stall?
Minakshi seems more prepared and realistic, having seen that her first plan was too hopeful.

Minakshi could ask a teacher or senior who ran a stall last year what went wrong for them, since they may know problems she has not met.

Vasudha probably felt useful, since adding the sugar risk showed that two people spot more than one.

Dear Kunal,
I know you think I'm being gloomy, but hear me out before Friday's fest.
Last night I tried something. I pretended it was Saturday and our bookmark stall had completely flopped. Then I asked myself: why did it flop? I wrote down whatever came.
1. People paid with big notes and we had no change, so they walked off.
2. It rained, and paper bookmarks got soggy.
3. We got the corner behind the stage where nobody walks.
None of these were in our plan. Our plan was only colours and prices!
So can you bring a bag of ten-rupee notes and coins from your dad's shop? I'll get plastic sleeves and a tarp. And let's ask Mrs Pillai tomorrow if we can swap for a spot near the food stalls.
Not gloomy. Just ready.

What did Keerthana plan to get to protect against rain?
Keerthana planned to get plastic sleeves and a tarp.
How might Keerthana have felt after writing down the three reasons?
Keerthana probably felt uneasy at first and then more confident and ready, since the list showed gaps the colourful plan had missed.
What else could Keerthana and Kunal do to test the stall before Friday?
They could do a short trial run at home, pretending to sell to family, to catch any other problems like slow counting or missing price tags.
How might Kunal see the letter?
Kunal might first think Keerthana is being gloomy, then feel reassured, because each worry now comes with a clear job for each of them.

So, Jagdish, you want to know why our ring-toss stall made the most money at the fest? It's because of one weird evening, the Wednesday before.
Your friend Arnab was sitting on the terrace feeling great about the plan. Rings, bottles, prizes, done. Then I thought, okay, imagine it's over and it was a disaster. Why?
First thing that came: nobody has change. Everyone brings a hundred, tickets are ten. Second: what if it rains, the bottles are on the open ground. Third: they'd put us near the toilets last year.
I actually laughed, because all three were so obvious and none were on my list.
So I got two hundred in coins from the vegetable vendor, borrowed a big umbrella from the canteen, and went to the fest committee on Thursday to ask for a spot by the main gate.
It drizzled at noon. We didn't even notice.

What did Arnab borrow from the canteen?
Arnab borrowed a big umbrella from the canteen.
Why did Arnab laugh while listing the reasons for a disaster?
Arnab felt surprised and a bit embarrassed that all three risks were so obvious yet missing from the list.
What else could Arnab try in next year's planning, and why?
Arnab could ask a friend to do the same imagined-failure exercise separately, since another person may spot risks Arnab overlooks.
How might the fest committee see Arnab's request on Thursday?
They may see a student who has thought ahead, which can make them more willing to give a better spot by the main gate.

In the incubator's meeting room, Disha read the survey scores aloud. "Weak. People said nice list and never came back."

Ritu had built a tool-sharing app for her colony whose first version only listed who owned what. She looked at the results for a long while. "Nobody could ask for a drill. That was the whole point." She opened her laptop and added one button: Borrow tonight. Then she set up two-week cycles: release on Monday, watch what forty residents actually tap for ten days, meet on the second Friday and change something.

In the first cycle, most taps landed on drills and ladders, and almost nobody opened the profile page. Ritu deleted the profile page and moved ladders to the top.

Disha nodded. "That's evidence, not opinion."

What one button did Ritu add?
Ritu added one button: Borrow tonight.
What was Ritu thinking as she looked at the results for a long while?
Ritu was thinking that the app had missed its whole point, since nobody could ask for a tool, and she looked disappointed but determined.
What could Ritu do if taps stay low even after adding the button?
Ritu could talk to a few residents about why they do not borrow, then change the next cycle's version to match.
How might Disha see Ritu's response to the weak scores?
Disha may be impressed that Ritu responds to what people do, as "That's evidence, not opinion" suggests.

messages.content:
Read this:

Dear Ojas,
Thank you for testing the first version of the tuition-finder app last month. Your honest feedback, "I don't see why I'd use this," stung, but you were right.
I went back to why I started. Parents in our colony don't just want a list of tutors. They want to know which tutors other parents trust. That was the whole idea, and I'd left it out to launch faster.
So I added one thing: short reviews from parents whose children have studied with each tutor. Nothing else.
Since then I've been working in two-week cycles. At the end of each, I look at what people actually did, not what they said. In the first cycle, most people read reviews but never messaged a tutor. So I added a "call" button. Messages doubled in the second cycle.
Would you try it again?
Vinita

What one thing did Vinita add after the first feedback?
Short reviews from parents whose children have studied with each tutor.
How did Vinita feel reading Ojas's feedback?
Vinita felt stung, but also saw that Ojas was right.
Why is looking at what people did better than only asking what they think?
Because actions show real use, like reading reviews but not messaging, which led to the call button that doubled messages.
How might Ojas feel being asked to try it again?
Ojas may feel respected and curious, seeing that the honest feedback led to real changes.

messages.content:
Read this:

Ganga, you asked on the show how our library-sharing app survived its first flop. So here's Aadhya's honest version.
Our first release was just a list of books people owned. Nobody used it. The feedback was polite and useless: "Nice idea," "Looks clean."
I sat with my co-founder and asked, why did we start this? Because people in apartment buildings have shelves full of books they've read once, and neighbours who'd love to borrow them. The magic was the borrowing, and the first version didn't even let you ask to borrow.
So we added one button: "Ask to borrow." Then we worked in two-week sprints. At the end of each, we looked only at what people did. First sprint, people asked but never returned books. So we added a gentle return reminder. Second sprint, returns went up.
We stopped guessing, and started watching.

What button did Aadhya's team add?
"Ask to borrow."
How did Aadhya feel about the first feedback?
Aadhya found it polite but useless, and seemed frustrated that it gave no real direction.
What else could Aadhya's team look at in the next sprint?
They could check which buildings borrow the most and learn why, so other buildings can be helped to do the same.
How might the neighbours using the app experience the new version?
They can finally ask to borrow and get gentle reminders to return books, so sharing feels easy and fair.

I'm Pranati, and for two years the certification exam lived in a folder called someday. Last September I made a plan: twelve weeks, one module a week. Then I asked Kamal, a colleague in the finance team, if we could meet every Friday at four for ten minutes. I would show what I had finished, and Kamal would only ask, "Is that what you planned?" No advice, no praise. The first Friday I had not finished the module and my face went hot. The second Friday I had. By week eight I noticed I was starting on Monday mornings just so my page would not look empty on Friday. I passed on the first try. I still keep Fridays with Kamal for other things.

When did Pranati and Kamal meet?
They met every Friday at four for ten minutes.
How did Pranati feel on the first Friday?
Pranati felt embarrassed, with a hot face, since the module was not finished.
What could Pranati do if a Friday module is missed?
Pranati could tell Kamal honestly and add a catch-up slot to the plan rather than hiding it.
How might Kamal see the Friday meetings?
Kamal might feel useful and glad that one simple question was enough to help.

messages.content:
Read this:

Team manager's note, quarterly review: Sangeeta

In March, Sangeeta told me she wanted to finish a cloud certification by June, alongside her normal work. She made a plan with six milestones. What I noticed was the next step. She asked Zeenat, a colleague who had passed the same exam last year, to meet her every Friday at five for fifteen minutes. Each Friday Sangeeta showed what she had done that week: notes, a practice test score, a lab screenshot. Twice she had nothing to show, and Zeenat simply asked, "What got in the way, and what's the plan for next week?" I saw Sangeeta rearrange her evenings after that. She passed the exam on June 18. I've suggested she share this method with the new joiners.

When did Sangeeta pass the exam?
On June 18.
How might Sangeeta have felt on the Fridays she had nothing to show?
She probably felt embarrassed and a bit guilty, which pushed her to rearrange her evenings.
How could the new joiners use this method?
Each could pick a colleague who has done the course, set a short weekly meeting and show real work each time.
How might Zeenat see her part in this?
Zeenat likely felt useful and proud, since fifteen minutes a week helped a colleague pass.

Friday

Fourth Friday with Disha today. I showed her my practice test, 71 out of 100, up from 58 last week. She circled the networking questions and said, "That's your weak spot." It felt good to have someone look at it. I know I would have skipped this week without her. On Wednesday I was so tired I nearly didn't open the book, but then I thought of sitting in front of Disha at five on Friday with nothing to show, and I did one chapter. It's a strange kind of help. She doesn't push, she just asks. And somehow that's enough. Next milestone: networking chapter plus one full mock test before next Friday. Himani, you've got this.

What was the practice test score this week?
71 out of 100, up from 58 last week.
What was Himani feeling on Wednesday, and what changed it?
Himani felt very tired and tempted to skip, but thinking of facing Disha with nothing to show was enough to push through one chapter.
What else could Himani ask Disha for?
A few tips on the networking questions, since Disha spotted them as the weak spot.
How might Disha feel about these Friday meetings?
Disha probably feels glad to help and pleased to see the score rise.

Lalit: You okay? You've yawned three times since first period.
Jagdish: Five am study slot. Day four.
Lalit: Five? You never wake before seven.
Jagdish: The topper does it. The whole class knows. If it works for him, it will work for me.
Lalit: How's the reading going?
Jagdish: I sit up with the book open and my eyes close. I read the same page four times.
Lalit: Did the maths test come back?
Jagdish: Fourteen out of thirty. Last month I got twenty-one.
Lalit: You do your best work at night.
Jagdish: I know. But five am is what toppers do.

How many marks did Jagdish get in the maths test?
Jagdish got fourteen out of thirty.
What does Jagdish want from the five am routine?
Jagdish wants to do as well as the topper and believes that if the routine works for the topper it will work for Jagdish, though Jagdish looks tired and unsure.
What could Jagdish try instead of the five am slot?
Jagdish could keep a night study slot, since Jagdish works best at night, and borrow only the topper's methods that suit him.

Lalit notices the yawns and the lower marks and remembers that Jagdish works best at night, so probably sees the routine as a poor fit.

messages.content:
Read this:

In Class 10, I tried to become Trisha. I'm Lokesh. Trisha topped our school every year, and in an interview for the school magazine she said she woke at five and studied maths before sunrise. So I set my alarm for five. The trouble is, I've always been a night person. My brain wakes up around nine at night. For three weeks I dragged myself up at five, stared at equations with heavy eyes, and fell asleep in the second period. The teacher caught me twice. My maths test score dropped from 68 to 55. Papa found me asleep at the dining table one morning and said, "Beta, that's her routine, not yours." He was right. It fit her. It didn't fit me.

What did Lokesh's maths score drop to?
From 68 to 55.
How did Lokesh feel during the three weeks of five-am alarms?
Lokesh felt exhausted and discouraged, dragging up with heavy eyes and falling asleep in class.
What would suit Lokesh better than copying Trisha?
Studying maths at night, when Lokesh's brain wakes up, and keeping mornings lighter.
How might Trisha see her routine being copied?
Trisha might be surprised, and would probably say it's what works for her, not a rule for everyone.

Class teacher's note: Kiran, Class 9, unit test review

Kiran's marks have dropped in three subjects this month. He has been falling asleep in the first two periods. When I asked him, he told me he started waking at 4:45 to study, because Francis, our class topper, does that. Kiran said, "If it works for him, it should work for me." But he also said he's never been able to sleep before midnight, and that his best studying used to be at night. So he's now getting about five hours of sleep. I spoke to his parents and suggested he go back to his own evening routine. Francis's timetable fits Francis. We will check his energy and marks again in three weeks.

What time did Kiran start waking to study?
Why did Kiran think Francis's routine would work for him?
He felt hopeful that copying the topper would make him a topper, without thinking about his own sleep pattern.
What would you advise Kiran now?
Return to studying in the evening, when he works best, and get enough sleep, as the teacher suggested.
How might Kiran's parents see the problem?
His parents may feel worried about his sleep and relieved to have a clear, simple fix.
