People who want beauty, long life, strength and a good memory should avoid harming others. The sages praise giving up meat, saying it brings as much merit as great sacrifices, and that a person who does not kill is a friend to all creatures.

Monday: At dinner Varun said the new colony parking rule was unfair to the guards. Papa waved his fork. "You'll understand when you're older. Eat." Varun ate.

Thursday: The class teacher kept Varun back for arguing in class. At home he told only his brother Eshaan. "Don't tell Papa. He'll just say I'm a child."

Two weeks later: The teacher phoned Papa. Papa came to Varun's door, phone still in hand. "Why did I hear this from her and not from you?"

Varun shrugged. "You'd have said I'll understand when I'm older."

Papa stood there a long moment. Then he sat on the bed. "Okay. Tell me about the parking rule."

What changes between Varun and his father? Briefly, please.

Varun's father keeps brushing off his opinions, so Varun stops telling him things, even about trouble at school. When the father hears about it from the teacher and learns why Varun stayed silent, he sits down and finally listens.

Write a three-sentence summary of this passage.

The day before Aaji went to hospital, she asked me to thread her needle, and I snapped, 'Can't you see I'm busy?' I was watching cartoons. I'm Madhuri, and I've never felt as bad as I did the next morning, when Papa said Aaji had had a stroke. For two days I couldn't eat properly. My brother Ujjwal found me crying behind the water tank. 'You're not a bad person,' he said. 'You're sad because you love her.' On Sunday we visited. Aaji's mouth was a little crooked, but her eyes knew me. I held her hand and said, 'Sorry I was rude about the needle. I love you, Aaji.' She squeezed back. I still feel a little bad, but it's lighter now.

The day before Aaji went to hospital, Madhuri snapped at Aaji over a needle, then felt terrible when a stroke was reported. Madhuri's brother said the sadness came from love. On Sunday Madhuri apologised at the visit, and Aaji squeezed back.

Summarize this in two or three sentences.

Several months passed in this manner. Her father grew worse; her time was more entirely occupied in attending him; her means of subsistence decreased; and in the tenth month her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and a beggar. This last blow overcame her, and she knelt by Beaufort's coffin weeping bitterly, when my father entered the chamber. He came like a protecting spirit to the poor girl, who committed herself to his care; and after the interment of his friend he conducted her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relation. Two years after this event Caroline became his wife.

Caroline's father grew worse, and after ten months he died, leaving her alone and poor. The narrator's father found her weeping at the coffin and took her to Geneva, where he placed her with a relative. Two years later she became his wife.

What is the main idea of this passage? Answer in a couple of sentences.

The evening altogether passed off pleasantly to the whole family. Mrs. Bennet had seen her eldest daughter much admired by the Netherfield party. Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been distinguished by his sisters. Jane was as much gratified by this as her mother could be, though in a quieter way. Elizabeth felt Jane's pleasure. Mary had heard herself mentioned to Miss Bingley as the most accomplished girl in the neighbourhood; and Catherine and Lydia had been fortunate enough to be never without partners, which was all that they had yet learnt to care for at a ball. They returned, therefore, in good spirits to Longbourn, the village where they lived, and of which they were the principal inhabitants. They found Mr. Bennet still up. With a book, he was regardless of time; and on the present occasion he had a good deal of curiosity as to the event of an evening which had raised such splendid expectations. He had rather hoped that all his wife's views on the stranger would be disappointed; but he soon found that he had a very different story to hear.

The Bennets return from the ball happy, because Jane was much admired and danced twice with Bingley. Mr. Bennet, who stayed up reading, is curious and soon finds out that the evening went much better than he had hoped.

Retell this extract briefly in two sentences.

"Oh, the evil is that I am not jealous, is it?" cried Catherine. "Well, I won't repeat my offer of a wife: it is as bad as offering Satan a lost soul. Your bliss lies, like his, in inflicting misery. You prove it. Edgar is restored from the ill-temper he gave way to at your coming; I begin to be secure and tranquil; and you, restless to know us at peace, appear resolved on exciting a quarrel. Quarrel with Edgar, if you please, Heathcliff, and deceive his sister: you'll hit on exactly the most efficient method of revenging yourself on me."
Catherine says she is not jealous and accuses Heathcliff of enjoying others' misery. She says that quarrelling with Edgar and deceiving Isabella, just as her home is calm, would hurt her most.

"Oh, my dear Mr. Bennet," as she entered the room, "we have had a most delightful evening, a most excellent ball. I wish you had been there. Jane was so admired, nothing could be like it. Everybody said how well she looked; and Mr. Bingley thought her quite beautiful, and danced with her twice. Only think of that, my dear: he actually danced with her twice; and she was the only creature in the room that he asked a second time. First of all, he asked Miss Lucas. I was so vexed to see him stand up with her; but, however, he did not admire her at all; indeed, nobody can, you know; and he seemed quite struck with Jane as she was going down the dance. So he inquired who she was, and got introduced, and asked her for the two next. Then, the two third he danced with Miss King, and the two fourth with Maria Lucas, and the two fifth with Jane again, and the two sixth with Lizzy, and the Boulanger----"

Describe this for a small child in three sentences.

A woman is full of joy after a ball and tells Mr. Bennet it was wonderful. She says Jane looked lovely and Mr. Bingley danced with her twice, which he did with no other girl. Then she goes on to list the others he danced with.

Cut this extract down to two sentences.

The two gentlemen left Rosings the next morning; and Mr. Collins having been in waiting near the lodges, to make them his parting obeisance, was able to bring home the pleasing intelligence of their appearing in very good health, and in as tolerable spirits as could be expected, after the melancholy scene so lately gone through at Rosings. To Rosings he then hastened to console Lady Catherine and her daughter; and on his return brought back, with great satisfaction, a message from her Ladyship, importing that she felt herself so dull as to make her very desirous of having them all to dine with her.

The two gentlemen leave Rosings, and Mr. Collins, who waited to bid them goodbye, reports that they are in good health. He hurries to console Lady Catherine and her daughter and returns with her invitation for them all to dine, as she feels dull.

"'"The Brahmana continued, 'Unto them assembled together, the Lord of creatures, Brahma, said, "No one of you is superior to others. Ye are all endued with particular attributes. All are foremost in their own spheres, and all possess special attributes." Thus said unto them, that were assembled together, the Lord of all creatures. There is one that is unmoving, and one that is moving. In consequence of special attributes, there are five life-winds. My own self is one. That one accumulates into many forms. Becoming friendly unto one another, and gratifying one another, depart in peace. Blessings to ye, do ye uphold one another!'"'"

What's the short version of this excerpt? Two sentences.

Brahma tells the assembled beings that none of them is superior, as all have special attributes and are foremost in their own spheres. He ends by telling them to be friendly, please one another, leave in peace and support each other.

Vaishampayana said, "After he had lost his century of sons, king Dhritarashtra, afflicted with grief on that account, cheerless, and looking like a tree shorn of its branches, became overwhelmed with anxiety and lost his power of speech. Possessed of great wisdom, Sanjaya, approaching the monarch, addressed him, saying, 'Why dost thou grieve, O monarch? Grief does not serve any purpose. Eight and ten Akshauhinis of combatants, O king, have been slain! The earth hath become desolate, and is almost empty now! Kings of diverse realms, hailing from diverse quarters, united with thy son (for aiding him in battle) have all laid down their lives. Let now the obsequial rites of thy sires and sons and grandsons and kinsmen and friends and preceptors be performed in due order.'"

Wrap up this extract in two sentences.

After losing his hundred sons, King Dhritarashtra is grief-stricken and cannot speak, looking like a tree stripped of its branches. Sanjaya tells him grief is useless, since eighteen armies are dead, and urges him to perform the funeral rites.

Retell this section briefly in two sentences.

My father had often, during my imprisonment, heard me make the same assertion; when I thus accused myself, he sometimes seemed to desire an explanation, and at others he appeared to consider it as the offspring of delirium, and that, during my illness, some idea of this kind had presented itself to my imagination, the remembrance of which I preserved in my convalescence. I avoided explanation and maintained a continual silence concerning the wretch I had created. I had a persuasion that I should be supposed mad, and this in itself would for ever have chained my tongue. But, besides, I could not bring myself to disclose a secret which would fill my hearer with consternation and make fear and unnatural horror the inmates of his breast. I checked, therefore, my impatient thirst for sympathy and was silent when I would have given the world to have confided the fatal secret. Yet, still, words like those I have recorded would burst uncontrollably from me. I could offer no explanation of them, but their truth in part relieved the burden of my mysterious woe.

During the narrator's imprisonment their father heard them accuse themselves, and sometimes asked for an explanation and sometimes thought it came from delirium. The narrator stayed silent about the creature, fearing to be thought mad and unwilling to fill anyone with horror.

Make a three-sentence summary out of this.

One morning, about a week after Bingley's engagement with Jane had been formed, as he and the females of the family were sitting together in the dining-room, their attention was suddenly drawn to the window by the sound of a carriage; and they perceived a chaise and four driving up the lawn. It was too early in the morning for visitors; and besides, the equipage did not answer to that of any of their neighbours. The horses were post; and neither the carriage, nor the livery of the servant who preceded it, were familiar to them. As it was certain, however, that somebody was coming, Bingley instantly prevailed on Miss Bennet to avoid the confinement of such an intrusion, and walk away with him into the shrubbery. They both set off; and the conjectures of the remaining three continued, though with little satisfaction, till the door was thrown open, and their visitor entered. It was Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

A week after Bingley and Jane become engaged, an unfamiliar carriage with four horses drives up the lawn, too early for visitors. Bingley persuades Miss Bennet to walk with him into the shrubbery, while the other three guess who it is. The visitor is Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

He was away three weeks. The first day or two my charge sat in a corner of the library, too sad for either reading or playing: in that quiet state she caused me little trouble; but it was succeeded by an interval of impatient, fretful weariness; and being too busy, and too old then, to run up and down amusing her, I hit on a method by which she might entertain herself. I used to send her on her travels round the grounds—now on foot, and now on a pony; indulging her with a patient audience of all her real and imaginary adventures when she returned.

Could you recap this paragraph for me? Two sentences is enough.

A man is away for three weeks, and the narrator's charge first sits sadly in the library, then becomes restless and fretful. Too busy to play with her, the narrator sends her to explore the grounds and listens patiently to her adventures, real or imagined.

Boil this letter down to one sentence.

Dear Naveen, You asked why I'm not joining the design college with you this August. I owe you the true answer. In January I had two options: design in Ahmedabad or the engineering seat here in Nagpur. I told everyone, including you, "I'll sleep on it." And I did. For weeks. But sleeping on it meant nothing new. I didn't visit either college. I didn't call any seniors. I didn't ask my parents about fees. I just kept waiting for the answer to appear one morning. The design application closed on 28 February. I noticed on 3 March. So the choice got made anyway, by the calendar. I'm in engineering by default, not by decision. Next time I say I'll sleep on something, ask me what date I'm deciding by. Farhan
Farhan tells Naveen that putting off the choice between design and engineering meant missing the design deadline, so engineering happened by default.

Describe this short passage in just three sentences.

In the Hitec City office, Yogesh pinned a single page above the team's shared desk. The Tuesday before, Ritu had run a bulk refund script meant for the test system on the live one, and 212 customers got refunds they hadn't asked for. It took the whole week to recover. Yogesh didn't give a speech about carefulness. He changed things. The refund tool now asked for a second person's approval before any bulk action. Test and live logins were split: different passwords, and the live screen turned red. And the page above the desk was a checklist: 'Which system? Which login? How many rows? Who reviewed? Backup taken?' Ritu read it twice. 'Would this have stopped me?' 'At step one,' Yogesh said. 'The screen would have been red.'

Ritu ran a bulk refund script meant for the test system on the live one, and 212 customers got refunds they had not asked for. Yogesh then made bulk refunds need a second person's approval and gave the live system a separate login and a red screen. He also pinned a checklist, and says the red screen would have stopped Ritu at step one.

Distil this bit of text into two sentences.

His words had a strange effect upon me. I compassionated him and sometimes felt a wish to console him, but when I looked upon him, when I saw the filthy mass that moved and talked, my heart sickened and my feelings were altered to those of horror and hatred. I tried to stifle these sensations; I thought that as I could not sympathise with him, I had no right to withhold from him the small portion of happiness which was yet in my power to bestow.

The narrator pities him and sometimes wants to comfort him, but the sight of him turns this feeling into horror and hatred. The narrator tries to fight these feelings, thinking that there is no right to refuse him the small happiness within reach.

Sum this diary entry up in one sentence.

Saturday. Found Papa's old torch in the drawer that doesn't work. I asked Keerthana didi if I could open it. She said yes, but first took the battery out and gave me the small screwdriver from her box. Inside there was a spring, a tiny round bulb and a metal strip! I pressed the strip and the spring pushed back. My heart went boom. I took out everything and put it on the table in a line. Then I could not put it back. The spring jumped away twice. Keerthana didi found it under the cupboard. We put it together, and on the third try the light came on. I clapped. Arohi
With Keerthana didi's help, Arohi opens an old broken torch, struggles to fit the parts back together, and finally gets it working on the third try.
My coach said the match was "called off". Will it happen later?

Probably not. "Call off" means to cancel something that was planned. If the match will happen later, people usually say it was "postponed".
Example: The match was called off because the ground was flooded.
Find out: does it mean the same as discover?

Mostly, yes. "Find out" means to learn a fact or a piece of information, often by asking or checking. It is more common than "discover" in everyday speech.
Example: Shreya called the office to find out when the results would be announced.
Can "get over" be used for feelings?

Yes. "Get over" means to feel better after something unpleasant, like an illness, a shock or a sad event.
Example: It took Noor a few weeks to get over the loss of her pet cat.
How do you spell the word for a person you work with: colleage or colleague?

The correct spelling is "colleague", ending in -gue, like "league". Both words have the same "eague" pattern.
Example: My colleague Wei helped me fix the spreadsheet.
Buisness or business? I can never remember.

The correct spelling is "business". Think of it as "busy" plus "ness": the y changes to i, giving bus-i-ness.
Example: Harpreet's uncle runs a small business selling handmade candles.
Formally or formerly: which should I pick for "my ___ school"?

Neither fits exactly. "Former" is the adjective that means earlier, so say "my former school". "Formerly" is an adverb meaning in the past, and "formally" means in a formal or official way.
Examples: She was formerly a teacher. The prize was formally announced today.
His name "rings a bell", but I can't remember where from. What does that mean?

If a name or fact rings a bell, it sounds familiar and reminds you of something you have heard before.
Example: Her name rings a bell, but I cannot remember where we met.
Our manager said a new project is "in the pipeline". Where is the pipeline?

There is no real pipeline. If something is in the pipeline, it is being planned or prepared and will happen soon.
Example: A new library is in the pipeline for our town.
My brother says filling in the form twice is "a pain in the neck". Does his neck hurt?

No. A pain in the neck is an informal way to say that something, or someone, is very annoying.
Example: Standing in two queues for one ticket is a pain in the neck.
Is it "pasttime" or "pastime"?

The correct spelling is "pastime", with only one t in the middle: pas-time.
Example: Reading is her favourite pastime.
When I wanted to ask about the old quarrel, my mother said "let sleeping dogs lie". Why?

It means do not stir up an old problem that is quiet now, because you may cause more trouble.
Example: The two neighbours have not argued for years, so let sleeping dogs lie.
Our teacher said that Nina and Pooja are "birds of a feather". Are they both birdwatchers?

Not necessarily. The full saying is "birds of a feather flock together", and it means that people with similar interests or characters tend to become friends.
Example: Both of them love chess and old films, so they are birds of a feather.
When do I write "anyone" and when "any one"?

Write "anyone" when you mean any person. Write "any one" as two words when you mean a single one from a group.
Examples: Is anyone at home? You may choose any one of these books.
I got a call from an unknown person who asked for someone else. How can I say politely that they have the wrong number?

You can say, "I think you have the wrong number." Or say, "I'm sorry, there is no one here by that name." Both are polite.
Example: I'm sorry, I think you have the wrong number.
Parents can "opt out" of the school trip. What does that mean?

"Opt out" means to choose not to take part in something.
Example: You can opt out of the email list at any time.
Is it a "rucksack" or a "backpack"?

Both words describe a bag carried on the back. "Rucksack" is common in British English, while "backpack" is American and also widely used in India.
Examples: She packed her rucksack for the trek. She packed her backpack for the trek.
The librarian helped me "track down" an old book. Did she follow footprints?

No. "Track down" means to find something or someone after a careful search.
Example: After a long search, we tracked down the owner of the lost bag.
When should I use brackets like ( ) in a sentence?

Round brackets, also called parentheses, hold extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
Example: My cousin (who lives in Pune) is visiting us this week.
The notice says "sorry for the inconvenience". Who is saying sorry for what?

The people who wrote the notice are apologising because something, such as a delay or a change, causes trouble for readers.
Example: Sorry for the inconvenience; the library will be closed on Monday.
Do I put the title of a short poem in quotation marks?

Yes. Titles of short works such as poems, short stories and articles usually go in quotation marks. Titles of whole books are usually written in italics or underlined instead.
Example: We learned the poem "The Road Not Taken" in class.
Indefatigable is such a long word. What does it mean?

Indefatigable means never getting tired, or never giving up. It is an adjective. You can break it up: in-de-fat-i-ga-ble.
Example: The indefatigable volunteers served food to the guests for twelve hours.
What does remonstrance mean?

A remonstrance is a strong protest or complaint. It is a formal noun, mostly found in older writing. The verb is remonstrate.
Example: In spite of her remonstrance, the council cut down the old banyan tree.
In my notebook I wrote conference but forgot what it means. Help?

A conference is a large meeting where many people gather to discuss a subject. It is a noun.
Example: Teachers from many schools came to the conference on reading.
Found athwart in an old sea story. What did the writer mean?

Athwart means across, from one side to the other. It is an adverb or preposition, and it is old-fashioned.
Example: A fallen tree lay athwart the road, so the bus could not pass.
Is evermore a real word? I saw it in a poem.

Yes. Evermore means always, from now on and for all time. It is an adverb, used in poetry and old writing.
Example: In the song, the sailor promises to love his village evermore.
Why did the speaker talk with such vehemence?

Vehemence is strong, forceful feeling that is shown when speaking or acting. It is a noun.
Example: The girl argued with vehemence that the playground should be repaired.
Hair tangles are a daily problem for my sister. Is that the same word as in 'tangles in the wool'?

Yes. Tangles are twisted knots of hair, thread or rope that are hard to separate. It is a noun, the plural of tangle.
Example: Mum combed the tangles out of her daughter's long hair.
My teacher said that stories pass down through generations. What does the word generations mean?

Generations are groups of people born and living around the same time, or the time between one such group and the next. It is a noun, the plural of generation.
Example: Three generations of her family lived in the same house.
Can downhill be used for a bike ride and a bad situation?

Yes. Downhill means going down a slope. It is an adverb or an adjective. If things go downhill, they get worse.
Example: The cyclist rode downhill with the wind behind him.
When we reach the top, you will get a panorama. What will I see?

A panorama is a wide view of a large area that you can see all at once. It is a noun.
Example: From the hilltop, we saw a panorama of fields and the river below.
Is lethargic the same as lazy?

Not really. Lethargic means tired and slow, with no energy, often because of heat, illness or boredom. Lazy means not wanting to work. Lethargic is an adjective.
Example: The heat made the whole class feel lethargic after lunch.
The sign says do not obstruct the gate. What does obstruct mean here?

To obstruct is to block a path, view or process so that something cannot get through or move. It is a verb. A sign like that asks you not to leave anything in the way.
Example: A parked lorry obstructed the narrow lane.
Can a plant be thirsty or only a person?

People say a plant is thirsty as a way of saying it needs water. Thirsty means wanting or needing a drink. It is an adjective.
Example: The thirsty plant drooped until we watered it.
What does excursions mean in 'school excursions'?

An excursion is a short trip taken for pleasure or learning, usually by a group. It is a noun, and the plural is Excursions.
Example: Our school excursions this year include a visit to a fort and a visit to a planetarium.
What are hammers? My uncle has three of different sizes.

A hammer is a tool with a heavy metal head on a handle, used for hitting nails or breaking things. Hammers is the plural. It is a noun, and it can also be a verb that means to hit hard.
Example: Uncle's toolbox holds three hammers of different sizes.
The cricket club wants to contest the umpire's decision. Doesn't contest mean a competition?

As a noun, yes. As a verb, to contest means to argue against something and say it is wrong or unfair. It is a verb here.
Example: The team decided to contest the result because the scorer had made a mistake.
The chief guest will deliver a speech on Annual Day. Is she bringing it in a van?

Ha, no. Deliver also means to give a speech or talk in front of people. It is a verb. The other main meaning is to take goods to someone's home.
Example: He delivered a short talk about kindness to the whole school.
Everyone says the green kurta flatters me. Does flatter mean to say nice things that are not true?

That is one meaning. Here, to flatter means to make someone look better than usual, as with clothes or light. It is a verb.
Example: The soft evening light flatters the old stone building.
The report described the village as having relative calm after the floods. I only know relative as an uncle or cousin.

As an adjective, relative means judged by comparison with something else, not on its own. The noun is a member of your family.
Example: After the heavy rains, the weekend felt like a time of relative quiet.
What is apprehension?

Apprehension is a noun meaning worry or fear that something bad may happen. Older books sometimes also use it to mean understanding.
Example: Ravi felt some apprehension before his first flight alone.
Describe a foggy winter evening in Delhi, in about 70 words.

By six in the evening, a thick fog has swallowed the city. Streetlights glow like blurry yellow moons, and cars crawl along with their hazard lights blinking. People hurry home with mufflers wrapped over their noses. At the corner, a group of rickshaw pullers warms their hands over a small fire. The smell of roasted peanuts and wood smoke hangs in the cold air. Sounds seem softer, as if the whole city is whispering.
Write a simple poem, 4 lines, about a sleepy cat in the sun.

The cat lies down in a golden beam,
And blinks her eyes as if in a dream.
She stretches long and gives a yawn,
Then purrs herself to sleep till dawn.
In around 75 words, describe a mountain lake covered in morning fog.

The lake lies silent under a thick white blanket of fog. You cannot see the other shore, only the dark outlines of pine trees that seem to float in the air. The water is still, like glass. A single duck glides through the mist and leaves a thin ripple behind. Cold air touches your cheeks, and everything sounds soft and far away. Slowly, the sun rises, and the fog lifts like a curtain.
Write a story, around 85 words, for primary school children about two friends who quarrel over a toy and then solve the problem.

Sameer and Raju both loved the red toy truck. One day, they pulled it so hard that a wheel came off. "You broke it!" cried Sameer. "No, you did!" said Raju. They sat far apart and did not talk. Soon, they felt sad and lonely. Then Raju picked up the wheel and said, "Shall we fix it together?" They found some glue and worked side by side. The truck rolled again, and both boys smiled. After that, they took turns playing with it.
Please write a story, about 100 words, about two neighbours who built a wall between their houses and then made a little door in it.

Two neighbours quarrelled over a mango tree, and one of them built a high wall between their houses. For months they did not speak. One day a ball from one garden flew over the wall and landed in the other. The boy next door knocked on the wall, calling for his ball. Nobody answered. His father felt sorry and took a small hammer. By evening there was a little wooden door in the wall. The other neighbour came through it with the ball and a mango. They both laughed, and shared the fruit.
School library notice, please: it will be closed on Thursday for stocktaking and will reopen on Friday. About 35 words. Sign it Librarian.

NOTICE
The school library will be closed on Thursday for stocktaking. It will reopen on Friday. Please plan your visits accordingly. We apologise for the inconvenience. Thank you for your understanding.
Librarian
Invite my uncle to my piano recital on Sunday at 5 pm. Keep it warm and short, about 45 words. I'm Meghna.

Dear Uncle,
I am playing in my piano recital this Sunday at 5 pm, and I would love for you to be there. It would mean a lot to me to see you in the audience. I'm a little nervous, but excited too. Please do come!
With love,
Meghna
Prepare a story, about 80 words, about a village that has no clock. A boy makes a sundial, and the story ends with everyone meeting at the same time.

In a small village, nobody owned a clock. People met whenever they pleased, and meetings were always late. One day, a boy named Gopal noticed that the shadow of a tall pole moved slowly across the ground. He pushed a stick into the ground and marked the line where the shadow fell at noon. Soon, he added more marks. He had made a sundial. The villagers were amazed. Next morning, everyone gathered by the sundial together at the same time.
Write a short rhyming verse, around 45 words, about being brave on the first day at a new place.

My heart goes thump, my steps are slow,
I do not know the way to go.
But I will smile and take a chance,
And soon my fear will learn to dance.
A friendly face will say hello,
And then I'll feel the courage grow.
Write one paragraph, 55 words, about why trees are like quiet friends.

Trees are like quiet friends. They give us shade when the sun is harsh and fruit when we are hungry. They hold the soil in place and give homes to birds. They never ask for anything, and they stand with us year after year. All we have to do is look after them in return.
Hopeful, with a little humour: a farmer waiting for rain.

Farmer Gopal looked at the sky every morning, and every morning the sky looked back at him, blue and empty. He had sown his rice, and the seedlings were turning brown.

His wife, Revati, told him to stop staring. "Staring does not make it rain."

"Neither does washing the cow," said Gopal, but he wiped his face and went to look at the field. He wore his oldest hat, for luck.

The next afternoon, a single cloud appeared, then four. The cow lowed. A gust of wind snatched his hat and carried it into the paddy.

The rain came while he was still chasing it. He caught the hat at last. His wife ran out with a pot on her head, and the two of them stood laughing in the downpour while the field drank.
How does a boy get the whole class quiet by whistling a tune? Tell it as a story.

The Class 7 room was as noisy as a market. The substitute teacher, Mr. Kishore, tried shouting, but it only made things worse. At the back of the room, a boy named Prasad cleared his throat and began to whistle a slow, gentle tune, the kind his grandfather played on the fields. One by one, the chatter faded. A few heads turned. By the time he reached the second line, every face was calm, and the whole room had gone quiet. Mr. Kishore, astonished, waited until the tune ended. "Thank you," he said. "Please do that again every time I need you." Prasad grinned. He whistled for the rest of the year.
Fashion a story about a boy who was mean to his friend and finds a kind way to say sorry.

Bipin laughed when his friend Ashok tripped over his own bag and everyone looked. Ashok did not laugh. He picked up his things and walked off without a word. Bipin felt a stone settle in his chest. The next day, Ashok avoided him in class. Bipin thought hard about what to do. At lunch, he walked up to Ashok's desk and quietly put down a small paper boat. Inside it, he had written, "I should not have laughed. Can you forgive me?" Ashok read the note, folded the boat into a pocket and said, "Next time, help me pick up the books." Bipin nodded and promised.
About 120 words, please: a boy loses his school shoe in the mud.

During the rainy season, Anwar's left shoe came off in the mud outside the school gate, and no amount of pulling brought it back. He hopped around on one foot, soaking his sock. A group of Class 6 girls came by and laughed, and he turned red. A girl named Jaya, however, found a long stick and began poking the mud near his foot. Another girl found a second stick, and together they dug until the sole appeared. Anwar pulled out the shoe, covered in brown sludge, and shook it triumphantly. They washed it under the tap. He walked into class with one very clean shoe, one muddy sock and a loud, happy squelch with each step.
Make up two friends who meet outside the exam hall and exchange good luck charms.

Outside the Class 10 exam hall, Rasheed and Ketaki stood in the queue, both pale. Rasheed was holding a small green pencil he used for luck. Ketaki had a tiny brass elephant in her pocket. They spotted each other and burst into nervous laughter. "Swap?" said Rasheed. She nodded, and they traded. He took the elephant with a bow, and she tucked the pencil behind her ear. Inside, the paper was hard, and both of them felt the funny weight of the other's charm in their hands. Afterwards, they met on the steps and compared notes. "Elephants do not forget," Rasheed said, holding up the answer sheet. They exchanged the charms back and agreed to repeat it next time.
Narrate a story about a girl who lights a lamp for her grandmother on the first Diwali after she is gone.

The first Diwali without Ajji felt wrong. Tanya's house was quiet, and her mother had not made any sweets. Tanya found Ajji's old brass lamp in the cupboard. She polished it for an hour until it shone. Then she filled it with oil and set it by the door. When she lit the wick, a gentle flame rose. Her mother came and stood beside her. They said nothing for a while. Then her mother began to cry, and Tanya hugged her. After a while, they walked to the kitchen and made a small batch of Ajji's favourite sweet, kneading the dough together.
Pen a tale about a sugar cane juice seller and a hot afternoon.

Ganesh pressed sugar cane through his old iron machine and filled glasses with green juice and a squeeze of lime. It was a very hot afternoon, and the line was long. A delivery boy on a bike pulled up, sweating. He had no money left, only a few coins. Ganesh looked at his flushed face. "Take a glass," he said. The boy drank it in one go. "I'll pay tomorrow," he said. The next day, he came back and not only paid but also brought two friends. By evening, Ganesh had sold three hundred glasses and could not feel his arm.
Could you invent a tale about a clock tower that gave away spare minutes?

The clock tower in Dharampur had a secret. Every evening at six, it let a few spare minutes drip from its hands like honey.

Most people never noticed. But a boy named Yash, who was always late, caught one in his palm. It was warm and tiny, shaped like a seed.

"What's this?" he asked.

"A spare minute," said the tower, with a deep gong. "Use it well."

The next morning, Yash was running behind again. He remembered the seed and let it open. Time seemed to stretch. He tied his shoes, packed his bag, and had a moment left over to wave to the dog.

He reached school early. Then he came to the tower every evening and held out both hands.
Two raindrops race down a window. Write the story.

Drip and Drop were two raindrops sliding down the window of a school bus. They had agreed to race to the bottom.

"Ready, steady, go!" said Drip.

They slid. Drip went straight. Drop wobbled left, then right. A tiny speck of dust caught him.

"Wait!" Drop called. "I'm stuck!"

Drip paused. Winning would be easy now, but it felt lonely. So he slid back up a bit and joined Drop, and together they grew heavy and round, and rolled past the dust.

At the bottom of the window, they reached the edge at the very same moment and dripped off together onto the road.

A girl on the bus, named Zara, had been watching. She smiled, because it was a tie.
Help me write a diary entry of about 100 words about my grandmother visiting us after a long time.

Dear Diary,
Nani came to stay with us today after almost two years. The moment she walked in, the whole house smelled of the laddoos she had brought from her village. She looked a little smaller than I remembered, but her laugh was just as loud. After dinner, we sat on the terrace, and she told me stories about Ma as a naughty little girl. I laughed so much my stomach hurt. She is staying for three weeks, and I already know it will feel too short. Tomorrow she has promised to teach me her pickle recipe.
